Page 1: Oṃ tat sat. Salutations to Śiva, whose form is self-luminous bliss.
Now begins the *Śrīparātriṃśikā* text, accompanied by the commentary titled *Tattvaviveka* composed by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
The Mother is the great new creation, the refuge of the stainless digits (*kalā*), whose body is full; and the Father is he whose splendor is hidden within the five faces and whose form is replete.

May my heart, consisting of the emission (*visarga*) of the state that flashes forth from the union of those two, which is the family of the nectar of the Absolute (*anuttara*), manifest intensely. [In the *Abhinavasṛṣṭi*: She is the Mother, whose nature is the pure path, in whom resides the light characterized by fullness, who rests upon the stainless digit, and whose essence is supreme awareness.]

"Śakti likewise has five faces"—meaning that Śiva, the progenitor whose nature is full, possesses a desire fulfilled by the five powers; because he is devoid of anything further to be desired, his body is complete. "That both"—referring to the vibration of being arising from the friction of their essential identity (*sāmarasya*), which is the emission (*visarga*) whose nature is the impulse to overflow outwardly, possessing a manifest existence.
"May that such primordial nature, the family of unsurpassed nectar whose form is absolute freedom, which is my heart,
manifest radiantly"—
for here, everywhere, the word "I" has as its sole domain pure consciousness alone.

Thus, by this Mīmāṃsā statement, may that ultimate reality—which is the heart of the cognition "mine," which bestows existence, whose characteristic is absolute freedom (svātantrya), and which is denoted by such terms as "world-bliss" (jagadānanda)—fully blossom;
for a cognition devoid of freedom is indeed non-cognition (abodha). Therefore, that which constitutes the non-cognitive nature of cognition—

The meaning is: "having cast aside that lack of autonomy, may [it] shine forth as consciousness. Furthermore, it is well known that Abhinavagupta’s mother was named Vimalā and his father was Narasiṃhagupta. As for the detailed commentary on this *Padma*, it is found in the *Tantrālokaviveka*; therefore, it should be consulted from that very source. || 1 ||

I bow to that one Goddess, the self-awareness of my own being, within whom this entire universe shines forth as an external appearance during the process of emanation; yet who remains as the unsurpassed state when agitation has subsided.
The meaning is that within her, because she is endowed with the characteristic of being a reflection, although she is transcendent (*atirikta*), she is nonetheless non-transcendent (*anatirikta*).

The entire universe, appearing as "this" (*idantābhāsa*), shines forth. Regarding the term "agitation" (*kṣobha*): when the agitation characterized by the appearance of "this-ness" has subsided, there occurs self-awareness—awareness (*saṃvitti*) which is the light (*prakāśa*) of the Self (*ātman*) by means of the Self itself, residing within the Self alone.
Thus ends the description of the nature of the Unsurpassed. I pay homage; I enter into it. || 2 ||

I bow to the Supreme, the Unsurpassed, my own self-luminous manifestation—the wonder of intuitive insight (pratibhā)—which, having established within the heart the Triad consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, illumines them [meaning: it makes manifest externally that which resides within]. (3)
Victorious is the illustrious primordial Guru, Śambhu, the Supreme Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, whose greatness is priceless and who has liberated the multitude of bound souls. 4.
(On page 3:

For the awakening of his own disciples [meaning: so that their awakening may occur without dependence on other treatises], and for the recollection of those already awakened [meaning: for the sake of reminding those who have been awakened by other treatises].
This slight effort [or: this slight error characterized by the scriptures] is being made by me, Abhinavagupta. (5)
The Śrīdevī said:
O God, how is the unsurpassed [teaching] that immediately bestows the *kaulika* accomplishment, by the mere realization of which one attains equality with the *khecarī*? (1)

The Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of the fivefold act, is constantly pervaded by His supreme form of power (*parā-śakti*), which is essentially grace—even while the manifestation of creation and the other acts continues. In reality, He is of one essence with grace alone; for power cannot be conceived as distinct from Śiva. And that power, consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of grace toward the worlds, manifests first.

[It is] undifferentiated from the hundreds of infinite powers that are about to be manifested by the *paśyantī* [speech], which consists of reflective awareness; [the meaning is that they have not yet emerged externally].

First of all, firmly established in consciousness— which consists of the supreme mantra and is not limited by space or time— the Paśyantī [speech] exists precisely as an undifferentiation between the speech and response that are yet to arise. And that very [consciousness],
consisting of the non-duality of the consciousness of all subjects, remains eternally so [even during the manifestation of Paśyantī and the other stages].

Then, Paśyantī, appearing in the form of the present, reflects—by means of the thread of consciousness alone—upon whatever desired object is sought, such as that which is wished for and so forth, once it has been awakened by the restriction of appropriate causes (the causes being desire and so forth). For since Paśyantī is the common ground of all, how could there be a sequence of desire and so forth therein? [This refers to the objection: "How can there be a sequence of desire and so forth there? [The answer follows: "Because Paśyantī is indeed the universal ground of everything."

To clarify the point there, he states an example with the words "just as" (*yathā*). This is because the seed of memory within the variegated cognition— the cognition of blue— is awakened by the suitability of one or another factor that awakens memory, such as the perception of a similar object, reflection, or the like, for that cognition has been conditioned by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of cognitions regarding the presence and absence of many entities.

Memory reflects upon only something [already perceived], for there is no differentiation here at the time of the first cognition; [in the *paśyantī* stage, differentiation does not manifest through the desired object and so forth.

In that state where there is non-difference between the specific signified and the signifier, it is *madhyamā*; furthermore, *madhyamā* reveals the difference between those very same signified and signifier through the operation of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that is, identity (*tādātmya*);
whereas *vaikharī*, however, consists precisely in the manifestation of the difference between those two—such is the established order.

In that which is established by one's own self-awareness— [the sense being that because the manifest distinction therein is established by one's own direct experience, this is not something accessible through external means of knowledge (pramāṇa)]— that very ground of supreme speech (parāvāgbhūmi) is the essence of the non-conventional, uncreated, ultimate, and refined latent impression (saṃskāra), whose nature is the ultimate reality of the power of the word pertaining to the realm of Māyā.

Impelled by the portion that constitutes the vitality (*vīrya*) of the mantra according to the method to be explained hereafter, she remains established in reality even within the subsequent states such as *paśyantī* and the rest; for otherwise, since there would be a lack of manifestation in *paśyantī* and the other levels, the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatā*) would follow.

In that regard—[the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the very first ground]—by means of the sequence beginning with "this" (*idam*) and so forth, [she manifests] the non-conceptual and conceptual [realms], as well as space and time.

[This is the definition of its essential nature: And herein, at this very moment—there is no conceptualization whatsoever of distinctions such as "thus" or "now. Precisely for that reason, beginning from the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*), which consists in the emission of the potency of the supreme mantra (meaning *paśyantī*), and extending up to the manifestation of the distinctions of states projected as *vaikharī*, this is the ground of the Supreme Speech (*parā vāgbhūmi*).
Consisting of its own self-astonishment,
it flashes forth after coming to rest within itself alone, which is the nature of luminosity; thus it is.

The "I" is the supreme reality of uninterrupted vibration; this will become clear further on. However, within that very [reality], there are two forms consisting of the powers of knowledge and action—the essence of Sadāśiva and Īśvara—wherein, in the Paśyantī stage, there is no outlining of the element of duality, and wherein, in the Madhyamā stage, there is the manifestation of duality.

[By the metaphorical treatment of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power, Sadāśiva is the possessor of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), while Īśvara is that in whom the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has emerged. That very [power] is the wonder of "I am this," a state full of the wonder of the internalization of the infinite universe as its own limit;
it consists of the *paśyantī* and *madhyamā* stages, and [perceives] its own self alone, characterized by the non-emergent and emergent states of objectivity (*idantā*).
The meaning is "form" (*rūpa*). In reality, that which consists of supreme consciousness reflects upon itself, and that very supreme consciousness is called the Goddess.

To this extent, by means of the process of emanation beginning with *paśyantī* and extending to external objects such as blue, through the play whose nature is the non-dual self-reflection of her own consciousness—wherein "play" refers here primarily to a vibration (*spanda*) that follows joy according to her own will—[she acts].
The intended meaning is precisely the description of His own nature as both consisting of all things and transcending all things.
Because He abides in a state of supreme excellence by virtue of transcending all things, the Lord Bhairava is thus [in that manner, through His supreme excellence].
By the desire to abide with the nature of a victor,
through the performance of such worldly transactions as infinite knowledge, memory, doubt, and certainty,

and by means of the manifestation in the form of the appearance of that very blue and so forth within all things— such as the blue— which appear everywhere, [he acts] through all those penetrations of its light.
Because it is praised by those who are inclined toward that [state], it has been said:
"There is no other entity called 'praise' apart from the all-pervading Supreme Lord;
for the praise consists in [the realization]: 'I am Śiva,' in a form that transcends everything."
Thus: "And according to one's desire, by attaining the state of being the Self of all through the limitation of space and time.

One should not suspect here that there is a contradiction in the phrase "by attaining the state of being the Self of all through the limitation of space and time," because whatever is all-pervasive necessarily exists in all directions and at all times; however, it is not the case that the state of being the Self of all occurs without being limited by space, time, and so forth.
For it has been said by the venerable Somānanda:
"Pervasiveness is obstructed by such characteristics as direction and time;
for that which is necessarily pervasive exists in all directions."
Thus:
"Salutation to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and for whom self-experience alone is the sole means of knowledge."
Thus, that definition of "being the self of all" which was formulated by the venerable feet of Bhartṛhari has been refuted by this [text].
For this very reason, primarily... (p. 8)
The divinity of Bhairavanātha alone is intended [here], while that of his Śakti, the Blessed Goddess, is her very nature as the Goddess (Devī). As it has been said:

"The root *div* is used in the senses of playing, desiring victory, worldly transaction, splendor, praise, and motion. And likewise, through the grace of even a fraction of a fraction of that divine state consisting of such supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*), [it is present] in Viṣṇu, Viriñci, and others.
As has indeed been determined elsewhere by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda: "When the group of Tattveśvaras has dissolved, at the time of creation again,
those who seek that state, or those beloved by Śiva, occupy that station."

That which is called *brāhmī* is indeed the power (*śakti*) of another; he who causes that [power] to descend thereon is, respectively, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, starting from the Vaiṣṇavī [and other powers].

Thus ends the discourse on the deities. In this way, when the Blessed Goddesses Paśyantī and Madhyamā reflect upon their own self, thinking, "I alone am composed of the deity Parāvāk; thus have I spoken," then, by virtue of that form, through the unfolding of Māyā, this pair—characterized by the manifestation of the appearance of "this-ness" (idantā)—is indeed the commencement of Māyā.

This is the meaning: by virtue of being dependent upon one's own self, and in accordance with the differentiation belonging to its *māyā*, that very supreme ground (*parābhūmi*), which consists of one's own self, [is perceived].
Considering it as a reality— that is, as a common temporal state—

it is "indirect" (*parokṣa*) because it transcends the paths of the internal and external senses, which are the life-force of the manifestation of difference; for the definition of the indirect is that which is beyond the senses (*akṣebhyaḥ yat param tat parokṣam*).

The meaning is as follows: since the division of days is determined by the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, how can there be a designation of "present" (*adyatana*) in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), given that it is not delimited by such movement?

For the world of Brahmā is situated above Mount Meru, whereas the sun is situated below; therefore, how can the present time be defined there by the movement of the sun and so forth? Furthermore, a day of Brahmā is measured by many *kalpas*. From that [day], too...

[Because it exists above that,] starting from Viṣṇu; and as for the end, regarding the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, [one should infer for oneself that in an external day there are twenty-one thousand six hundred movements of the prāṇa, and within that very [period], the emergence of sixty years occurs];
even in a hundred-thousandth part of the vital breath, there is the conventional usage of "day"—thus [the day] is established and yet conceptual.

According to the principle that "how could there be 'presentness' in the non-conceptualized nature of consciousness?", one should reflect by means of the sequence of the third person singular (parokṣottamapuruṣa), which fulfills the requirements of a past, non-present, and remote object: "I myself am she, the Goddess Parāvāk, who, being undivided from all that is expressed and the expression itself, spoke thus"— this is the intended meaning.

(10) "I indeed spoke while asleep"—this is precisely how it is logically established. For instance, he does not remember that past state because it was previously unperceived; [he now knows it] through the greatness of what has been told by another person.

Or rather, one experiences that state through the immersion in bodily transformations such as stammering produced by activities like excessive lamentation and singing, due to the resulting wonder; for this is not merely a lack of cognition, as in the thought, "I indeed lamented while intoxicated or asleep.

For in states such as intoxication, sleep, and fainting, there is a state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) because of the non-apprehension of specific objects of knowledge; however, in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), it is different.

There is simply an absence of any specific object of knowledge (*vedya*) here; this is because, through the realization of identity with the subject (*vedaka*), it possesses the nature of the Fourth State (*turya*).

However, in states such as intoxication and the like, there is a predominance of the onset of delusion (*moha*); this is the only distinction. As for its being beyond direct perception (*parokṣatā*), that is indeed the same in both cases. Thus, every subject whatsoever—whether situated in the roles of teacher, disciple, and so forth, or in other worldly transactions—is at all times [in this state].
Whatever one does, by entering into this very consciousness, one becomes a vessel for all worldly activity;
therefore, it is that very [consciousness] which one must investigate in reality. Thus the Goddess said: "I alone am always everything, in a state of non-duality. This is what is meant.

11) I reflect upon this on the supreme level (*parābhūmi*); otherwise, this clear manifestation belonging to the intermediate level (*madhyamābhūmi*) would not occur. Thus it is said: "The Goddess said. In the same way, [it will be stated] later regarding Bhairava.
It should be understood as follows: even there, it is the very self of Bhairava, consisting of the non-differentiation between one's own power and that of another, who said "I"—this is the meaning.

However, when there is a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the nature of emanation, where power is predominant, the reflective awareness of the Goddess as "I" is appropriate; whereas, when there is a reflective awareness of the immersion in withdrawal, where the possessor of power is predominant, [the awareness] is "Maha-a."

The wonder of the form of Bhairava will be made manifest. And this—[referring to all that was previously stated, he says "this"]—is precisely the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) within the supreme consciousness consisting of the power of will, which exists within the very ground of the powers of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) known as *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*. And that alone...
Therefore, the purpose of the entire treatise, reaching its ultimate conclusion, is precisely this: within the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) which consists of Sadāśiva,

through the manifestation of the sequence of preceding and succeeding words and sentences, there occurs the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the true, supreme potency of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), namely the letters *da*,
*e*, *va*, *ya*, *u*, *va*, *ā*, *ca*, *bha*, and *ai*.
(The construction of words and sentences beginning with the letters *repha*, *akāra*, *vakāra*, and *akāra*. And it is said in the *Svacchandatantra*:
"The Lord Sadāśiva himself, assuming the roles of teacher and disciple..."

By means of sentences consisting of preceding and following words, he introduced the *tantra*— [the *tantra* being the scripture characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), situated in the state of teacher and disciple, which is characterized by Śiva and Śakti].

Thus, the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*) is indeed eternally unsetting within all subjects; for it has been said that [having entered into consciousness itself, it becomes the vessel of worldly transaction]. This very [power] is the supreme relation, which is the sole life-force of the *Ṣaḍardhasāra* scripture, as it has been stated:
Of Śiva, who is perfect, supreme, and of immeasurable splendor,
there is his power called Sādākhya, which is the domain of his own will and agency.
The wise know that through that [power], the first connection with *sattva* is attained;
and furthermore, by means of intermediate conjunction, it is gradually attained from the state called *sādākhya*.
The second was proclaimed by him as attained by the god Ananteśa;
and the third, O Goddess, was [attained] by Śrīkaṇṭha together with Nandin.
Because it was received from the gods by two [means], it is proclaimed as "divine" (divya);
and it was briefly expounded to the sages by Nandin.
The fourth [empowerment] was proclaimed by the Blessed One as both divine and non-divine,
through the application of the sequence of exposition, for the worship of the Vidyāpīṭha.
The fifth is the mutual relationship in the form of disciple and teacher;
thus, this fivefold connection has been fully described.
Thus, because even a trace of duality has dissolved within this absolute oneness (*aikātmya*),

and because it possesses the fullness characterized by the state of being the self of all (*sarvasarvātmatā*), the relationship is indeed the Supreme (*para*) one. Here, within the Absolute (*anuttara*),
[there is no room for] other types of relationships.
13) Because, through the aforementioned teaching, the great interval between the divine and the non-divine and so forth consists solely of the Supreme; as it is said in the *Trikahṛdaya*:
"The Supreme Lord is eternally intent upon emission within His own power."

He is the creator whose nature is grace, the destroyer, and one for whom emission is supreme; being solely intent on that, he is of the form of the creator as "I," and by its opposite, he is of the form of the destroyer, and remains unconditioned.

Thus, in this manner, because the Supreme Lord— the *cittattva*— is eternally emergent and consists of such ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that very internal object which flashes forth in undivided unity is, upon the level of *paśyantī*, grasped with the desire to differentiate it into phonemes, words, and sentences; and on the level of *madhyamā*, it remains as differentiated, preceded by the [internal] object.

From the *saṃnanna* up to the end of *vaikharī*, [it consists of] the "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) and so forth, ending with the arrangement of phonemes, words, and sentences belonging to the differentiated level of *māyā*. This very [reality], which is unperceivable as such, is the mouth of Bhairava; it consists of the reflective awareness of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and its essence is the Unsurpassed state of "I-am-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*).
It is characterized by the agitation arising from the attainment of the union of Śiva and Śakti, whose forms are the letters *a* and *ā*, the essence of which is the Unsurpassed.

The seed of the expansion of the Trika scriptures is the primordial *dhruvapada*, which is the singular life-force of all living beings; for this very reason, because there is no differentiation, designations such as "place" (*sthāna*) are inapplicable. [Now, according to the rule of the *paratantra* [Tantras], first some devotee, having made known the person to be initiated, provides a designation of the place for the Goddess and Bhairava.]
Just as [the description] "seated on the peak of Kailāsa" and so forth applies to [the deity] in his aspect of purity (svacchatā) and the like, why is it not applied here as well?

For this very reason, he says: "because there is no exclusion" (vyavacchedābhāvāt), and so forth. Furthermore, one should not think that this description of the location and so forth is appropriate only for the gross (sthūla) level and not for the internal form (antārūpatā); for even in the case of "Kailāsa" and so forth...

Because it is precisely the subtle reality that must be explained; for instance—what is the *elā*? It is the throbbing power (*śakti*) at the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*) at the crown of the head. Upon that is the seat (*āsana*), the state of being situated above, belonging to the Peak (*śikhara*) whose nature is the pervasive (*vyāpinī*) and the equalized (*samanā*).
That peak is the summit of Kailāsa, existing above all paths; seated there is that which has transcended [the levels].

Regarding the phrase "the reality of manifestation": it is not logical for [this reality] to be preceded by location and so forth. Furthermore, the reality—which consists of the question and its answer—is eternally risen; first, it is undivided. Therefore, this alone is the intended meaning here: one's own Self, which is the intrinsic nature of all things, being self-luminous, [manifests] its very own Self through that which is non-different from itself.

15) Through the question and answer, [the teacher], by means of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) consisting of his own self as both questioner and respondent, experiences wonder and reflects: "It is I alone who, desiring such manifold wonders, while knowing it to be so, become exactly thus."

Thus, from the point where the Goddess asks "How is it unsurpassed? up to where Bhairava says "Listen, O Goddess," this is the *Rudrayāmala*. Alternatively, all the scriptures beginning with the *Pañcasrotas* up to this worldly convention—that is what is called the supreme relationship (*para-sambandha*).
This secret essence of instruction, which immediately leads to the state of Bhairava,
has been constantly explained by me, Abhinavagupta, as the "Treasury of Questions."
Out of a desire for the welfare of our disciples, however, we shall state this very point in summary:
whatever is to be known or to be accomplished in all worldly transactions,
that unfolds, free from duality, in the supreme fourth state (*turya*).

In Paśyantī, which consists of the subtle outlining of distinctions and possesses sequential order, [the Word] partakes of those very distinctions; in Madhyamā, where there is no manifest connection with sequence within, it likewise partakes of their differentiation.
The intermediate [state] sees the supreme and the intermediate; then, through their intense non-differentiation,
one should contemplate that state at that moment as if it were imperceptible, like one who is intoxicated or asleep.

In the midst of those who have abandoned the practice of killing living beings, whose minds are first awakened by the realization of the self, who have cast off all worldly attachments, and who shine with the splendor of the discernment of the soul;
in their midst, may [the Lord] manifest.
By means of desire, through the semblance of a horse,
and by the terrifying appearance of a phantom, he causes the doubt of those whose minds are fixed upon their own state to vanish.

In this very way, he will explain this state of unsurpassedness— thus it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānanda-pāda immediately after the first *śaktispanda* of the Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka, who is intent upon the fivefold act (*pañcakṛtya*).

Thus it is stated in his own commentary. For the purpose of shattering that knot—[the "knot" being the non-explicit statement of the meaning, and its "shattering" being its discernment]—this is our effort, we who have been purified by his teaching. The relationship has been stated. As for the subject matter (*abhidheya*), it is the *Triśikā*, which refers to the three powers: will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

17) [The powers] whose names cannot be fully expressed by terms such as "creation" and so forth— namely, creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace (sṛṣṭi-sthiti-saṃhāra-tirodhāna-anugrahaḥ),
as well as "exertion" and so forth.

[They are] worthy of being defined by other names such as "the radiance of arising," "the color of time," "the devouring of time," and "resting in one's own nature. [The term *īśikā* means] the Mistress (*īśvarī*) and the act of ruling (*īśanā*), which, because of the impossibility of the entry of objective portions [into it], is non-different from that which is to be ruled (*īśitavya*). It is thus "that which is to be" (*bhāvinī*).
The Supreme Goddess Bhaṭṭārikā Parā—the Blessed Consciousness who transcends these three divisions of power and consists of the non-differentiation from those powers—is the signified (*abhidheya*).

And precisely through connection with her, this signifier (*abhidhāna*) is called the *Triśikā*. The teachers also read it as *Triṃśakā*, and they explain its etymology based on the similarity of the syllables: "It proclaims (*kāyati*) the three powers (*tisraḥ śaktīḥ*)," thus it is *triṃśakā*; it is not [derived from] *triṃśat* (thirty).

However, because it consists of thirty verses, it is called the *Triṃśikā*. This is because even this [work], which contains two hundred thousand [verses]—this being the meaning of the term "even so many"—possesses the thirty topics (*triṃśakārtha*). For it is said in the *Śrītantrasāra*:
"The meaning of the thirty [topics], though its extent is one and a half crores [of verses], has been proclaimed by you."
Thus, it has already been stated that the relationship between the signifier and the signified is precisely one of identity (*tādātmya*).
And the purpose [of this] is for all cognizers.
For those who, by virtue of the grace of the Lord’s supreme descent of power (*paraśaktipāta*), have become fit vessels for this much unsurpassed knowledge, there arises—

through the internalization of their own true nature within the heart— the realization that the entire multitude of principles regarded as bonds is merely a manifestation of difference brought about by the play of the abundance of one's own innate fragrance.

Liberation while living consists of an immersion into the non-dual nature of Bhairava, which is the identity with the "I-ness" (ahantā) full of the wonder of one's own self. Indeed, for one who is established even within the sphere of the vital breath, the body, and so forth— which are the objects of the internal and external senses, characterized by impulse, effort, strength, and life— there is liberation from those things considered to be bondage.
—thus it is sung. For even when the illusory [world] has been shattered, what is this linguistic convention of "liberation," and with reference to what?
As it is said in the venerable *Spanda*:
"Or he whose consciousness perceives the entire universe as a play..."
Seeing thus and remaining constantly disciplined, he is undoubtedly liberated while living.
Thus it is said. And this will become clear very shortly:
"Kill, kill! Run, O jackal, wherever you may be!
Stay with your feet raised upward; you who desire the fruit of this world!"
p.

19) Therefore, since the very purpose here is this self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which culminates in the fulfillment of all human goals, there is no room for a further purpose for that purpose. As it was said in the *Stotra*:
O Lord, the ultimate fruit of actions or ritual injunctions is indeed nothing other than absorption in You;

however, for those who desire fruits here, their state remains that of the deluded, characterized by an endless cycle of rebirth. Thus, the connection, the subject matter, and the purpose have been stated.

Now the meaning of the text is explained. "Anuttara" means that there is no *uttara*—that is, nothing superior or additional—to it. For, just as the thirty-six other principles, from the *anāśrita-śiva* up to [the earth], attain their respective states of perfection by entering into the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava and thereby surpass the [lower] consciousness, they do not do so in this case.
The supreme, perfectly full consciousness of Supreme Bhairava does not admit anything else as distinct from itself,

because its essence is always the wonder of its own unimpeded and independent manifestation. Likewise, there exists no "answer" in the form of a response to a question therein, precisely because it is the ocean of Great Consciousness.

The disciple becomes a vessel for the manifestation of questions, insights, and so forth, from the abode that is the limit of infinite, shimmering creative intuition (pratibhā); that indeed is, in reality, the eternally arisen Tattva.
What else, indeed, could this be but the Master’s answer? Crossing over (*uttaraṇa*) refers to liberation (*apavarga*) as conceived by the proponents of dualism;

for that, in reality, does not transcend being animated by necessity (*niyati*). To explain: first, having entered from the body into the level of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then having ascended from there to the level of the intellect (*buddhi*), and even from there to that which is called vibration (*spandana*).

Having superimposed the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), and from that state having ascended to the stage of the void (*śūnyapada*) characterized by the dissolution of all objects of cognition, and further, upon reaching the culmination of the progressive attenuation of all impurities (*mala*), the individual soul (*aṇu*) attains liberation through the manifestation of its Śiva-nature, because the superimposition [of limitation] has been rendered purposeless. It is precisely of such a nature [that this is].

The sequence of ascending upward, attained through the successive stages of presiding over the centers (adhiṣṭhāna) beginning with the navel, heart, throat, palate, the abode of Brahmā, and the cavern of Bhairava; likewise, according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), as stated in the *Tantrāloka*.
For that which is pure consciousness alone, whose ultimate reality is light,
shines forth as the distinct void after having cast off the object of knowledge from itself.
That very self of space, when this object of cognition is differentiated, becomes oriented toward appropriation;
falling [into manifestation] as an upward surging, it is designated by such terms as the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Therefore they say that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath (prāṇa),
and thus the wind becomes the substratum for the principle of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
This is that power of vital breath (prāṇa-śakti) which bestows the longing for internal exertion;
it is considered to be vibration (spanda), radiance (sphurattā), repose (viśrānti), the individual soul (jīva), the heart (hṛt), and intuitive insight (pratibhā).
That function of the vital breath, by making the body its own through its five forms beginning with prāṇa,
becomes filled with consciousness by that very means.
Thus, this is the upward progression through the contemplation of dissolution according to the manner of its manifestation.
"Such" (*īdṛśam*) is the exclusion by way of direct perception (*pratyakṣatayā*); "so" (*tādṛśam*) is the exclusion by way of indirect perception (*parokṣatayā*).
[Regarding the term *uttara*: it is called *uttara* because they cross over (*uttaranti*) in that manner; thus, *uttara-bandha* is bondage, and *uttaraṇa* is liberation.
Where there are no such *uttaras* (subsequent states or further descriptions), and where there is no further verbal expression—that is, in every respect, "such" and "so"—is the exclusion. [48]

One should perform that [action] wherein this unsurpassed [reality] does not exist as uninterrupted; for even the notion "this" has its very life in the exclusion of what follows it—thus, because it functions as an exclusion, it is essentially conceptual in nature.

Therefore, as long as the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātā*) desires to enter into the unsurpassed form (*anuttara-rūpa*), he remains merely imagined (*kalpita*) within that specific nature; however, that which is non-conceptual (*avikalpita*) therein—because the imagined form does not manifest apart from its inseparable correlate—is alone the truly unsurpassed. For in that state, the practice of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth is simply untenable in reality. Thus it is said.
The state of being devoid of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and ritual action (*karaṇa*) has been stated [as follows] by the venerable Śrī Somānanda:
"What need is there for cultivation or ritual action for Śiva, who is ever-arisen? Once gold is known, what is the use of cultivation, ritual action, and the like?"
Truthfulness consists in maintaining a firmness toward [the teacher] equal to that toward one's mother, father, and so forth, at all times;
this occurs once through valid means, whether from the scriptures or from the words of the guru.
Once Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, has been known through firm realization,
there is no further need for any ritual instrument nor even for meditative cultivation.
Thus [it is said]. But it is not merely due to a lack of utility that such a supreme state exists even within the functions of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) in this very manner.
As I have stated myself in a hymn:
"As if bowed down in the sky, yet without being severed..."
A thin stream of falling water is not clearly perceived;
however, by means of such factors as trees in the grove, the roof of a house, or the base of a mountain, it is distinctly observed.
In the same way, Supreme Bhairava, due to His extreme subtlety,
never at any time comes within the range of experience.
Then, through their connection with place, form, time, arrangement, stability, vibration, and agency,
they suddenly produce a derivative consciousness that eclipses the awareness of Bhairava.
And so forth. And thus it will be stated later: "The answer to the answer as well. This is also explained:
in this very way, for the individual soul (*narātman*), the Śākta is the answer; beyond that, the Śāmbhava;

and likewise, even among those [levels], by means of the distinctions of the elements (*bhūta*), the principles (*tattva*), the self (*ātman*), the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*), the powers (*śakti*), and so on, there is a state of being progressively higher within one's own self, even regarding the elements and the rest.
For one who is awake in the form of earth and so forth, dream follows; from that, deep sleep; from that, the fourth state (*turya*); and even beyond that, the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*).

Even within the states of waking and the rest, there is a successive progression of higher and higher levels according to the fourfold division within one's own self alone. This very point has been explained in the *Śrīpūrvapañcikā*.
24) This has been determined by me in detail elsewhere; however, it is not stated here at length because it is of no use for the present purpose and would result in excessive prolixity.
Such is this state of being "subsequent" (*uttaratva*), which produces the delusion of non-duality regarding the sequence of higher and lower [truths].
Where there is no division based on the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or outcastes, nor any deficiency or excess;

where the latter term emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*): the "higher" powers (*uttarāḥ śaktayaḥ*) are Paśyantī and the others—namely Aghorā and the rest, and Parā and the rest—which are established as Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī according to their subtle, intermediate, and gross forms.

And by this sequence, there are the powers (*śakti*) consisting of will, knowledge, and action; the powers characterized as the presiding deities, namely the non-terrible (*aghora*) and the terrible (*ghora*); and the nature of the Supreme (*parā*) and the others, as stated elsewhere: "That by which the Supreme Lord sustains, perceives, and illumines this entire universe from Śiva down to the earth as nothing but non-conceptual pure consciousness—that is His [power]."

She is the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*). By her, [the universe is perceived] through both difference and non-difference, like a reflection of an elephant and so forth in a mirror; thus she is the "Supreme-Non-Supreme" (*parāparā*).

By her, [the universe is perceived] through difference alone, as mutually distinct entities; thus she is the "Non-Supreme" (*aparā*). That power by which these three are swallowed—through their integration within herself by means of unifying consciousness—is also the Supreme herself, designated by the alternative name *Kālakarṣiṇī*. Where those [powers] reside...
They would not exist; for [the root] *nud* means "to impel," thus *noda* is the impelling (*nut*), by which there is crossing (*taraṇa*) through the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*).
The teacher's consciousness is the crossing (*taraḥ*) into the consciousness of the disciple.

[The Guru should, at the time of initiation, effect the grasping of the Self by means of the intellect; according to this principle, one's own awakened consciousness is impelled into the unawakened consciousness of the disciple.

By that [means], through the sequence of the various locations such as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the void (*śūnya*), and the equinox (*viṣuvat*), [the consciousness is projected] whether into the state with parts (*sakala*) or the partless (*niṣkala*).
By means of the performance of the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) and other rites—[as for "joining," it is stated in the *Tantrasāra* regarding the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*]:

"Initiation is of the nature of joining with Śiva"]—he ordains the initiation that bestows liberation. Now, in this regard, how can there be [a process] for consciousness, which is self-luminous, all-pervading, and not differentiated by specific qualities of space, time, or form? [In this sequence...]
The causal relationship must be established as follows: since [the Lord] is not distinguished by form, how can there be a connection with that which is both whole and partless?
Since He is all-pervasive, how can there be a conjunction? Since He is not limited by space and time, how does He bestow liberation?
And since He is self-luminous and independent, how could any ritual injunction be possible therein? Regarding this:

The sequence of initiation is as follows: the yoga of both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*) is for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), whereas the unmanifest alone is for the sake of attaining liberation exclusively.
These are mere farces; thus, that in which there is no crossing over—that is, no liberation—through such an impelling force is the "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*). As it will be said:
Thus, for one who knows this according to reality, initiation becomes the means leading to Nirvāṇa.

Thus: from the verbal root *an* (to breathe), with the suffix *kvip*, we have *an-aṇuḥ*, meaning the Self (*ātman*) which is not subtle, such as the body, the city-of-eight (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth. Likewise, *ananaṃ* is life (*jīvana*).
Life is a function (*vṛtti*) residing within the body and other such things, which is for the most part devoid of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) associated with various distinct powers and so on. (p. 26)

The void subject— that very reality of Light which manifests as the non-differentiation of the universe consisting of the triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge, and which is not yet differentiated by the powers such as will— is, through its own sovereignty,
desirous of manifesting within itself the object of knowledge that constitutes the universal self, while remaining undivided from itself.

Having distinguished himself from everything through the realization "I have transcended all," he is proclaimed in the Āgamas as the *nirāvaraṇa-pramātṛ* (the subject free from veils), because he is devoid of all objective existence (*sakalabhāva*). Furthermore, this "voidness" (*śūnyatva*) here results from the cessation of all objective states, but not of consciousness itself; for if consciousness were likewise absent, everything would become blind and mute. And it has been said:
Except for all objective phenomena, all principles in their entirety,
and all latent tendencies of the afflictions, it is empty; yet from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is not empty.

Thus it is said: the state of being its very response, its absolute supremacy as the ultimate reality, wherein—in this world filled with both the insentient and the sentient—those who are insentient abide as if immersed solely within the individual soul (jīva). [The intention here is as follows:
what is the meaning of "the jar manifests to me"? It means that my own manifestation, my own vibration, has entered [into it].]
For it has attained the very form of the "I" (madrūpatā) because it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*). And it has been stated by the venerable master Utpaladeva:

Thus, even those others who are known as "living" among the insentient are themselves indeed insentient, insofar as their forms consist of the body, the vital breaths, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the void; what then can be said of them? This being so, that which appears as something attached—consisting of the jar, the body, the vital breaths, the subtle body, pleasure, and its absence—is precisely that [consciousness].
Truth is that which has become the very form of the living soul (jīva). Likewise, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it is said:
"For the foundation of insentient things rests upon the living soul."

27) Furthermore, that which is called "life" for living beings is the single supreme sovereignty of the Lord, consisting of knowledge and action as previously described, which exists in all even in other states. For it is only the body and so forth that appear, at first glance, as either "not living" or "living," but not [the true life itself].

The meaning is: [it appears] as distinct within the nature of consciousness. That which, however, is the act of breathing (prāṇana) is self-luminous precisely through non-duality, and this alone is the ultimate reality. As it was said by the venerable Utpaladeva:
"Knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings."

Thus, life consists of nothing other than knowledge and action. And this "A" is that which is non-illusory, non-scriptural, innate, and of the nature of the wonder of one's own self— the waveless ocean of consciousness resting in the Great Light.

The first stage consists of the power of manifestation (*kalā*) belonging to that very [consciousness], which reaches its ultimate consummation in the state of the perfect "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), whose nature is the reflective awareness (*amarśana*) of the universe as consisting of the outpouring of Śakti. [Note: The first stage consists of the power of manifestation; the meaning is that the stage of the perfect "I-consciousness," which consists of the reflective awareness of the universe as "I," is the ultimate stage. It is the *kalā* (power/aspect) of that very [consciousness].
By the method to be explained, that which is this state of ending in *visarga*—the crossing over (*taraḥ*) of that very [state], that is, its existence as revolving above all—is where [this occurs].

That in which there exists no *anut*—that is, no impelling activity (*preraṇā*) consisting of sequential action that depends on duality such as going to or coming from a place and time—is the *anuttara*. It is superior even to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, which are well-known in the world; he states that it is indeed superior even to that *anuttara* with the words "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) and so forth.

In the case of space and so forth, such a sequential action might indeed occur due to the influence of diverse limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pots that possess conjunction, and through connection with inherent qualities (samavāyin) such as sound; however, in the principle of consciousness— which consists essentially of the sovereignty of all-pervasive, unconditioned, and full autonomy— there occurs a repose consisting of a fragmented aesthetic wonder (camatkāra).

In the Self— which is devoid of appearance yet eternally manifest, which is filled with a multitude of states that are the locus of all "this-ness" (idantā) whose status as limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is accepted though suspected, and wherein non-appearance is made to appear as if accepted— there is no succession whatsoever, because there is an absence of sequence dependent on space and time, which consist essentially in the appearance of "this-ness" and its non-appearance. Thus, it is indeed without succession (akrama).

The action called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), consisting of the intensity of self-reflection and well-known from the *Matsyodarīmata* and other sources, is that very *anuttara* (the unsurpassed). Here, the suffix *tamap* expresses a mere degree of excellence; according to Pāṇini’s rule regarding the comparative suffix *tarap*, it is used when a dual or a distributive word is present.
In this regard, concerning the statement "this is white, this is white, and this is whiter than these two," the meaning is as follows:

between these two white things, this one is whiter—that is, *śuklatara*; but regarding the statement "among these white things, this is whiter," what is the additional meaning? For instance, [in the case of] "this palace":
"This cloth is white; this swan is also white; among these, that which is most white is the one with the excellence of whiteness.

In this case, since both the palace is white and the cloth is white, what would be said as being more so? To apply such a statement even to that [palace] would be entirely improper, for the suffix *tamap* cannot denote an excellence greater than what is already expressed by the suffix *tarap*.

Thus, it may be argued as follows: the suffix *tamap* is not employed when the specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not intended to be expressed; however, when there is a requirement for a specific counter-correlative, the suffix *tarap* depends precisely upon that counter-correlative.

For the referent of the dual number and the comparative suffix (*vibhajyopapada*) must be a single counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), as in "of these two, this one is whiter by excess. A third [correlative] is not perceived; rather, it is perceived that only the first [member] functions as the counter-correlative through the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Nor does there arise a dependence on two or more [members], for it is held that a single [entity] depends on each [other] simultaneously; thus, it occurs sequentially.

There is no further meaning [to be derived]. As for the usage *tāratamya*, it is simply a conventional term (*rūḍha*) established for the excellence of a sequence, and not [derived] from following the meaning of the suffixes *tarap* and *tamap*; for if it were so, forms such as *tāryam* or *tāmyam* would also have to occur. Enough, then, with this display of skill in citing fragments of scripture at an inappropriate time. Here, however, when there is a requirement for a subsequent successive correlate, [the term used is] *anuttama*.
This is also the meaning in this application. For instance, in another scripture:

"That which even today is not known by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) who possess awakening, yet nothing whatsoever remains unknown to anyone—this one thing is unsurpassed. (The word *adyāpi* refers to the attainment of perfect illumination.)
"Of the Siddhas" means those in whom the tradition of the Guru and the scriptures has blossomed by virtue of the descent of the supreme *śakti*;
for this very reason, they are endowed with awakening—that is, they possess the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) rooted in the awakening known as absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).

That which is not known by them of itself—because it is the nature of both the support (*ādhāra*) and the supported (*ādheya*), and thus is not known as an object of cognition (*vedyatayā*)—is likewise not known to anyone else.
And it is not unknown to ordinary people, because without it the accomplishment of anything is impossible; it is indeed known and worthy of being known.
For this very reason, because its nature appears contradictory at first glance, it is called "something"—meaning that which is supreme among all.

Thus, Anuttara (the Unsurpassed) has as its body the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which is permeated by the essence of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). This was stated by the venerable Utpaladeva: "And there is succession in worldly [action]... [By "worldly" is meant that which consists of the raising and lowering of the hands, and so forth.]

"From the power of Time" means from that specific power of the Supreme Lord which consists in the capacity to manifest the differentiation of appearances. "Eternal" means not having abandoned its primordial nature. "Belonging to the Lord" means non-different from the Lord. Herein is the intended meaning:
The power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is the Lord’s capacity to illuminate the knower and the known, which are the root of worldly cognitive activity;
that very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose essence is sovereignty over conjunction and other operations, is indeed action (*kriyā*).

This [action], however, appearing as a succession, consists in the infusion of the shadow of the object of cognition; though it is transparent, it accepts limitations and thus manifests as sequential.
"In reality, even though there is no succession"—since it is not delimited by time, its state of non-succession remains established; what, then, is being said here?

Even when the multitude of objects of knowledge has emerged, and even while the Lord occupies the station of the subject constituted by *māyā*, as long as the entire collection of knowable things, both external and internal, [remains] within his own self...
The repose of light within itself;
thus,
this [notion] of "this-ness" is fragmented.
By this method, [the Lord] brings [the universe] to rest and devours it; at that point, even the sequence of manifestation centered upon that [universe] is itself swallowed.

Thus, that activity—which is characterized by specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and extends from the initial stage of conjunction (*saṃyojana*) up to the final stage of the withdrawal of the manifestation of all diverse entities as "I"—is indeed nothing other than the emergence of the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) from action (*kriyā*).
But it does not apply to that which is eternal; for [the power] of the eternal would be like that of a Lord, belonging to the Lord himself.
Thus it is said. This Anuttara has been explained as being sixteenfold. As it is stated in the *Sāraśāstra*:
"The Anuttara is the Heart; in the Heart lies the nature of the knot.
Having known the knot to be sixteenfold, one may perform ritual action according to one's pleasure."
Thus [it is said]:
"Likewise, the knot that resides in the heart... [and so forth].

And so forth. In what manner is such an *anuttara* (the unsurpassed)? Is it by way of abandoning the form of an answer (*uttara*), or rather otherwise? [The term "manner" (*prakāra*) refers to a specific distinction that excludes generalities. "In the form of an answer" means by way of a nature transcending the universe; "otherwise" means by way of accepting a nature consisting of the universe. And what is this manner, whereby this entire [universe] is the *anuttara*?

The world is indeed twofold by way of the distinction between knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). For the entire collection of knowledge and its objects is perceived everywhere as consisting of mutual difference and opposition; and from that, this hierarchy of superior and inferior must necessarily arise. Thus, in whatever manner it may be—whether in liberation itself, or even in what is considered bondage, or perhaps only in liberation—[it remains so].

The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is as follows: whether such a supreme nature (*anuttara-svarūpa*) is perceived [in liberation], or even in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which is considered bondage; for according to the principle stated that "the world does not exist in reality," the cycle of existence is in fact impossible, though it is regarded as bondage through the power of the deluding force (*mohanī-śakti*). Thus.

Since the suffix *-tha* (in *devatha*) is prescribed merely in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) without restriction to a specific case-meaning (*vibhakti-viśeṣārtha*), this question pertains exclusively to the sense of "manner. The term *deva* has already been explained. *Kula* [is so called] because it consists of a collection of gross and subtle vital breaths, senses, elements, and so forth, and because of the relationship between cause and effect.
As it was stated on page 33:
because they act in combination.

Thus, the *kula* (the family or aggregate) of consciousness itself, by way of its solidified form—namely, that the light which is Śiva becomes solidified as far as the five elements according to the sequence beginning with Śakti and Sadāśiva—becomes so because the nature of the knower has been eclipsed. Solidification (*styānībhavana*) is thus a state of hardness consisting in the predominance of the object of knowledge (*vedyatā*). Such is the nature of the process.

And while this is so, the bound person (paśu) imagines that very [reality] to be bondage within his own self. Even in its state of solidification, it never abandons its own essential nature, just as ice does not abandon its nature as water; thus he says "not indeed," and so forth. And it has been said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
Due to the force of activity within the coagulated state of the light of Śiva, which is like sugarcane juice,
even the five elements do not abandon their sweetness, just as they do not lose it when formed into balls of molasses.
Thus, because of its very state of being and because of the sovereignty of consciousness itself, there arises the conceit of bondage for this [consciousness]. For it is said in the *Kula*:

"The root *bandh* [is used] in the sense of gathering (*saṃstyāna*) and in relation to kinsmen" (*ghā*, *bhvā.*, *parasmaipada*). Indeed, because [all things] have the single nature of consciousness whose sole essence is light, [this occurs] only for those entities that do not abandon their identity with the pure, conscious subject.

Therefore, manifestation is established because memory, conceptualization, and so forth are rooted in the power of cognition; this very point must be understood in the same way. And it has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"The manifestation of entities appearing as present..."
This is possible only for those things that already exist internally, appearing through an external form.
Thus: apart from this,
there is nothing among these that is non-manifesting— [meaning that the collection of objects such as blue and so forth is non-manifesting].
If being blue and so forth is nothing other than the state of being manifest, and if this manifestation does not transcend the very body of the object,
then— just as when a cognition does not arise, that [object] is called "blue" for everyone or for no one at all;
or, in reality, it would be blue only for itself, since it is impossible for it to reside in another, and yet it is neither blue even in its own self.
Since that which is not blue cannot be established without the favor of manifestation, its non-manifestation would likewise follow;

thus, the consequence of non-manifestation is brought to an end. In that context, the Kauliki Siddhi—belonging to the Kula—is realized as the form of bliss, having transcended the firmness of such [dualistic] states.

The identity with the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Śiva, whose nature is the supreme consciousness that is the essence of the Heart—[“the essence of the Heart” means the essence of *spanda*]—bestows that accomplishment (*siddhi*). For when there is identity with the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara*), the *kula* becomes such.
As it has been said:

For the determination of the other and one's own nature occurs through both exclusion and inclusion— namely, the absence of the other when one exists, and the existence of oneself when the other is absent.
This establishment, being firmly grounded, is called "accomplishment" (siddhi) or "cessation from activity" (nirvitti).

Thus, the word *sadyas* functions in the sense of "on the same day," according to the principle stated [above]: "And how could there be a conceptual 'this-day-ness' in the non-conceptual body of consciousness?"—this is the stated principle. Because the day is not fixed, [it is said] "on the same [day].

In this context, the word *kṣaṇe* functions in the sense of "at the moment. Furthermore, the identity (*samānatva*) of the moment does not consist in similarity, but rather culminates in absolute oneness (*tattva*). This is precisely how the understanding arises from the word *sadyas*.
Therefore, by the phrase "in that very same moment," the present moment is defined with such restriction that all other past and future moments are excluded.

When even the present time—which has its life-force in the conceptualization dependent upon both [past and future]—is cast aside, then that very *kula*, which is said to consist of the circle of rays of the Supreme Lord Bhairava-Bhānu and is composed of the expansion of His own light, enters into cessation; that is to say, it attains identity with the inward-turned consciousness of the Supreme Bhairava. At that moment...

That very state consists of the tasting of the nectar of supreme bliss; it is beyond space and time, unsurpassed, eternal, of the nature of emission (*visarga*), and perpetually arisen. As it is said in the venerable *Vādyatantra*:
"This alone is 'confinement' (*saṃrodhana*) here—that which [consists in] the confining of the mass of objects, such as blue and so forth, once they have become solidified."

Through the pride of being a cognizer [limited to] the body, vital breath, and so forth, objects of knowledge appear as superior; yet by immersing oneself in that [consciousness], even that [cognizer] becomes, according to the stated method, submerged solely within the Light. Having drunk the unsurpassed nectar of its own circle of rays—which is not delimited by the two times—one becomes happy in the present.
Thus [it is said].

And the non-delimitation of both time and space has been elaborated at length by me elsewhere. Likewise, the accomplishment (siddhi) that has come from the *kula*—from the vital breath, the body, and so forth—is of the nature of ascertainment regarding those things whose life-force is duality, such as blue, pleasure, and the like; that [accomplishment]...

"He gives"—expounding upon this which was stated briefly as "the body and so forth," he says: "The body and so forth," etc. The meaning here is this: as others have said, all worldly transaction proceeds solely from the connection with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); by that very quality of desire (*icchā*), even insentient instruments proceed toward their respective functions, and not otherwise.
[The doubt is raised: "Is it not again due to that presiding [power]? [The response is: "Instantly" (*jhagiti*)—the meaning is that it is not through the mediation of will (*icchā*) and so forth.

Indeed, by means of the sudden immersion into the potency of the unsurpassed, eternal emission (*anuttara-dhruva-visarga-vīrya-āveśa*), which is unconditioned by time, one attains the accomplishment (*siddhi*) consisting of the certain realization of the true nature of all things, precisely by ascending the middle ladder of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so on.
They bring about [this state]. As it has been said:

"However, through contact with his own power, a person may become equal to Him" [meaning he becomes equal to the Lord, characterized by sovereignty that is independent of any other subject]. (Spanda-kārikā 1.8)
Thus,
"the senses are like those of embodied beings" (Svacchandatantra 2.10).
Likewise, although Śiva and Śakti are present within the Kula, it has been stated that accomplishment consists of the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*).
The ground for the production of the desired powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth: "Aṇimā, mahimā, laghimā, garimā, as well as prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis."

Thus, it should be understood that the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) herein have non-duality as their very essence. For instance: because the nature of consciousness alone is capable of containing everything within itself, it is *aṇimā* (atomicity); because of its pervasiveness, it is *mahimā* (magnificence);

because of the absence of the weightiness inherent in duality, it is *laghimā* (lightness); because it is the place of ultimate rest, it is *prāpti* (attainment); and because it grasps the manifold variety of the universe, it is *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will).

Because it is unbroken, there is lordship (*īśitva*); because it endures everything, there is mastery (*vaśitva*) and the power of determining things according to one's will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*). Thus, these perfections (*siddhi*) exist there in truth and in their fullness.

It bestows that [state] immediately, without even being perceived, precisely by being devoid of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), ritual means (*karaṇa*), and so forth. As it was said by the venerable Somānanda: "What need is there for mental cultivation or ritual means for Śiva, who is eternally manifest? [In the absence of mental cultivation and ritual means...]"
The state of being perpetually manifest is itself the cause; even in the appearance of various forms, that alone is the cause.
Thus, "once" (ekavāram)—as it is said in the *Tantrāloka*—means:

When the cloud of doubt has dissolved— either through the words of the Guru, by virtue of the cleansing process of composing a collection of reasonings, or from the confidence gained toward the scripture—
touch the feet of the Lord, whose splendor shines in the sky of the heart like that of the sun.
Victors over darkness.
Thus: "By means of valid cognition" refers to that which one has inferred for oneself; [it may be] by means of valid cognition derived from scripture or from the words of the Guru.
When Śiva-nature, which resides in all things, is known through a firm-minded realization, [one attains liberation]. (p. 38)
"There is no purpose whatsoever served by ritual action (*karaṇa*) or even by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Thus, within the *Kula*—which consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti—that very desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*), existing internally, takes the form of an outward orientation; this is the power (*śakti*) characterized as emission (*visarga*). Once this has arisen, it is the accomplishment of the Empowered (*śākta-siddhi*).
Starting from the initial emergence in the form of *hādi* up to the expansion of the external layer of existence, it bestows the manifestation of duality;

for that very Absolute (*anuttara*), whose nature is the Great Light and which has internalized the expansion of all objective existences consisting of consciousness, unfolds duality out of its own state of being the Absolute—that is, from the abundance of the wonder of its unsurpassed sovereignty and freedom. Indeed, it is not otherwise.

If that which is non-luminous in nature were to become the cause for the manifestation of the expansion of existence, it would necessarily be of the very nature of the Supreme Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka; what need then is there for anything else—whether this be Māyā, Prakṛti, atoms, or the like? If it is luminous in nature, then enough with speaking of it; and if it is not, [it cannot be the cause].
Nevertheless, how could that which has not yet attained existence within itself become a cause for another? [This is answered] by means of a web of words:

likewise, those "measures" (*mātrā*) whose protection (*trāṇa*), preservation (*pālana*), and lordship (*patitva*) are known through that unsurpassed distinction—by the measure (*māna*), that is, the cognizing subject (*pramātman*)—those measures, consisting of the forms of the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing, are thus fully understood.
By that [means], it is merely known. Likewise, that which is known through the firm binding of realization by means of specific distinction is indeed already manifest;
it is not to be cultivated further, because its nature is once-and-for-all manifest (*sakṛdvibhāta*). Thus, it is merely known.
That which is known is indeed of the single nature of the knowable, for it never possesses the nature of a knower; likewise, objects such as jars and the like do not possess the nature of a knower.
This *māyā* consists of duality, wherein the knower has the form of the knowable. That state where both of these have vanished is "pure consciousness alone" (*vijñātamātra*).
It is that state where objects such as jars and the like are self-luminous by virtue of having the single nature of the knower, and wherein *māyā* no longer has power.

By the mere recognition of that, having remained in the *kha*—the Brahman whose nature is non-duality—one moves; that is, one perceives the object, likewise performs activities such as rejection and acquisition, and abides in one's own true nature. Thus, *khecarī* consists of the internal and external senses, their objects, pleasure, and forms such as blue, for it is in the state where the relationship between the known and the knower does not arise.

In the void, when there is the unfolding of the vision of pure consciousness alone; when there is the unfolding of differentiation as it is being indicated by the unity of the internal distinctions residing within the objects of cognition; and when there is the intensification of manifest differentiation—these are, respectively, the powers that have become Vyomacarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī.
In reality, according to the principle stated, they are indeed inseparable from the power whose nature is the *carakhecarī* (the moving and non-moving); thus, she is one alone.

For she is the single, ultimate power of the Supreme Lord, non-different from His own essential nature; yet, appearing through the differentiation of various forms born merely from the distinction in the reflective awareness of "this," she manifests as a plurality of divided entities.

It is worthy of being designated even by means of plurality. Furthermore, the purpose of designating the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) by the word "power" (*śakti*) is precisely to demonstrate the non-difference from the Supreme Lord, who possesses that power. The Supreme Goddess is Power. As it has been said:
"His powers are the entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power.

Therefore, there is a designation in the feminine gender; for neither the differentiation nor the establishment of the self, the mind, the senses, and external objects—which constitute the domain of distinction—is tenable, because of the impossibility of intentional application (*abhisaṃdhāna*) [in such a case].
And because it is non-manifest, that very *khecarī* is perceived through the imbalance of forms such as desire, anger, and so forth;
its equanimity, however, exists everywhere due to its nature as the perfectly full Bhairava.

Even the slightest lack of awareness of the unexcelled (*anuttara*) nature—which is entirely undivided—is itself the imbalance of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), and that alone is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

[Saṃsāra consists of the nature of going and coming, and so forth. He confirms this very point with the words "incomplete" (apūrṇa). The conceit of incompleteness is twofold: one is the loss of the autonomy of the Light, and the second is the nature of consciousness [arising] from that autonomy.
Therein, it is designated as a single entity because of the identity [of both] in the forfeiture of one's own true nature.]
(41) Due to the conceit of being incomplete, one brings about a state of atomicity (*aṇutva*) within oneself; thus, the impurity of atomization (*āṇavamala*) arises.
Furthermore, when there is a longing for that incomplete form to become complete, desire itself is here [defined as] the impurity (*mala*).

According to this principle: because of the perception of duality, that which is called *māyā*—which consists precisely in the manifestation of diverse objects of knowledge—is what bestows birth and experience.

However, when there is ignorance regarding the agent, that which is called *kārma* (karmic) arises; thus, through the power of *māyā* alone, this triad [of *māyā*, *kalā*, and *vidyā*] comes into being.

Thus, due to the grasping of the impurity (*mala*) through those auspicious and inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and due to the manifestation of the impurity of action (*kārmamala*), [the state] up to this limit—even by so much as an atom—is merely reinforced; this must be understood through subtle scrutiny.
Upon the cessation of that inequality, which consists in the non-recognition of one's own true nature, [there occurs] the cessation of the inequality of that Absolute (*anuttara*).

Because of the absence of the threefold impurity (*mala*). Due to the absence of impurity, the mental fluctuations such as anger and delusion are indeed of the very nature of the consciousness of the Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭāraka in his state of perfection. As it was said by the venerable Somānanda-pāda:
Thus:
"Likewise, whether in pleasure—which is the effect of the qualities *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—or in pain and delusion, I remain as the Supreme Śiva.
Thus it is said.
"Even in suffering, through expansion and by means of the union with fortitude for the sake of stability," and so forth.
For mental states such as anger [arise] because of their identity with the wonder of consciousness; otherwise, there would be no attainment of their very nature at all.

And because they are not separate from Him, these supreme sovereign goddesses are indeed the deities of the instruments (*karaṇadevatā*); performing various divine sports, they are the very rays of the sun that is Śiva. Likewise, they alone—[namely, the internal functions such as anger and so forth]—assume innumerable forms through their mutual intermingling, and [they manifest as] those respective acts of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
In rites such as those for killing or pacification, there are various peaceful or wrathful forms conceived as appropriate to each specific task—

such as the different types of *kṛtyā* (as in the phrase "Vāmā because she vomits forth saṃsāra," etc., the distinctions among the *kṛtyās* should be inferred by oneself)— who exist as deities [and their retinues as powers (*śakti*)]. As it has been said:
Those functions which have been proclaimed for the mantra that is extroverted are themselves proclaimed as the powers (śaktis) of this [mantra] when it is introverted.
Thus, those to be worshipped have been described as they appear in the scriptures of the Mata and other traditions, forming the retinue of the venerable Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka.
As it has been said on page 43:
"Kākavaktrā [is used] for eradication (*uccāṭana*)," and so forth; having begun thus, [it continues]: "These very rays of the God of gods are the bearers of the letters beginning with *ka*."

And so forth. However, those whose true nature is not fully understood conceal the wonder of consciousness— which, even within conceptual thought, has non-conceptuality as its sole essence— by entering into a state of anxious doubt through various forms of conceptualization, whether consisting of diverse clusters of phonemes and syllables, or taking the form of extremely terrible deities.
They bestow the state of being a beast bound by the snares of saṃsāra. As it has been said:
"The mistresses of the sacred seats (pīṭheśvarīs), who are most terrible, delude [beings] again and again.
Likewise:
"Causing the subtle elements (*aṇu*) to fall further and further down, being completely absorbed in the sense objects," and so forth. Likewise,
regarding that which arises from the collection of sounds (*śabdarāśi*)— [the collection of sounds beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*]— of the group of powers (*śaktivarga*):

Through the *kalās* (energies) of the *kādi* group—that is, by means of the letters beginning with *ka*—the state of being an object of enjoyment belongs to the group of powers (*śakti*). Having had his power eclipsed by these *kalās*, he who has fallen into that state is known as a bound soul (*paśu*).
(p. 44) Thus it is said.

Those very [energies], whose true nature has been known through the aforementioned reasoning, bestow the state of liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā). It has been stated accordingly: "When, however, in one place... [The term *ekatra* refers to the general *spanda*. The term *tasya* refers to the *ka*-group and so forth. The term *cakra* refers to that which begins with *ā* and ends with *ha*.].
When he has become firmly established, then, by restraining both dissolution and emergence, he attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, he becomes the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara).

Thus, the thorough knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) consists precisely in this: that within these mental states (*vṛtti*)—namely, anger and the rest—which at the moment of their arising are of a single non-conceptual form, as it has been said:
"When, even in those states where there is contact with the knower and the full range of cognitions..."
And she is perceived as remaining present through that repose in the fruit in that very manner.

Thus, even as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises— though it is colored by various specific words composed of a collection of phonemes— it is not joined with such a wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) whose nature is a mass of phonemes; for that [conceptual construction] belongs to the subject who consists of the prior, non-conceptual, and singular linguistic usage.
It would undermine its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are neither distinct from direct experience (*anubhava*) nor from one another;
rather, it is that very same single Lord who, through the coloring of various states differentiated by His sovereignty, is the master of the wheel of cognitions bearing names such as "the past."

Thus, liberation is indeed the very state of equality with Khecarī, and that is precisely the thorough knowledge of the nature of the Anuttara. Regarding the term "Anuttara," this is the intended meaning here: one should not think that if the essential nature itself is liberation, then there is no need for Khecarī;
for Khecarī is taught in the traditions as the state of Śakti, while the nature of the Anuttara exists above all paths.

Since liberation here consists in the thorough knowledge of one's own unsurpassed nature, and that is accomplished only through Khecarī, who is the form of the most subtle reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); there arises the state of being established in the bliss of both types of reflective awareness through the union and absorption (*samāpatti*) of the Supreme Goddess within the Self of Śiva, which is eternally manifest. For Śiva is...

It consists of the emission of the great mantra-power of the speech of others; it exists in identity with that which is filled with the flowers whose nature is the destruction of that power, emitted by the Supreme Goddess through the vibration (parisphuraṇa) of the power of that light of unsurpassed form, as well as its external power.
This blossoming, characterized by the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) and externally well-known, is joined with a creation that is intensely full and agitated,
consisting of such an activity; for indeed,
[it pertains] to all the internal and external organs.
