46) Whatever it enters, that very thing exists upon the ground of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), because it abides as the most internal of all; thus it is called "central" (*madhya*).

"That which does not find rest therein becomes like a flower in the sky"—by this statement, one should not think that a "flower in the sky" is something entirely separate; for even that, due to its identity with light (*prakāśa*), is not so [distinct]. That which exists as the vitalizing essence of all limbs, in the form of consciousness (*cetana*) by way of the life-force (*prāṇa*), is *ojas*.

That very [consciousness] is said to exist in all limbs as the animating principle, its vital energy (*vīrya*) being inseparable from them; furthermore, through the doors of the senses such as sight and hearing, it again enters into forms, sounds, and so forth, which serve to nourish it.
Precisely because they nourish it, those objects become awakeners of the fire of desire, which consists of the agitation of that vital energy. This is the intended meaning here.

From the mutual union of the network of faculties— consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), whose nature is speech and so forth, as well as the ear and so forth— there arises, through the conjunction of the grasped and the grasper,
the fire named *śuci*, produced from the friction of the moon and the sun.

According to this principle, through entry into the central abode (*madhyadhāmānupraveśa*), the bliss of emission (*visargānanda*) unfolds; and by virtue of being a semblance thereof, whatever other bliss is metaphorically designated—by means of which even that [other bliss] becomes a cause for entry into supreme consciousness—this is the meaning.
As it has been said:
From conversation and from the touch of the body... [text missing] ...from [the touch of the body].

And so forth. Furthermore, by means of even a single form—such as visible form (*rūpa*) or another—one who is augmented by previously accumulated power is capable of producing the aforementioned agitation regarding all objects; for everything is the self-nature of everything else.

Even through recollection, conceptualization, and so forth, agitation (*kṣobha*) indeed arises by virtue of the expansion of infinite objects such as sound that have entered the mind consisting of all things (*sarvamaya*).

Only that which possesses fully nourished great vitality (*mahāvīrya*) brings about the creation of nourishment (*puṣṭisṛṣṭi*), and not that which is incomplete or diminished—just as in the case of appropriate childhood and old age. And in the agitation of vitality, because vitality is one's own nature (*svamayatva*), [it is established].
Even though it is undivided, its nature consists solely of the great reflective awareness (*mahāvimarśa*) which is characterized by vibration (*spanda*) that transcends space and time;
it is essentially the nature of the perfectly full consciousness of Bhairava. [In this regard, the underlying intention is as follows:
"The knowledge of the bound soul (*pāśava-jñāna*) is said to arise through the degrees of contraction."
However, the cognition of the cloth, by virtue of the varying degrees of its manifestation, is a sublater [of that notion].
Such is the tradition of the Siddhas. In that regard, it is said:
"The universe shall be fully gratified by means of the desired Śiva-liṅga.
However, in the Kula and other systems of philosophy, this worship of the liṅga is prohibited; therein, regarding the worship of the liṅga—

They say that the supreme Lord’s *liṅga* consists of all the paths (*adhvan*) because it is through meditation that the entire expansion of the paths is internalized within it. Others, however, maintain that the body itself consists of all the paths;
therefore, direct realization is easily attained right there. What is the use of an external *liṅga* or other such objects, which are logically untenable? As they have said:

Having abandoned the Omniscient One who dwells within the chamber of the heart and is all-pervading, the one of limited intellect bows down to that which is inauspicious— such as stone and other such things— which is merely praiseworthy due to its association with the auspicious.

Thus [it is said]. Here, however, in the Trika system, there is no purpose whatsoever for the vision of supreme non-duality through either its affirmation or its negation. Furthermore, the presentation of the Kula system that has been made here serves solely to demonstrate [the author's] higher realization (*abhijñā*), as well as for the sake of illuminating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), since it is stated that "the Trika is superior to the Kula. As it has been said:
With this very intention, Bhaṭṭanāyaka also said:
"O Lord, how much fruit could this neuter Supreme Brahman bear,
were it not for Your beautiful Śakti, who impels its manly power?"
Thus, sovereignty consists of the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) and is the ground for the birth of happiness; for even the form [perceived] by the eyes [is of this nature].

By means of the method of separation from that great emission (*mahāvisarga*), which consists of the agitation of its own vitality (*vīrya*), [the following is the intended meaning]: first, within the Supreme Light— the emission that is the unsurpassed Self, resembling a waveless ocean, and unconditioned by the operations consisting of the desire to manifest and so forth at the prior limit— precisely because of the play of its initial manifestation...

Because there is no object of reflection distinct [from consciousness], the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cit-parāmarśa*) flashes forth, by which its sovereignty arises everywhere. Then, through the very majesty of its own sovereignty, the Supreme Lord—whose nature is the light of the Absolute (*anuttara-prakāśa*)—conceals His own true form by ascending through the stages beginning with the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
Emission (*sṛṣṭi*) is the externalization [of an object] in the form of blue, pleasure, and so forth; persistence (*sthiti*) is its relishing for some time;
withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the assimilation [of the object] into one's own self; dissolution (*laya*) follows from that, due to the pride of satisfaction in thinking "this object has been known";
and grace (*anugraha*) is resting within one's own self by means of the dissolution of even that externalized form. And it has been said:
"The separation from emission (*visarga*) is the supreme; the universe is said to consist of that.

Thus, it becomes a bestower of bliss. And for the ears, [there is bliss in] sweet songs and the like. In other senses as well, nothing else attains the state of being a complete creation, because [the consciousness] surges forth within its own self alone; and so it is.
For those whose vigor is not augmented by that [intense passion],
and who lack the intoxication consisting of the agitation of such vigor,
even the most beautiful form of a young woman, and even the low, sweet warbling of a woman’s voice trembling from her hips, are like stones.

(49) To the extent that [consciousness] does not culminate in full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) and does not become expansive (*vṛṃhaka*), it culminates in a limited aesthetic wonder (*parimitacamatkāra*). For where there is no wonder at all, there is mere insentience; whereas the penetration of excessive wonder constitutes [the state of consciousness].

Thus, that which consists of the agitation of *vīrya* (vital energy) is called "sensitivity" (*sahṛdayatā*). For one whose heart is nourished by an infinite expansion of *vīrya* established through the practice of attachment to enjoyment, there arises for him an extraordinary aesthetic wonder (*camatkriyā*) even in the face of suffering; this very state is the true aesthetic wonder, for it is that which is established within.

That very [pleasure] consisting of beloved children, happiness, and so forth—which is of the nature of *vīrya*—having attained expansion through the awakening of lamentation and the like that correspond to its cultivation, becomes of the nature of agitation; yet, because it will not exist again, it is the true essence of suffering, characterized by a special wonder born of the power of detachment. As it has been said:
"Even in suffering, through expansion...

[as it is said]. When, through the complete filling of the winds and other elements within all the channels of the senses, one enters the state of the great central Suṣumnā, one attains identity with the agitation of one's own power (*nija-śakti*). At that time—

When all duality has dissolved (p. 50), there occurs an entry into the wonder consisting of the I-consciousness (*ahantā*), which is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) overflowing with one's own perfect power.
Through entry into the union of the *Rudrayāmala*, whose nature is the bliss of the perfected creation,

there occurs the manifestation of the state of Bhairava— unwavering, waveless, and undisturbed— consisting of the firm ground (*dhruvapada*), by means of the dissolution of the emission (*visarga*) which is the potency of that Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*). For it is thus:
Even for that which consists of both genders in the form of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), and which has gained its support through the vigor, enthusiasm, and power of that [central channel],
at the time of trembling there arises an internal tactile bliss consisting of the desire to emerge from the agitation of all vital energy (*vīrya*),
which is witnessed by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). And this is not merely based upon an imagined body.

By means of the instruction on that direct realization (*abhijñāna*), there occurs an entry into this very state— the supreme *Parābhaṭṭārikā*, whose nature is the bliss of the union of Śiva and Śakti consisting of the Supreme Brahman, which is the firm ground attained through the dissolution of the emission of the power of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*). This will now be explained.
Then, one should worship the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*)...
[and so forth]. Likewise, (p.
"Just as [the tree] resides within the seed of the nyagrodha," and so forth;
likewise, "in such a way," and so forth.
It is also stated elsewhere:

O Queen of Gods, through the recollection of the fullness of a woman's pleasure—arising from licking, churning, and striking—even in the absence of external power (or even when external power is lacking), there occurs an immersion into that state through intense contemplation preceded by such remembrance; this is the meaning. Thus, there arises a flood of bliss.

Thus, for the reason that contact, when remembered from the past, is reflected within the channel of the central, uncreated power (*anāhata-parā-śakti*) in the field of that contact—even in the absence of its primary *śākta* contact—it becomes the agitator of the vitality (*vīrya*) consisting of the *śākta* contact existing within it; this is the intended meaning. Likewise:

That bliss of the Brahman-reality which concludes with the immersion into power (*śaktyāveśa*) following the agitation caused by the union of powers—that bliss is one's own; it is the bliss that arises at the end of the immersion produced by the joy of sexual union, which, having abandoned the conceptualization of "woman" and "man," rests solely in one's own Self. It belongs to the Self alone.
One should not conceive of harm from any other relative; rather, union with a woman is indeed the cause of manifestation—this is what is being stated.
Thus,
and likewise, it was also stated by the Great Hero, the Blessed Vyāsa,
on page 52.

"Of mine"—that is, of me whose nature is the Supreme Brahman—"the great" (mahat) means the gross (*sthūla*), which is perceived as an object of cognition; "the womb" (*garbha*) refers to the transferral of one's own potency characterized by pure consciousness (*saṃvit*).
"From that"—meaning from the essential nature (*svabhāva*) which is perceived as "this-ness" (*idantā*). The intended meaning here is: while perceiving the nature of the Supreme Brahman...

I illuminate the reality characterized by primordial nature (*prakṛti*), because even in its state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), it lacks luminosity without the penetration of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). Its nature as Brahman is excluded because it consists of a delimited object of knowledge;
yet, it is the Great Brahman (*mahadbrahma*) which is of the nature of "this-ness," serving as the cause for the differentiation of all the various states of the world, and is thus called "gross."
"For that which desires to produce the world, the womb is its locus. The womb is the Great Brahman; into it I place the seed.
From that, O Bhārata, arises the birth of all beings.

Thus it has been sung. Furthermore, in his own commentary, Somananda-pāda stated that the question regarding the Goddess as the stable state of passion (*rata-sthāyī*) was posed with the intention of referring to the great internal space consisting of that [passion], even though she is essentially one with the Supreme.

Thus, enough of this excessive elaboration regarding the discourse on the secret teachings of the Trika scriptures. This very Anuttara bestows the *siddhi* of the Kaulas, by the mere knowledge of which one attains equality with the *khecarī*, according to the method already stated. || 1 ||
O Lord, tell me this secret, the great secret;
for it is a secret because it is not manifest, existing within the cave of *māyā*, which consists of the non-recognition of one's own true nature.
"Even though it is present" (*sthitam api*); here the intention is this: for the Self, whose very nature is luminosity, shines forth in every respect;

it does not fail to shine in any part whatsoever. Thus, "unmanifest" (*aprakaṭam*) means that it has not attained a state of being fully realized within the heart. And yet, it is great and not hidden from anyone.

Because it consists of such wonder, the Blessed Lady Śuddhavidyā herself—who possesses the non-differentiation of the divisions consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—is Māyā, insofar as she is the power of the Supreme Lord whose nature is the reflective awareness characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), wherein the apprehension of difference is intensely reflected within the form of the triangle. I, having no other refuge, take shelter in that Goddess whom the sages declare to be the ancient Prakṛti, and whom those who know the secret Upaniṣads of the Vedas extol as Vidyā— she whose form bears the seal of Śaṅkara with half his body budding forth.

Thus [it is said]. And the Goddess Māyā, because she is of the nature of the "I-consciousness" (*idantā*) which has blossomed forth while being veiled by the "this-ness" (*iyam-idantā*), consists of the clear form of the cognition "this is I. For this very reason, her status as the "vital potency of mantra" (*mantravīryatva*) has been described elsewhere; for it is when a mantra rests within this state that it becomes possessed of the capacity to bestow its appropriate fruit. And it has been stated elsewhere:
One should not employ a mantra in the male principle (puṃstattva) nor in the supreme reality (paratattva);
for in the male principle it becomes inert, while in the supreme reality it is fruitless.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"This *yoginīhṛdaya* is the *liṅga* characterized by bliss;
through the union of the seed (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*), it gives birth to an indescribable consciousness."
Thus, [it is said: "It exists" (p.
Even *māyā*, the ground for the production of the world, is in reality nothing but *vidyā*; this is because it has been stated that it is to be understood as being of such a nature.
Because it is not fully known, and because its three corners—the knower and so forth—are concealed by the majesty of non-duality, it is called the "Great Cave" (*mahāguhā*).
In reality, that very [Cave] is the locus of worship, the trident (*triśūla*) in the sense of the Triad (*trika*). As it has been said:
"That Great Vidyā is triangular; she is the Triad (*trikā*), the abode of all aesthetic flavors (*rasa*)."
This very state of emission (*visargapada*)—by means of attaining that abode, the stream of bliss flows forth from the Kaulika power known as autonomy;
thus he says, "the state of emission. Her state of being the state of emission is explained in the *Tantrāloka* as follows:
"And that very [power] is her state of emission, because of the sequence of the arising of bliss."
The surging state of being extends as far as the power of action (kriyā-śakti) has become manifest.
Thus, by virtue of surging forth in succession, the universe, even as it surges outward, appears ever-new; and it has been stated elsewhere:
"Sprinkled by the stream of the bliss of emission resulting from absorption into this *liṅga*, that very universe becomes eternally ever-new."
Thus, the sequence of withdrawal is attained here through contemplation alone. "All flavors" means the nature of both enjoyment and liberation.
The greatness of creation here lies precisely in the absence of duality. Therefore, one should worship the Triad.

Thus it is said. And so, within such a great cave—which consists of the heart of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), which is the form of the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*), and which is the birthplace of the universe—one exists as one's own creative wonder in the form of *maha-a*.
This which is the secret: by means of this, there is that sovereignty (*svātantrya*) which is the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), characterized by the uninterrupted radiance of Bhairava.

For the light of consciousness (prakāśa), whose nature consists of the wonder of the innate, unartificial, supreme power of mantra (vīrya) beyond speech and mind, finds its rest in self-reflection (ātmavimarśa) through the process of withdrawing from all objective entities (bhāva) back into its own essential form; this is the characteristic of the "I" (aham),
the full subjectivity (pūrṇāhantā), as described in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*.
This supreme Speech (Parā Vāk) is consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness, flowing by its own inherent force;
it is the true I-consciousness in which the entire multitude of phonemes has been withdrawn from beginning to end.
Thus it is said:
"The resting of consciousness within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahaṃbhāva).
That very thing is the secret, the supreme mystery; for instance, according to the sequence of emanation:

Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka, who rests in an unmodified, unsurpassed, and eternal form, who is the life-force of the entire web of kalās, who is the primordially established and partless essence of all—He alone is [the ultimate reality].
"By way of expansion" (*prasarātmanā*) means by way of the surging forth of one's own self in the form of vibration (*spanda*). As it has been said:
"The unified form of those two is known as *saṃghaṭṭa*;
that alone is called the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), from which the universe is emitted."
Thus, the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*) alone is called the supreme emission (*paravisarga*). As it has been said:
"That supreme Kauliki power which is described as the internal desire to emit (*visisṛkṣā*), that very power, by virtue of agitation (*kṣobha*), certainly attains the nature of emission."
Thus it is said. In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
the Śakti-kuṇḍalikā and likewise the Prāṇa-kuṇḍalikā.
At the terminal point of the visarga, however, is what is called the supreme Kuṇḍalinī;
it is called the void of Śiva, the supreme Brahman, and the abode of the Self.
"The Lord's emanations alone are the fluctuations of creation and withdrawal.

Thus, assuming the state of *visarga* (the emission) through its form— since *visarga* itself consists of the power (*śakti*) of the letter *ha*, which is the nature of *kuṇḍalinī*— it further assumes, as the non-dual knower of the expansion of that power, the nature of the *bindu*, which is the form of the individual (*nara*).
It expands. Likewise, "again" means that just as previously everything that was to be done was emitted into the fire of emptiness,
immediately after that, this is called the *āṇava* [state], which is the resting of the mind.

The state of being directed toward objects such as those seen or heard within one's own consciousness is called the awakening of the mind (cittasaṃbodha); it consists essentially of the fullness of the unfolding of Śakti.
Therein, due to being oriented toward that [reality], through the impact of that object, and because of its firm rooting within the heart,
there occurs an immersion into Śiva by virtue of the fullness [of that state] and the dissolution of the limited mind.
This supreme Śāmbhava emission, known as the dissolution of the mind, arises from the immeasurable abode of the orientation toward the future, as previously described.

that for whom the universe does not exist at all as "mine" (*mama*), because [for him] everything is of the singular nature of the burden of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*).

Because its nature is solely self-luminous: *amā* means that where *mā*—which signifies "non-existent," "measurement" (*māna*), and "negation"—is absent; and because it is eternally risen, where there is no dissolution (*saṃhāra*), she is called the Blessed Lady *Amā*. A bahuvrīhi compound is [contained] within another bahuvrīhi. For the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), even in the conventional usage of means of knowledge and so forth, is composed entirely of supreme power (paraśaktimaya) because he is in every respect of the nature of non-duality (advaitarūpa); therefore, the address [to him] is indeed [an address] to oneself. 1½.

O Lord of Gods, tell me of that power residing in the heart, the Kaulikī, the mistress of the Kula, by means of which I may attain satisfaction.

The meaning is that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the foundation for everything—blue, pleasure, and so forth [where "blue" refers to the external and internal object of perception, and "body" refers to the subject; the point is that consciousness is the locus of support for both]. Furthermore, the supreme foundation for the body, vital breath, intellect, and so on, is the heart which is the self of consciousness. Its various and manifold forms are merely distinctions imagined through its own innate sovereignty.
The cognitions of jars and other objects are situated within that; this power, consisting of radiant manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), is the Mistress of the *Kula*.
She is the bestower of radiance upon the body, the vital breath, pleasure, and so forth; she is the vitality of the circle of deities beginning with Brāhmī;
she is the central-most form of the entire network of sense-faculties and channels; and she exists as the *liṅga*-nature of the pericarp, which is the place of birth.

And she is Kaulikī because she exists within that very *kula* (family/lineage) as its form; or rather, *kaula* is that which arises from *kula* and has *akula* as its essence— that which exists within her through identity is Kaulikī, for *kula* is indeed established upon the light of *akula*.
It is so. As it has been said:
"But rather, through the touch of the power of the Self" (Svacchandatantra, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, Kārikā 8).

The syntactic connection is as follows: "I obtain a satisfaction consisting of supreme bliss; I become one whose essence is the savor of sovereignty and the peace of supreme non-duality.

and by means of this instruction on the nature thus described, one recognizes one's own essential form as the Lord (*īśvara*).

The "sustenance of the universe" (*viśvasya dhāraṇam*) means its maintenance within one's own self, as well as its nourishment by way of being fixed upon the wall of one's own self; for it has been stated elsewhere: "By this very [Self] one sustains the universe through the application of sustaining and nourishing. Likewise, its "sustenance and nourishment by that" [the universe] occurs because it flashes forth everywhere as consisting of the universe, such that the universe is fixed upon the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*).

"The locus of the manifestation of consciousness," so say the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta elsewhere. Likewise, it is "of the nature of self-reflection (vimarśa) by its own self within itself alone. Furthermore, it consists of the resonance of the Great Mantra (mahāmantra).

Herein, there is the predominance of the Possessor of Power (śaktimat); however, in the process of expansion, there is the predominance of Power (śakti) in the form of Paśyantī and the others, while in the process of withdrawal, [there is the predominance of the Possessor of Power].

Furthermore, when there is a contraction of power (śakti), the predominance of the possessor of power (śaktimat) is indeed easily understood. It was stated previously that [the state] takes the form of "maha-a" by way of withdrawal; this will become clear on page 64.
And it is right at the beginning. This is the intended meaning here:

*parā* (the Supreme) means that which is of the nature of the Absolute (*anuttara*), free from desire, and full. The power of will (*icchā-śakti*)—which flows forth by virtue of its own essential existence because it consists of the act of acceptance—is also of the very nature of the Supreme Absolute; this is the meaning. He states the reason for this right there:
"Non-different from Bhairava. In this regard, the sequence is as follows: when she is oriented toward the *icchā* (will) power, she is that very *parā*;

when oriented toward the *jñāna* (knowledge) power, she is *paśyantī*; when oriented toward the *kriyā* (action) power while remaining [in that state], she is *madhyamā*; and when remaining [as such], she is *vaikharī*.
Thus, the Blessed Consciousness, expanding forth from her own essential nature...
It is called the power of the will (paricchā-śakti), which is non-different from Bhairava.
Its nature consists of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and so forth, which is the state of having the quality of expansion;
it assumes the forms of Parā, Parāparā, and Aparā, as well as Paśyantī and the others (by "and so forth," Madhyamā and Vaikharī are included).
Thus, O Goddess, this very investigation into the nature of the form of its expansion is called "the question," for you are the one who poses that question consisting of that very essence.
Having stated the true nature of that expansion, he speaks of the true nature of the mutual question and answer, beginning with "tasya" and so forth:
"That very act of reflective awareness which consists of the form of expansion is declared to be the supreme, taking the form of question and answer."
Starting again from that very point of non-recognition of the other, he describes the subsequent nature [in its distinct form] with the words "tadevāpara" and so forth:
"Again,
repeatedly, it effects the withdrawal into the dense bliss of supreme consciousness."
The form of Bhairava, in which every possible expansion is entirely contained,
perpetually unfolds through the very nature of each individual speaker.
Since these two— expansion and withdrawal— are not fashioned by time, this reality,
consisting of question and answer, is indeed of a single nature.

Thus, the venerable Gurus [the venerable Śambhunātha and others] have previously delineated this very essence of the heart of the Trika (Ṣaḍardha), which is endowed with the unsurpassed relationship to the Supreme.

"O Goddess" (*devi*) is as before. She whose "great portion" (*mahābhāga*) there is— she who, when cultivated through the study of the teachings already stated and those yet to be stated, bestows the great power known as supreme sovereignty (*pārameśvaryā*).
It is so. "Mahat" refers to that whose portion or part is the form of Anāśrita Śiva, who is renowned for his nature as the Great and the Supreme-Great;
for the power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī śaktiḥ) indeed contains within her womb the infinite thirty-six principles and so forth.
This is the intended meaning here, as it has been stated:
At the end of his own time, Sadāśiva, having seized all that is moving and unmoving, ascends through the Bindu, Ardhendu, and Nirodhikā, and dissolves into the Nāda.
But by means of the function of the end of sound (nādānta), the Sound (nāda) forcibly pierces the aperture of Brahmā and,
having taken up all that is moving and unmoving, goes to dissolution in the principle of Śakti.
Śakti dissolves again into Vyāpinī when its own time has passed;
thereafter, by that very same sequence, it dissolves into Anāśrita.
That too goes to dissolution in the state called Sāmya (Equilibrium), which is beyond the mind;
that power known as Sāmya remains eternal, undecaying, and composed of subtle parts.
"That form which is united with the mind (sāmanasa) is the all-pervading Brahman, the state of equilibrium.

The "Great One" (mahān)—the specific principle consisting of the intellect (buddhi) and so forth—is the "part" (bhāga), whose form depends upon the subtle division (vibhāgakalā); for the supreme consciousness is indeed a single, dense power (ekaghana-śakti).
When it serves as the locus for the effects of diverse objects of knowledge fashioned by its own sovereignty, it is called *buddhi*.
As it was said by the venerable Somānanda:

Regarding another point of contention, some here have formulated the following alternative view: "Pure light is devoid of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*); for if it possessed reflective awareness, it would follow that it is conceptual (*savikalpa*). To explain: knowledge (*jñāna*) is that which knows; it is consciousness (*bodha*), which is a function of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).

How could there be such a thing without an intellect possessing functions? Therefore, the intellect is born from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and is insentient (*jaḍa*); and by that [insentient intellect], [pure light cannot be known]."
The connection with that Śiva-tattva is as stated by the venerable Somānanda-pāda in the *Pūrvapakṣavyavasthā*:
"Without the intellect (buddhi), how can there be cognition? That intellect is born from Prakṛti."
And if it is argued that there is no connection between him and that [action]...

Thus it is said. Here, others have offered this reply: "In the state of *apara* (the lower), when differentiated objects manifest through non-recognition (*akhyāti*), it is called *buddhi*; but in the undifferentiated, consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), its innate nature is *bodha* (pure awareness). Here, moreover, the intended meaning is as follows:
for subjects consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka*, *buddhi* [is that which exists] within the state of the full subject (*pūrṇapramātṛtā*) as a form that is not an object of cognition.
By the phrase "mere consciousness" (*bodhamātra*), it is shown that even at the time of cognition, the existence of Śiva persists.
That intellect (*buddhi*) which is again subtle, all-pervasive, and situated everywhere—
that knowledge consisting of pure consciousness belongs to that Śiva as his innate nature, since it exists even when the ordinary intellect (*prākṛtabuddhi*) arises.
Because that [effect] does not exist without that [cause], it is always [present].

Thus: "part" (*bhāga*) means division; where that exists in a form, by the word *bhāga* ending in the possessive suffix *-aka* (i.e., *bhāgavat*), a differentiated form is expressed. And since in a differentiated body, delimitation occurs precisely through mutual exclusion, the ascertainment of an object consisting of clarity, which arises in the intellect, [pertains to] those things existing in the world such as the beautiful and the non-beautiful.

[The word "another" (*apara*) means distinct. It arises not by touching entities at all, but rather by excluding them; for the cognition of the state of pleasure consists of such forms as mastery over the *dharmas* and so forth.

It is sung that [the world] consists of *sattva* and is an outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) of the *guṇas*. However, if one penetrates even into its innermost core, then by means of that very gateway, there would indeed be a constant arising within the abode of supreme bliss (*paramānandadhāman*) which resides at its root.

For this very reason, [there arises] the Great Bliss (*mahas*), which consists of the joy of the universe, characterized by omnipresent, indivisible, perfect, unobstructed, and independent sovereignty. Ā—

The Lord’s Portions: [In this context, indeed, by the statement "the non-empty is empty," one should rest in the state of consciousness itself—which is not a mere support and is untainted by the differentiation of objective entities—and having attained repose within the functioning of the quality of *sattva*, one should remain resting in innate bliss, directly realizing one's own self in its absolute isolation. 1. Thereafter, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the limited consciousness (*rāksaṃvit*):

According to the principle that "they have undergone transformation," when the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), arises from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* by way of exhalation (*recaka*),
it may somehow, due to its outward orientation, depart from its own bliss— which is recognized as the subject (*mātṛ*)—

and remain in a state devoid of bliss (*nirānanda*). Then, it arises again through another [process] within the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is of the nature of the downward breath (*apāna*).

One should contemplate the bliss produced by the object of cognition (*prameya*), so that even during the stage of the emergence of the object of cognition, one may abide in supreme bliss (*parānanda*). Then, having rested for a moment in the heart,
through the friction (*saṃghaṭṭa*) consisting of the mutual fusion of the various objects of cognition appearing as blue, pleasure, and so forth—

One should abide established in the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda). 4. Even beyond that, intent upon swallowing the flood of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, and devoted to their union, one should contemplate the bliss recognized as the subject (pramātṛ);
one should reflect upon it as being essentially resting within one's own self alone, and thus abide as consisting of Great Bliss (mahānanda). 5. Even beyond that...

One should abide in the bliss of the universe, which is the manifestation of one's own self that synthesizes all this; as it is stated in the *Tantrāloka* regarding the nature of the bliss of the universe:
"That wherein there is no differentiation whatsoever, and from which the universe radiates forth."
That which is unappropriated consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar.
"That which possesses no primary connection whatsoever with meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the like—
Śambhu has declared this to us as the bliss of the world (*jagadānanda*). [This refers to the definition of bliss on page 69.]

Since whatever pleasure there may be is obtained by entering into the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*)— the supreme abode of great bliss and liberation— and by being perceived in that manner as a mere partial form; so it has been stated by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa:

"I bow to that God, the ocean of bliss, whose single drop (*bindu*) is whatever joy whatsoever is seen here in the three worlds, consisting of existence, non-existence, and the state beyond existence. (Verse 61) Thus,
according to the previously mentioned method, that very form which is called *maha-a* is indeed what is to be worshipped by the Supreme Lord.

That which is "I," nourished by its own wonder (*svacamatkāra*), is itself the Śākta body, and it is said to be the very form of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*). For this very reason, she alone is the Supreme Sovereign who hears everything,
abiding through her existence known as hearing (*śravaṇa*).

The sovereignty known as the synthesis and contemplation— which consists of bringing about a state of identity with the entire mass of sounds, each distinct in its own sequence and clearly manifesting within the cavity of the ears— is [the means]; for without it,
even while hearing specific sounds lost in a tumultuous din, one thinks, "I do not hear."

Thus the cognizer employs the conventional expression [“I heard it”]. However, since the synthesis has as its object merely the general clamor, the conventional usage “it was heard right there” occurs. In reality, however, that sound of clamor, upon entering the space of the auditory organ, does not [reveal] the phonemes.
If one were to cause [the letters] to enter [into the cognition] in that manner, there would only be a confused clamor (kalakala) exceeding those [individual] phonemes.
Therefore, it is the single, sequential-less, conceptualized, and unreal portion—the sentence-sphoṭa—that produces a cognition regarding its own denoted object of such a kind.
Those various phonemes, which are by nature fleeting and established solely through conceptual construction, do not produce a cognition regarding that meaning; enough of this.
By means of discourses on that.

Thus is the doctrine of *sphoṭa* accepted by the grammarians. Furthermore, when there is a desire to express specific phonemes (*varṇa*), a confused din (*kalakala*) would simply not arise due to the absence of its cause; for even if it were the effect of a word consisting of distinct phonemes produced by that desire to speak, the production of a similar sound [as a confused din] would be impossible. In every respect, those very phonemes exist in that distinct form.

For one who is intent on attending to that synthesis, there will indeed be a perception of some degree of clarity regarding those things which, being in the process of being synthesized, are designated by the term "clamor" (*kalakala*).
Thus, it is *saṃkalana* alone that is effective here; and it is that very Goddess, the Supreme Parā Parameśvarī, who performs this *saṃkalana*.
As it has been said:
"Having seized that power, the mantras... (*Svacchanda Tantra* 2.10).
And so forth. In reality, indeed, the forms of hearing, seeing, speaking, grasping, and so on, belong to the Blessed Lady alone. As it has been said:
"By means of this very [consciousness], one perceives form, taste, smell, touch, sound, and sexual union; what remains here [that is not she]?"

Thus it is stated by the Supreme Lord in the Vedānta (*Kaṭhopaniṣad* 2.3). However, "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) does not merely consist of listening to phonemes in the form of distinct, indistinct, high-pitched, or faltering sounds. For instance, the venerable Supreme Lord—
In the *Śrī Svacchanda Śāstra*, at the very occasion of determining the divisions of recitation (*japa*), he has described it in this same way:
"That which is heard by oneself alone is known as 'whispered' (*upāṃśu*); for here, in the state of the middle channel (*madhyamā-pada*), one hears it oneself and no other."

As it has been stated (p. 72): when the effort of the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and so forth becomes distinct, through the conjunction and separation of the lips, teeth, and other parts, even if the utterance of sound is extremely subtle, there would be hearing by those standing very close by; thus, the consequence is that the sound necessarily possesses audibility.
"That which is heard by others is proclaimed as 'with sound' (saśabda)," so it has been said; for in this case, there is no distinction such as "near" and so forth.
However, even when there is a conjunction of the lips, palate, and other organs—which is the object of perception solely for another subject—the [sound] belongs to the self alone.

Even if there were hearing [of the sound] by another, nevertheless this results only in a middle state—because there is no acquisition of an external nature for the phoneme (*varṇa*). For indeed, it is only when produced from the impact of air that the phoneme becomes manifest; yet in that case, the impact of the air does not extend to the point of attaining externality. Furthermore, the movement of the lips and so forth is also not present there.

One may enter into the aspect of the [external] colors; however, that [state] would remain established solely within one's own self, occupying the place of momentary gestures, winks, manual movements, and so forth.

However, even when phonemes are produced through the conjunction of distinct articulatory places (*sthāna*), instruments (*karaṇa*), and efforts (*prayatna*), if there were a distinction between high and low pitch (*tāra-mandra*) among sounds according to their degrees of intensity, and if they were heard from far or near, they would be heard by others in every respect; thus, this [state] belongs strictly to the level of *vaikharī*. This is what follows from the context. That very same [level]...
[The characteristic of hearing: The Supreme Goddess (Parameśvarī), through the application of address, is clearly stated to be of the nature of Śakti.
She clarifies this very point through reflection—stating that she is "clearly of the nature of Śakti" by means of the passage beginning with "nara-śakti"—that she consists of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva.
Among these, Nara is characterized primarily by duality, while Śakti is characterized primarily by both duality and non-duality.
Śiva is solely characterized by non-differentiation. As it has been said: "And when there is the manifestation of division, His body is declared to be threefold.
Here, the nature of will, knowledge, and action is easily understood through the sequence of emanation; for all this [is Śiva].

In that context, that which is merely the threefold form abiding within itself is primarily (mukhyatayā) associated with an insentient nature. (The intention of the word "primarily" is this: that which is insentient has not yet attained its own existence within itself.)

In the ultimate sense, that which is essentially attached to light is primarily "insentient" (jaḍa) by virtue of appearing as something external at this moment. Just as one says, "The jar exists as a human being" [the distinction here is that "jar" refers to conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), while "this" refers to non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*)], this alone is the remainder concerning the subject of the first person (*prathamapuruṣa*). That which...
Furthermore, even that which appears as "this" finds its fulfillment in the reflective awareness of "this-ness," which is a distinct discernment;
that resting within one's own essential nature, the reflective awareness "I am this," is precisely what constitutes the self.
Thus,
through that [power], this determination "this is a jar" appears as the supreme power of the Lord, which is not distinct from name and form, just like the Self itself, and not as a mere "this-ness."
Thus it is said. Herein is the distinction: those which are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) constitute the cause of differentiation within the nature of the Person (*nara*).
Furthermore, that power of determination which thinks "this is [it]," being non-differentiated, is the very essence of power;
for this [power] is non-distinct from the Self (*ātman*), because it is veiled by the sense of "I" (*ahantā*). This is so because it is addressed as the object of invocation.

That empowered form (*tacchāktaṃ rūpam*) which is designated by the word "you" (*yuṣmacchabda-vyapadeśyam*), wherein the state of "this-ness" (*idaṃbhāva*)—which is distinct from that [pure subjectivity]—is covered over by the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) through the act of addressing (*āmantraka*), is indeed what stands as "thou" (*tvam*). For in this context, this very thing is the meaning of the word "you" and the reality of the act of addressing. To illustrate: just as "I" stand, so too does "this one" [stand]; thus, it belongs to him as well.

Identifying himself with the freedom (*svātantrya*) that is the wonder of the sense of "I" as delimited by our own form, through the very wonder of an uninterrupted "I," he addresses [the disciple] and designates him with the second person used in its literal sense; for this is indeed...

The Blessed One, who is both supreme and non-supreme, abides as "I" within the self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃvimarśa*) of absolute freedom that is entirely uninterrupted and independent of external manifestation. (And so it is stated in the *Vīrūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"The three types of persons—the lowest, the middling, and the highest—are mutually distinct.")
But from me, the Great Person, who consists of self-reflection, nothing exists externally.
That form which appears as "I," seemingly divided and characterized by the exclusion of what you call "other," is merely a distinction of parts; for I am one and eternal.
Thus [ends the section on] the arising of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā). In this regard, the supremacy of the Person (Puruṣa) has been stated:
"Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)."

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the use of the word "I" (*asmi*), it is stated that I am superior even to both the perishable and the imperishable forms; for [one might object]: "In the phrase 'I remain,' it is clearly perceived that only the egoity of the body and so forth is intended; how then can there be the emergence of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) here?
To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth. This, however, is the underlying meaning here:

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is indeed the essence of the imperishable entity, which is a dense mass of autonomous luminosity (*svatantra-prakāśa-ghana*). That very reality, through its own sovereignty, even when assuming the state of identifying with the body, is called "I" (*aham*), in order to illuminate that it does not abandon its primordial nature.
As for the body and so forth, their ultimate reality is clearly one of fragmentation; how, then, could there be the designation "I am" (*asmīti*) with respect to them?
In all these cases (p. 76), the limited body and so forth are designated by the word "I," because their identity [with the Self] is contradicted by direct perception itself.

Thus, such a form, which is essentially self-manifesting— meaning it is self-luminous and not dependent on manifestation through distinctions such as the forms of humans or powers— is of the nature of Śiva; for this very reason, there is neither anything deficient nor anything additional in this consciousness, which consists of the manifestation of its own self-awareness.

[Consisting of both difference and non-difference: Since that which is of the nature of non-manifestation does not enter into the pure consciousness (cinmaya), whereas that which is of the nature of manifestation does indeed enter into the essential nature of consciousness—the meaning is thus established. Furthermore, in relation to that, even neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) is nothing at all—this being so, by means of attaining a firm foundation in the state of "non-existence" which is indefinable as "this-ness" (*idantā*), and which stands as the middle point between increase and decrease.

[Accretion (*upacaya*) belongs to the light (*prakāśa*), diminution (*apacaya*) to the jar (*ghaṭa*), and neutrality (*mādhyasthya*) to "you" (*yuṣmad*). The referents of "I" (*asmadartha*) consist in the non-interruption of that cognition; the referent of "you" (*yuṣmadartha*), even when interrupted, is exactly like this. For this very reason, "you" and "I" are said to be without gender (*aliṅga*). Through the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of number and so forth residing in the body, they incorporate within themselves the powers of the supreme (*parā*) and the intermediate (*aparā*).
The application of number, however, is logically consistent (p.
For instance, one should contemplate that which appears as differentiated through the projection of its own sovereignty as being one with its infinite bodies and so forth.

The forms "we two," "you two," "we," and "you"—which arise from increase and so forth—are impossible to apply even figuratively to that which resides within the body, because it is impossible for the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) to possess deficiency or excess; for indeed, everything is of the nature of all things.
Thus, even insentient human bodies, having abandoned their former form, become partakers of the Śākta and Śaiva forms—just as when one says, "O stones, listen!"; "Meru! [is heard].
For there is the cognition: "I am Śikhariṇā," and "I, Caitra, speak.

Thus, even that which is of the nature of *Śakti* (the power), though its form is that of the referent of *yuṣmad* (the second person pronoun), indeed assumes the nature of the human subject (*narātmatā*). In this way, having abandoned its form as *Śakti*, [the word] "you" (*tvaṃ*)—whose power of fearlessness and fortitude has departed—is understood even through the non-addressive mode (*anāmantraṇayoga*). By the term "bhavān" (your honor), the feet are the teachers.

Because there exists a cognition through such specific notions as "it" (*iti*) and so forth— which has as its object the first person (*prathama-puruṣa*) consisting of the human nature appropriate for the subsequent state— even for one who has abandoned the form of Śakti, there would also be the nature of Śiva consisting of the "I" (*ahaṃ*). Friend.

Because of the conviction that "I am indeed the very essence of the body and mind within my beloved," one enters the body— which consists of the human (nara) and power (śakti)— even though it is of the nature of Śiva, as if its conscious nature (cidrūpa) were abandoned. For in such expressions as "Who am I?",
"This is I," "Oh, I!", "Shame on me!", or "Oh, for me!", the sovereignty (svātantrya) is made manifest as the uninterrupted "I-ness" (ahamiti).

Primarily, however, it is precisely a fragmented "this-ness" (*idantā*) that is perceived where the emergence of the goddess Aparā occurs, as in [the utterance] "O, I am," and so forth; this is merely the touch of the vibration of the Parāparā Śakti. But in the case of Śiva, each preceding state is invariably present in the subsequent one; thus, the human form is perceived with manifest clarity.
One would indeed be able to ascend the path of Śākta and Śāmbhava, but not by ascending in the reverse order;
for such an ascent consists of clear perception, as each [level] retains its own specific nature.
Because it consists of three aspects, each of these triads assumes the form of one, two, or many. For it has been said:
"A single reality becomes twofold; being twofold, it becomes manifold.

Indeed, when there is oneness of essence, because there is no counter-correlative (*apratiyogitva*), Śiva-hood arises; whereas when there is multiplicity, Śakti-hood arises upon the possibility of a counter-correlative to Śiva-hood.

Indeed, within the very nature of the one human being, there exists differentiation: "a jar," "two jars," "jars," and even "jar, cloth, and stone"; likewise, "he stands," "they two stand," and "they stand. This is the manifestation of the power of action through the one alone; as it has been said:
"Having made the manifold into one, who would not be liberated from bondage?"

Thus, for this very reason, when there is a simultaneous reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the three—Nara, Śakti, and Śiva—in a single locus, there is indeed an entry into the nature of each subsequent one, because in reality that [subsequent state] alone constitutes its ultimate essence. This is the sequence of cognition: "He and you both remain," and "He, you, and I all remain."

Just as that which is the essence of uncreated refinement (*akṛtaka-saṃskāra*) is followed by grammarians through their technical definitions, so too, even in the case of words in one's own vernaculars— such as those of the Buddhists, Andhras, Draviḍas, and others, where not even the name of refinement remains— it is this very same [principle] that applies.

The sequence of the recitation and the sequence of the words follow from the very root the realization within the heart; since that realization consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it causes even the verbal expression itself to be understood as having such a nature, as I have said:
"Speech that does not reach the heart is no speech at all."
Thus, in every respect, this cognition is indeed uncreated, as it has been said:
"Without them, there would be no word, no object, nor even the movement of consciousness.
This is also stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara-tantra*.
Thus, having presided over the entire aggregate of atoms,
Śambhu has declared that the power of Śaṅkara is indeed one, existing exactly as it is.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śrītantrasamuccaya*:

"This entire universe always exists as the immersion (*āveśa*) of Man, Śakti, and Śiva, in every respect, for those who follow the sequential path (*kramin*) and for all those possessed of omniscience during worldly transaction."

Thus [it is said]. That very [reality], consisting of the nature of Man (nara), Power (śakti), and Śiva, has been shown through the instruction of the tradition for clear realization as "Man, Power, and Śiva. Indeed, this entire sequence of realization is created by the sovereign freedom of the Supreme Lord’s will.

Thus, enough of this [discussion] which captivates the hearts of only a few sensitive people who are purified by the descent of the supreme power (para-śaktipāta), possessed of great learning, and guided by instruction—[“sahṛdayāḥ” meaning sensitive listeners; “katipayāḥ” meaning a few]. As it has been said:
"Worshipers exist by the hundreds; devotees exist by the thousands."
"Only two or three are worthy vessels of grace and have attained confidence, not five.

[Thus it is said. This has been explained as a consequence of what followed from what preceded; listen, O Goddess. Regarding what was stated concerning "the answer also"—namely, how there can be an "unsurpassed" (anuttara) answer—the reply to that is: that which is unsurpassed even in relation to the proximate answer.

For, according to the sequence previously stated, even the "subsequent" (uttara) must exist as identical with the "supreme" (anuttara), and not otherwise. Therefore, even disregarding the subsequent—using the genitive case in the sense of disregard—the very form of the subsequent is indeed the form of the supreme, its state being disregarded. For this differentiation, which takes the form of the subsequent, is in fact utterly [non-existent].
p.
82) Having resorted to the state of non-duality (*abhedabhūmim adhiśayya*—that is, having taken recourse to it), one should become such [i.e., assume the form of differentiation].
As it has been said:
The determination of "otherness" [is the rule of differentiation; "others" refers to distinct entities]:
as long as an other has not been made one's own, it cannot be established as such, because an other that is not cognized remains merely an other.

Thus, the same applies to the subsequent portion of the text (referring to that which is yet to be stated)— it is *anuttara* (transcendent), for even by that it cannot be transcended. Even by the *paśyantī* level (referring to the fact that the reality of luminosity is indeed the reality of reflective awareness, and that very reflective awareness takes the form of the first unfolding— as it has been said):
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
it is the light of its own nature within, subtle, and never departing from its state.

Thus, that very [power], which exists in the mind as the nature of *vivakṣā*—consisting of the desire to communicate a meaning—and which is called "the intermediate" (*madhyamā*), resides in the form of consciousness (*vijñāna*). And this is eternally one and common to all, situated between the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. As it has been said:
"In its state of being consciousness, that word exists here through the desire to speak (*vivakṣayā*)."
That very [energy] is called the Middle One (madhyamā) through the sequence of the drop (bindu), the sound (nāda), and the breath (marut).

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, that very same [power], having reached the vocal channel (*vaktranāḍī*), is called *vaikharī*, which is unique to the phonemes such as the letter *ka* differentiated by locations such as the throat;
she alone takes the form of the book (*grantha*). Therefore, since this [book] is of the nature of its expansion (*prasara*), how can it be used to determine [the truth]? And it has been said:
When the wind is released through the various locations [of articulation], speech— assuming the form of phonemes—
is produced by speakers and is bound to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus,
because the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) is the first to manifest, this very [state] is the unsurpassed (anuttara) even for my subsequent [work].

The ultimate reality is that which follows the impelling of the trident and so forth; just as the divisions of the directions and such are known by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun, O Dear One, Śiva is known through his power in the same way.
Thus: [this refers to] that supreme immersion (*samāveśa*) which arises through the trident (*triśūla*), consisting of the three powers (*śakti*) in a state of mutual fusion (*lolībhūta*).
As it has been said:
"Therefore, the three powers in a state of fusion constitute that very trident."
By swiftly entering into which, the yogi becomes stainless.

Thus [it is said]. As to what that unsurpassed place of rest is, he says: "From which this Kaulika rule arises"—the *kaulika* being of the nature of *Kula* and *Akula*, as previously explained; and because it is being prescribed, it is a "rule" (*vidhi*) consisting of the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*), which is the form of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), wherein hundreds of millions of emanations and so forth are internalized.
From which this very thing has issued forth—
that which was stated on page 84:
"That in which all is, from which all is, who is all, and who is from all."
And salutation to that Self of all, who is eternally composed of everything.

In that regard, since this entire collection of effects originates from a single agent, the statement "from whom all [proceeds]" establishes the universal agency of the one reality; likewise, the statement "in whom all [resides]" establishes its omniscience with respect to this multitude of entities consisting of extremely diverse appearances.

The meaning is this: within that luminous Self—which possesses the nature of being solely the single cognizer persisting through all states such as pleasure and so forth, existing as this or that by virtue of the mere condition of being perceived—this very multiplicity resides, which flashes forth by its power; this [is indicated] by the phrase "that which is everything."

By the phrase "independent of any other material cause (upādāna) distinct from his own mere will," its independence is stated. And by the phrase "he who [shines] everywhere," the meaning is that since he alone shines forth within every object of knowledge, there is no modification of his essential nature (svarūpa). Furthermore, by the phrase "he who is eternally composed of all," the fact that he is the self of all is established even when no effect is being produced; such is the sense here.

The intended meaning is as follows: "All is one; the omniscient, the creator of all, devoid of material cause and devoid of limiting conditions, eternally manifests as the self of all"—thus it is stated in the commentary by the illustrious Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha. Regarding the word *sarvam* (all):
for instance, this entire universe...

[The term *cit* refers to the subject who is emptiness. Whether in this [consciousness] or in the other, the supreme sovereign Bhairava-consciousness—which consists of consciousness, mind, vital breath, body, pleasure, pain, the senses, the elements, jars, and so forth—[all this is indeed of the nature of light; otherwise, there would be the consequence of the world being blind. So why was it said "in consciousness" as non-different? (Note: The bracketed portion clarifies that the term *cit* refers to the subject who is emptiness (*śūnyapramātā*). The commentary addresses the objection that since everything is of the nature of light, the qualification "in consciousness" as non-different seems redundant.)

"By means of a form consisting of consciousness"—this is the intended meaning here: although it is true that nothing manifests without the existence of light, nevertheless, those [objects] are mutually distinct; however, in the supreme (anuttara) nature, there is no mutual distinction, and thus its state is "supreme. It abides precisely as an undivided form consisting of consciousness.
Although the nature consisting of awakening never sets— since if it were to set, the consequence would be its non-manifestation— nevertheless...
In that state, there is no limitation consisting of mutual non-existence; rather, the Self of the universe— the all-pervasive Śiva, whose consciousness is blissful as He shines within all beings,
whose flow of will is unobstructed, and whose power of vision and action is ever-expanding— is present.
When he remains as one whose knowledge consists solely in the experience of the joy of consciousness,
his will extends to that same degree, and his knowledge and action extend to that same degree.
Then the Supreme, whose nature is consciousness and whose essence is supreme bliss, exists as a seamless whole through the perfect equilibrium of the three powers, well-strung like a bowstring.
Thus, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "In that [state], if these entities were not present, then even the initial synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) and so forth would not be capable of impelling the senses;

therefore, the entire collection of entities is non-different from the mere reflective awareness of 'I' (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), in which the notions of 'this' and 'that' have appropriately not yet arisen."
Free from the conceptualization of division, nothing whatsoever remains there as a limitation; likewise, if this Kaulika method stands here clearly manifest.

Having attained rest, all this— which consists of thirty-six principles— is indeed reposed within that very own nature of Śiva, which is primarily characterized by supreme power, whose essence is the consciousness of universal vibration, and from whom everything was emitted by his own power;
though thus emitted, it rests therein, within the specific vibration of Bhairava, which is primarily characterized by power.

That very state of things being established in their own intrinsic nature is what was referred to by the phrase "in which all [exists]. That [reality], whose essence is Śiva and Śakti, consists of both the universal and the particular; and though it is a single essence, it is manifested by the Supreme Lord alone.
When analyzed and defined separately for the sake of entering the means of instruction, it is in reality only one:

the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), whose essence is the power of sovereignty—the "I" consisting of autonomous consciousness. Abiding in what kind of own-nature is this? It is that which is called "mine" in the space of my heart; this heart is [the ground] of all existents.

Indeed, the locus, the foundation, and the abode of blue and other objects—extending ultimately down to even a worm—is nothing at all that possesses the form of blue and so forth; rather, it belongs solely to the cognizer. (p. 87)

The state of being mounted upon an uninterrupted portion of the wonder [of consciousness] as "mine"—expressed as "blue has appeared to me"—is precisely that which constitutes the form of blue and so forth.

That which is the "void" (*vyoma*) of this "mine" (*mama*), which is the heart of all infinite existents such as blue and so on, is where the universe—which consists of the sense of "mine"—is *vīta* (specifically gone or entered) and perfectly sustained; for this very reason [it is called the void].

Wherein the sky (*vyoma*) is of the nature of emptiness because its own distinct form has been abandoned; likewise, the "heart" (*hṛdaya*)—which is the abode of ultimate support for that which consists of the self-awareness of the supreme and non-supreme, both distinct and non-distinct from the notion of "mine" (*mama*)—is also a sky. Through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), even that "I" (*ahaṃ*) dissolves into the power whose essence is the *bindu*, becoming the human-natured "Ma Ha A."

Having entered the "Ma"—which is the form of the digit of the letter *Ha* within Kuṇḍalinī—one enters the "A," which is the uninterrupted, all-pervasive, and perfectly full wonder; it becomes just so. This very thing is the sky of my heart, because from this [proceeds] this...
That wherein [the world] has spread forth and wherein it finds rest is itself eternal, its nature unobscured, self-manifesting, undeniable, and unsurpassed. As it has been said:
"That in which all this effect resides and from which it has emerged."
Because its nature is unobstructed, there is no cessation of it anywhere.

Thus: for even that which is considered an obstruction because it conceals, when manifesting through its own autonomy as that very concealment and so forth, is indeed the Supreme Lord whose nature is vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*). The particle *yat* functions in the sense of all case endings;
here, due to the suitability of its connection with the subsequent sentence, it remains fixed in a specific sense, functioning in the sense of both the ablative and the locative cases.
This is indeed the direct meaning—even without a detailed discernment of the subtle sense:

that which is this expansion of emanation (*sṛṣṭiprasara*) belonging to the Kaula tradition, and that which abides in the space of my heart, that alone is the Absolute (*anuttara*). Thus, it possesses the state of being both the locus of its own expansion and its own repose.

89) Having examined the nature of the process of expansion, he describes the emission (*visarga*) which is the vibration of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), beginning with the words "I shall tell," for that very form is indeed I.

"I shall speak"—this is the appropriate designation—of that supreme reality which is an uninterrupted oneness, unfolding through the sequence of *paśyantī* and the other stages consisting of the supreme (*parā*), the unsurpassed self (*anuttarātman*), and the supreme-cum-non-supreme (*parāparā*). I shall manifest this continuous stream of speech, comprising many divisions such as technical and worldly, extending from the arising of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*) down to the diversity of sounds (*vaisvarya*). Thus it has been said:
"And that which is from everywhere" means that in the ground extending up to the first level, within the nature of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) and within her own emanation,
which is the form of the goddess Parāparā, there is indeed the unfolding of the unsurpassed, eternal state (anuttaradhruvapada). Thus they have said in their own commentary.
In the *Śivadṛṣṭi* as well, it is stated:
"But when, through the blossoming of the joy arising from the expansion of the power of His conscious nature," and so forth.
This was also said by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.
Pulsating with your own self, you expand the entire universe;
perceiving your own form, you perceive the whole world;
for you yourself reel with your own inner essence.
From that, the mandala of phenomena shines forth.
Thus [says] the venerable Somānanda (p.
"I speak" means I utter [it], from the state of *utkalikā*; likewise, I myself am within all things as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
"I shall speak"—this very [truth] has been purified by us through the refinements of logical instruction and made heart-felt.

And the essential nature of this Supreme Lord is "immediate" (*sadyaḥ*). That which is the Supreme Lord, whose self is Bhairava, who exists as the unsurpassed, eternal abode of *Akula*—all this is precisely that.

The nature of the Kaulika ritual is not something distinct from the pure form of Bhairava, which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); for there is no existence (*sattva*) of entities whatsoever that transcends this.

Even the causes of existence proposed by others—such as the relation to existence (*sattā*), causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and so forth—are untenable when applied to existence itself, because they would require yet another existence and further causal efficiencies.
Furthermore, because an infinite regress would otherwise result, existence (*sattva*) consists precisely from the very beginning in a light whose life is such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);

and since that [existence] is filled with the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), whose essence is sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) and reflective awareness, it is indeed the form of Bhairava. Alternatively, "Sadya" means that which exerts effort (*yatna*) while existing in the state of being real (*sad-rūpa*), because its vital breath is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
91) Regarding the form *sat* with the suffix *kvip*, some teachers read it as a neuter designation. As it is stated in the *Śrīsiddhasantāna*:
"That which is existence (*bhūti*) as a manifest appearance is indeed *sat*."
Thus it is said; [this] also exists in the *Śrīspanda* from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus it was also stated by the venerable Śrī Somānanda-pāda.
"That which exists is the supreme object; for that reason, Śiva is the ultimate reality.
Thus, His essential nature has been described. As it is said:
"He who is everything..."
Thus [it is said]. He describes the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of this very [reality] with the words "bestowing Kaulika-siddhi. "Kaulika" refers to that which has been explained;

"siddhi" is the firmness of its suchness (*tathātvadārḍhya*). Since that [siddhi] arises from there—namely, from the supreme subject of ultimate reality (*paramārthapramātṛ*)—in that [subject], everything such as the *kula* and *akula* becomes such; for therein, everything being perceived attains the firmness of its suchness.
Thus it has been said:
"The Trika is higher than the highest.
Thus it is said elsewhere:

"Beyond the Veda is the Śaiva; beyond that, the Vāma; beyond that, the Dakṣa; beyond that, the Kula; beyond that, the Mata; and beyond even that is the Trika, which is supreme and the most excellent of all."
Thus it is said; and in the *Śrīniśācāra* as well:

"Even a teacher who has been consecrated in the Vāmamārga, if he knows the supreme reality (*paratattva*), must undergo purification in the Bhairava [tradition], and likewise in Kula, Kaula, and Trika."
Thus it is said in the *Śrīsarvācāra*:
"Even a teacher who has been consecrated in the Vāmamārga and knows the supreme reality (paratattva) deserves to undergo purification again,
in due course, within the Bhairava-tantras."
Thus, this is the very sequence as it has been stated: "In this way, [He is] the ultimate subject within the levels of the Sarva, Loka, Veda, Siddhānta, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Kula, and Mata systems.
As it has been said:
"And salutation to that Self of all, who is eternally composed of everything.
Thus it is said. This very Anuttara (the Absolute) has been described by the venerable Somānanda in his own commentary as encompassing all this;
for what more need be said? "The Absolute is indeed everything, because it is the Absolute. This is the intended meaning: [The rest of the passage would follow here.]
(93) Having abandoned all that is merely vibrating with intense spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*), one should now manifest the manifestation of the benefit [of the self]. Indeed,
this is the treasury of the nature of reality, which consists of the essence of spiritual agitation.

O you who have attained the state of liberation through the grace of the Lord of the Universe; O you whose fame has spread like a white umbrella over the entire earth; O you who are the refuge for those bewildered by the sixty-four arts;

O you who are the protector of those who have lost their way in the darkness of ignorance; O you who are the supreme goal for those seeking release from the bonds of worldly existence; O you who have destroyed the multitude of miseries caused by the venomous fangs of the serpent of worldly life;

O you who have once again withdrawn the world into yourself; O you who are the source of power for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; O you who are the incomprehensible, cool-rayed moon that puts an end to the heat of mental afflictions; O you who are the one and only sovereign!

"Having abandoned such an interpretation as 'the meaning of the cessation of the self which is not known by others,' [and] 'the state of the sword of the wise woman who has become very angry with another man'— even though a conversation held with those devoid of grammatical refinement and syntactical skill becomes a cause for shame, nevertheless, the demonstration of what has been interpreted by others is a refutation."

In order to awaken the conscious one to the unsurpassed, that is written down once for all—beginning with the words "the unsurpassed" and so forth, in a verse and a half concerning Śiva. [The meaning here is as follows: the analysis of the compound is "that whose object is Śiva" (*śivo viṣayo yasya*);
because by the mere realization of which, one attains equality with the *khecarī* (sky-farer).]
Thus it has been said. Likewise, the analysis of the compound should be understood as "that which has Śakti as its object" (śaktiviṣaya), since [it says]:
"Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods."

"Thus it has been said"—this is the explanation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). In order to refute that very point, he says: "In this regard, if... and so forth. Therein, he states the logical inconsistency with the words: "In that case... [This is the question. It resides in the heart. (p. 94)

By this verse beginning with "ityādi," the subject matter is *śakti*. Likewise, in the passage of the reply beginning with "Listen thus, O Goddess" (*tathā śṛṇu devi*), the meaning is that even the "higher" (*uttara*) is the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*); thus, it means "listen to the higher and the unsurpassed. If this were explained here according to the intent of the threefold meaning (*trikārtha*), then there would be the contingency of a third question concerning the human (*nara*). But if, on the other hand—

According to the intention of the *yāmala*, even there two separate entities consisting of Śiva and Śakti are not what is called *yāmala*— by which [the phrase] "by each [of them]" would imply a distinct nature for two separate things, thereby making the possibility of separate questions logically tenable; nor does the meaning of the word *atha* [as it will be explained in the passage beginning with "atha ādyāḥ"] cohere [with such an interpretation], for that [particle] functions as an indicator of immediate succession following a determination of a similar kind.
Furthermore, without determining the nature of the *uttara* (the answer), a single question concerning the *anuttara* (the unsurpassed) would be untenable.

For instance, regarding what they stated in the text of the reply—namely, "Listen to the *uttara* and the *anuttara*"—he says "the nature of the *uttara*" (*uttarasvarūpa*) in order to crush that [objection], and he supports that very point with the words beginning "for instance" (*tathā hi*). This is how it appears in certain ancient manuscripts.
Another verse is seen on page 95):
"O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, I have heard the great knowledge called Trika."
And likewise, the higher knowledge has been attained through your grace.

Thus, it is precisely according to the commentary formulated by the venerable Somānandapāda that whatever the gurus have instructed brings about the auspiciousness of all. This is the vow of uprooting the darkness of the mass of ill-conceived and unrefined commentaries [where *tāmasa* refers to the veil of *tamas*].
He causes the lotus of the heart to blossom, purified by the teachings of the Trika (the Six-and-a-Half [Tantras]).
The radiant sun of the commentary, which possesses a gentle luster that dissolves the mass of congealed and endless bonds— [where "congealed" means become solidified;
in the solar sense, the "mass of bonds" refers to the multitude of Piśācas and other spirits]—
has been illuminated by Abhinavagupta.

Thus, it has been stated that the Kaulika method is that from which this [universe] originates, that in which it finds its foundation, and that of which this Kaulika [reality] consists—that alone is the Anuttara (the Unsurpassed). In this regard, what indeed is the Kaulika method?
How does its expansion proceed from the Anuttara? And how is its establishment found in this very [Anuttara]? And how...

(96) The state of being the unsurpassed single form [is to be applied as the rule of the *kaulika*]. As for what was said—that even the "higher" (*uttara*) is the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*)—that is reasoning (*yukti*), which is the logic (*tarka*) conducive to direct experience; consequently, it is established here that [this is attained] from the Guru, from the scripture, and from oneself. All [of this is so].

Desiring to establish [the truth] in detail for those disciples who are skilled in the discernment attained through the realization of reality— the essence extracted from reasoning, scripture, and personal experience— the Blessed One introduces another work [with the words]:
"But for those whose manifold latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the conceit of duality have been crushed by such firm instruction..."
All this is [established] by this much alone; how so? This is concluded by the pair of verses beginning with "How [is it unsurpassed]? [The word "concluded" means:

Thus, for the sake of instructing others, I have set forth the method—the propositions, reasons, examples, applications, and conclusions—which are the causes of awakening. Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the demonstration of the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the probandum (*sādhya*), wherein the subject possesses the probandum in a state of doubt.

The *pakṣa* (subject) is, for example: "This mountain possesses fire. To establish understanding in another regarding that very subject, the indicator (*liṅga*) which makes it known is the *hetu* (reason), as in: "Because it possesses smoke. The cause for clear comprehension regarding that very subject is the *udāharaṇa* (example), as in:
"Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been observed in such places as a kitchen. This [is stated] with respect to the subject (*pakṣe*).

The application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption [of the subject] under the means of proof, as in "and so is this"; the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the subsumption of the probandum (*sādhya*) onto that very same subject, as in "therefore, it is thus. Regarding these, for those who possess firm conviction, comprehension is achieved through the conclusion alone; what need have they for anything else? For others, however, comprehension is achieved through reasoning (*tarka*) alone—this is the introduction to the passage to be cited.
