And by means of the answer determined in the verse and a half beginning with "Listen, O Goddess, through the question," [there is the attainment] of the state of those who are liberated while living, permeated by the power of reaching the unsurpassed state (anuttarapada). (p.
Since the task is accomplished, those purified by firm conviction should rest in that alone—
thus we cry out with uplifted arms.
Therefore, for the sake of entering the distinct state of Kaulika, which is reflected within the stainless mirror of the plane of the unsurpassed Supreme Bhairava:
It has been stated that another treatise is now being introduced. || 4 ||
For example:
the first lunar days (tithis) are all the vowels ending with the bindu;
within them, through the conjunction of time, the Moon and Sun are proclaimed. (5)
O virtuous lady, the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa are located,
in order, within the consonant groups beginning with Ka and ending with Ma.
There is a fourfold set of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on air, fire, water, and Indra;
above that is the well-known group beginning with Śa, and further ahead is the pentad of Brahmā.
(98) It should be known that, following that sequence, it is rootless; this is declared to be the emanation ending with *kṣāntā*,
O illustrious one, for all mantras and vidyās.
This source (yoni) is proclaimed in all tantras at all times.

Therein, the Akula is determined to be the unsurpassed (anuttara) Kaulika itself, in the form of emanation (sṛṣṭi). Now, the connection is that its emanation is [the source]; thus, that very unsurpassed state is the meaning of "emanation. And although, even regarding emanation, according to the previous method—

Although there would be no temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) dependent on time, nevertheless, as long as the distinction characterized by the relationship between the teacher and the taught is manifested by the Supreme Lord through His sovereignty within His own self, so long does temporal sequence also exist; with reference to that,
the word "atha" (now/then) signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

99) Immediately thereafter, it is precisely the *Akula* that takes the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*); however, the sense of immediate succession following the question and the thesis is not expressed by the word *atha*.

Because this [word *atha*] is inclined toward conveying a sequential intention based on a homogeneous set of objects of knowledge contained within a single section; otherwise, there would be scope for its use everywhere—even after silence and so forth—as in "this [follows] immediately after that. If it is asked, "What difficulty is there for you in this?", the answer is: none at all—except for... [the following].

Because they exist dependently, the very notion of "dependence" is itself the affliction (kleśa); this is the meaning. Therefore, there is no adventitious affliction, but rather only the root afflictions—this is the intended sense.
As for what the venerable Śrī Somānanda said:
"The letter *A* is called Śiva; the letter *Tha* is said to be Śakti."
By this demonstration of scripture, the response is simply "then" (*atha*). This being so,

according to the principle of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of a topic), whatever was previously stated— namely, that although temporal sequence is not possible, the same applies to silence and so forth— is now seen as a mere doubt that does not exist at all, since the single effect has been established.

"That in which other effects are established by themselves is *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*," they explained with the intention that [the letter *tha*] has an equal pervasion (*samavyāptikatā*) with the letter *ha*, because it consists of the non-differentiation from the power of creating an infinite-infinite array of entities expanding everywhere in the first unfolding (*prathama-ullāsa*).
Furthermore,
because the meaning of the word *atha* consists in its being based upon the supreme *nāda*, which is the life-force residing within all beings,
we have not analyzed this in detail, since we are not directly acquainted with such scripture (*āgama*).

By those [masters], who have directly realized such scriptures, the capacity of the Sūtra-text to withstand hundreds of various arguments has indeed been established. Even the demonstration of the distinction between the *dhūli* (dust) and [the *cūrṇi* (powder)] is [an exposition of the meaning of the *cūrṇi*]. With that very intention—that is, with the intention of [showing] equal pervasion—it was stated by them [by Somānanda-pāda]: "From this... [it follows].

"From that" means from those various scriptures characterized by the *Parātriṃśikā*. And "spread from there" [means it is diffused]. We, however, being purified by that teaching and desiring the purification of our own selves through the unraveling of the knots in its texts, remain entirely indifferent toward such matters as have been determined by them. This is also due to the distinctions between the [various] traditions (*dhūlibheda*) and so forth.

Even the dependence on imagined and conventional scripts might exist for someone; however, since the arrangement of letters is quite different in all regions, it cannot serve as a means for everyone. (p. 101)
And the distinction of time should be understood in this very same way. [This method] is not intended for disciples existing in all places and times;

therefore, we have not elaborated upon this at length. For those who have entered into the logic of direct experience, it is incapable of being performed by them; yet it is easily accomplished through their own conceptualizations, while for others it remains established as such.
For those who are ignorant of this instruction, the distinction here is as follows:
like a drop of water fallen upon a stone heated by the summer sun,
the song of instruction never produces any internal impression in the foolish.
And so it has been said by another:
"The words of instruction, even when accepted as objects of knowledge, are unable to take root in the hearts of those with deluded minds.
Can showers from the clouds, though falling incessantly, impart moisture to lotus leaves simply by clinging to them?"
Thus, even that instruction is ineffective; enough of this which creates an obstacle to the subject at hand.

Let us follow the topic under discussion: [the term] *athādi* refers to those vowels of which "a" is the first; or alternatively, with the letter "tha" added for the sake of easy pronunciation, it refers to those of which "atha" is the first.
And here, the word "first" (*ādya*) does not refer merely to a fixed position, nor even to proximity; rather, it means that which exists at the beginning (*ādau bhava*).
Nevertheless, this ground of the supreme speech (*parāvāgbhūmi*) among these phonemes is determined right here, wherein—

Their form is non-temporal, eternal, uncreated, and consists solely of consciousness (*saṃvit*). Within this body of consciousness, the state of being the self of all things is perpetually manifest; and she is the Supreme Goddess, the Most Venerable Parā (*parābhaṭṭārikā*).
Although she partakes in such unsurpassed non-duality, the [levels of speech] beginning with Paśyantī are [contained within her], like the juices within a peacock’s egg. (Parā...)

[The *paśyantī* perceives according to the analogy of the *vaṭadhānikā* (the seed-pod of the banyan tree); the *madhyamā* follows according to the analogy of the *māṣaśamikā* (the parched bean); and beyond that is the *vaikharī*.

Having internalized that which consists of an infinite variety of manifestations, beginning with the form of the venerable *Parāparā-bhaṭṭārikā*, it is not logical to say that "what is not there cannot exist anywhere" for one who contemplates the first [state]. [In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows:]

The statement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that "they are completely resolved through their establishment as objects"; and this is not established merely by resting in pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), which is the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) in its undifferentiated form, but rather through the medium of various forms of valid cognition such as distinct determinations (*niścaya*). This is so if these entities [are understood] within the single "I" (*aham*).

Otherwise, there would be no connection whatsoever among insentient objects, their cognitions, their conceptualizations, and their determinations, which are sequential in space and time and established solely in their own individual natures. And it has been said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

When all entities become established within the single cognizer through the various gateways of their distinct cognitions, this state of kinship (*jñāteya*) becomes possible. [This occurs] in the divine consciousness called *pratibhā*, which is devoid even of the slightest stain of the impurity of limitation. For instance, whatever—
And that [consciousness], whether in its moving or non-moving state, by virtue of its ultimate, imperishable nature whose essence consists solely of *vīrya* (potency),

exists as such through a state of being brought forth by the infinite variety of those very objects— be they extremely indistinct, more indistinct, or slightly indistinct— which are perceived in the manner of a stone polished by hundreds of things arising from it.

103) While consciousness—whose essence is the venerable Lord Bhairava-Bhaṭṭārikā—remains exactly as it is, for those who have ascended to the highest degree of such focused attention, [the following is the intended meaning]: "The determination of objects is grounded in consciousness"—this is the statement of the Siddhānta; and that is not [the case here].
This is established not merely by resting in pure consciousness whose nature is valid cognition (*pramā*) despite its diverse forms,

but rather through the medium of various cognitions whose nature is valid cognition in the form of distinct certainties (*niścaya*) and so forth; for these entities abide within a single essential nature of "I," otherwise there would be no connection between insentient objects, their cognitions, and the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding them.

There would be no synthesis whatsoever among those determinations which occur sequentially in space and time and are established solely in their own individual forms. And it has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"In a single cognizer, through the various gateways of distinct cognitions..."
When entities are established, this kinship is possible.
Likewise,
for objects that possess a sequence of space and time and are completed within themselves,
this synthesis is accomplished by their simultaneous appearance; otherwise, what kind of synthesis could there be?
Thus, in this manner,
within the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is variegated by the appearance of extremely diverse objects,
worldly transaction— whether defiled or pure— is experienced.
Thus, this has been stated as "attentiveness in that manner. With this very intention, it is said in the *Śivopaniṣad*:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings;
however, for yogins, this distinction lies in their attentiveness toward the connection [between them]."

Thus, even those who possess doubt— though purified by their altruism toward others and having ground away the stains of doubt through the friction of the whetstone of the gradual process of practice, which consists of the very nature of non-doubt— are indeed able to ascend to the stage of omniscience, which is uncontracted in its ultimate reality and whose nature is uncontrived.

"Contracted by the object given as merely what appears"—this is the intended meaning here: for one perceiving blue, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of sixteen *tuṭis*, arises up until the point of immersion in the object of knowledge (*vedya*).

Among these, the first *tuṭi* is of a single undivided nature; the second is of the nature of the emergence of the subject (*grāhaka*); and the last is non-different from the object (*grāhya*), being identical with it.

The penultimate [moment], however, has the nature of the manifest grasper; it is the middle of that twelvefold [cycle], which is half [of it] and consists of the non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) nature that covers conceptualization (vikalpa). Within that essential nature, there is one [aspect] as the covering, while within the conceptualization to be covered, there is a fivefold state: the desire to open (unmimiṣiṣā) and the opening (unmiṣattā). And this [opening], because its form is manifest activity, consists of two *tuṭis*.

Since vibration (*spandana*) lacks the nature of being a single moment, there are six moments that are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*): [the moments of] "having been opened," "performing its own function," and so forth—these five due to the objects to be concealed and one due to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Following those, there is the "process of perishing" (*dhvaṃsamānatā*) and the "perishing" (*dhvaṃsa*) of the non-conceptual, as well as the "desire to open" (*unmimipiṣā*) and the "opening" (*unmiṣattā*) of the conceptual (*vikalpa*).

The state of being "unblinking" (*unmiṣitatā*) consists of two *tuṭi*s; thus, there are six *tuṭi*s. However, the agency of performing its own function, which is said to be the nature of the subject (*grāhakarūpatā*), is not counted further. Therefore, when there is a decrease in conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is a corresponding decrease in *tuṭi*s. This being the case, as long as there is a decrease in duality—which is essentially the distinction of a manifest "this-ness"—the [count of] two *tuṭi*s diminishes until one reaches the immersion into Śiva (*śivāveśa*).

In this context, the first *tuṭi* is entirely full, while the second is permeated by the instruments of all-knowingness; when practiced, it leads to omniscience and omnipotence—not so the first. This very point has been handed down by Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa as "the fall of the *tuṭi*" (*tuṭipāta*);
the meaning is that the "fall" (*pāta*) of the first *tuṭi*—its diminution—is the subsequent *tuṭi*, the second one, and not something artificial.
As the venerable Kallaṭapāda has said:
"Upon the falling away of the *tuṭi*s, there is the attainment of omniscience and omnipotence.
Thus, although this object is of a single nature consisting solely of self-luminosity, it is [established] through reasoning.

105) It is demonstrated: whatever [is characterized by] the force of its truth being completely determined by the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā-yogyatā) arising at a subsequent time through its own power...

The nature of non-conceptual awareness— which possesses a congruent and unerring correspondence, which precedes the conceptualizations that establish blue and so forth as mutually exclusive and sequentially constructed,
and which is indivisible from the appearances of blue, yellow, and the rest that are conceived as contradictory by those respective conceptualizations— is such that, just as [it appears], so it is.

In the cognition of a variegated [object], the variegated form does not fail to appear—this being contrary to experience—and since that which is insentient cannot be manifest, this form must consist of cognition itself. Nor is there a division of cognitions due to a difference in forms, because a single variegated form lacks a plurality of forms; just as blue has a single form consisting of the nature of blue, so too [is it here].

The aspect of a single variegated [cognition] is precisely its variegated nature; and since cognition operates within that which constitutes its very self, it must operate in its entirety or not at all—it does not operate partially, because it is partless. As for those parts which appear as mutually distinct, they do not constitute the variegated form itself.
This is the state of being.

For even though there is a difference in the objects of cognition such as houses for one situated on a mountain peak, there would be only a single appearance of the city. The meaning is that "dark-blue cognition"—that is, non-conceptual knowledge of blue and so forth—is likewise entirely undivided therein.

That consciousness which resides on the peak of variegated cognition— consisting of the awareness of deep blue and so forth— is not divided from the appearances of blue, yellow, and other forms that are its opposites;
even though it precedes the conceptualizations of the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth, which arise from its own infinite inherent powers.

106) It does not exist in the manner of a cognition that directly perceives only blue; rather, this [cognition] arises as a flash of intuition (*unmeṣa*) existing in the interval between two conceptual cognitions—one concerning what has set and the other concerning what is about to rise.

That which is described in the verbal tradition (*śabdāgama*)— the grammatical treatises (*prakriyāśāstra*)— as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), occurring prior to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "blue" that are accompanied by correspondence or contradiction,
is therefore composed solely of an undivided manifestation immediately following that [perception]; and this is so for both [types of cognition].
The interval between two cognitions is undeniable; it exists precisely because of the difference between the two cognitions, and that interval is itself of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*).

Otherwise, if by that very [interval] the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of consciousness were destroyed—meaning that if, due to the destruction of impressions, ever-new appearances were subject to arising and passing away at every moment—then there would be a collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, when some object has been previously grasped...

That which was previously an outward-turned perception, its inward-turned nature as the essence of consciousness remains even at a later time; the power of recollection consists in this: it reflects upon that state residing within itself as being directed toward a specific external object.
Likewise, synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) consists in the attainment of a memory that has come to possess a single object;
[it is] the impossibility of such synthesis as recollection and so forth for the subject (*dharmin*) called "intuition" (*pratibhā*), according to all disputants.
There is no dispute [regarding this, for it has been said in the *Sūtravimarśinī* by this very author]:
"We praise that Śiva, whose nature is unceasing awakening, without whom not even all philosophical views would exist."
Thus, there is no lack of proof; and because this does not depend upon the time of learning linguistic conventions, it is indeed non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).
For its connection with innate, non-artificial reflective awareness (*tathāparāmarśa*) is inseparable from the nature of consciousness, which is distinct from insentient matter. [Now, one might ask:
"In the Blessed One, whose nature is pure consciousness, how could reflective awareness be equivalent to conceptual thought? To this, he says:
"Insentient," and so forth. And it has been said:
"They know that the essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (vimarśa); otherwise, even if it is colored by an object, light would be like an insentient thing, such as a crystal."

Thus it is said. Nor should it be argued: "How then could that not be of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpa)? For it is not equivalent to conceptual construction, because no differentiation is manifested. And so it has been stated:
"That reflective awareness of 'I', which, though consisting of light, has speech as its body..."
That is not conceptual construction; for it is defined as a definitive determination that entails a duality.

Thus: there is no equality with conceptualization—because [conceptualization] does not manifest difference, whereas [perception], by virtue of having acquired the essence of difference, brings about the manifestation of objects;
and for conceptualizations, there is no arising without non-conceptualization, because they lack autonomy, and this lack of autonomy is [the reason].

Since the recollection of conventions and so forth serves as the means [for cognition], and since such recollection of conventions and so forth cannot exist without a prior experience, and because— according to the previously stated reasoning— consciousness lacks delimitation by time and other factors, that supreme Lord’s intuition (*pratibhā*) is indeed one; it is of this nature, conceived through the power of our own teaching, and though its essence is undivided, it is the Self of all.
Even while existing in the present, it is precisely the source of the generation of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding past and future forms;

thus, according to that view—namely, "if the object were to have a nature manifested as separate from cognition, it would be perceived even in the absence of cognition, but this is not the case; therefore, there is indeed non-difference (*abheda*) between cognition and the object."
As they have said:
"Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof.
Therefore, it is cognition alone that appears in various ways in all instances; there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from it.
Furthermore, this entire conventional usage of the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is completed within knowledge alone.

For its state of possessing the form of the object is the object of cognition, its state of having the form of the apprehender is the means of cognition, and self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result.
As it has been said:

That which appears is the object of cognition; the means of cognition and the result, moreover, are the subjective form and the self-awareness [of that form]. Therefore, these three are not made separate from one another.

Thus, because the vision of reality has been subverted by the play of the latent impressions of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyāvāsanā*), knowledge itself appears as if possessed of the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject; however, upon the cessation of ignorance, this becomes purely transparent, or rather, it is nothing at all. As it has been said:
There is no other experience of that [consciousness] by means of the intellect, nor is there any further experience of it;
due to the absence of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, it shines forth by itself.
Thus,

although the nature of the intellect is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted by error.
Seeing that this is indeed mere consciousness, devoid of both object and form,
one casts off the succession of suffering and attains the fearless state of Nirvana.

Thus is the doctrine of the Sugatas; and by those skilled in discernment, it is precisely the *ālayavijñāna* that has been accepted, and its state of being accompanied by correspondence (*sasaṃvādatva*) has already been demonstrated through the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that arise immediately thereafter. Thus.

The reason is not unestablished with respect to the subject of the thesis; for that which is cognized by a cognition which produces a conceptual representation appearing as a single unity does not differ from it—just as the self does not differ from its own cognition. Blue and other objects are cognized [by cognition]; if there were a difference, their status as being cognized by that cognition would not obtain, because of the absence of identity (*tādātmya*), which is the necessary cause [for such a relation], since one thing cannot be related to another through identity.

If that which is unrelated were knowable, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, since the cause of restriction—namely, *relation*, which is the pervader—is not perceived in the case of difference, knowability, which is excluded from the dissimilar class (the vipakṣa) of difference, is thereby pervaded by non-difference. Furthermore, as for this appearance of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and consciousness as distinct: [End of provided text]
It is like the error of perceiving duality in a single moon. As it has been said:
"And difference would appear in non-erroneous cognition, like two [moons] in the moon.
Thus, it exists either always or at some time in the absence of conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*), which is its counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and there is no exclusion of it from that.

It is "doubtful"—thus it is neither contradictory (*viruddha*), nor inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), nor is its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) doubtful. (p. 110) Just as the act of cutting is connected with and distinct from that which is to be cut, so too...

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that even the cognition and its activity will be both conjoined with and separated from the object of knowledge; thus, the exclusion of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) remains doubtful. To this, [the reply is]:
because the rule of the simultaneous appearance of blue and its cognition is established merely by the fact that cognition is self-cognizing and cognizes others.
The counter-argument is that because external objects do not exist, cognition cannot be the perceiver of another [object].

Furthermore, even in the case of the subject of the example, such as variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*) and so forth, defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason are likewise avoided.
Indeed, once the defects of the reason have been eliminated, defects of the example and other such factors find no footing at all; and so forth.
Since this has already been extensively determined by others, what is the point of the labor of restating it? This much, however, is established:

that which is intuitive (*prātibha*), which precedes and follows all objective cognition, and which is the totality of all things—in that [state], for one whose body has dissolved and who shines as the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), exhaustion would be possible [i.e., it would reach its cessation].
Is it established by the power of non-existence? [Regarding "non-existence"—as others have said:
"One should meditate upon non-existence until one attains identity with it."]
(111) Not beholding the body, the vital breaths, and so forth, nor the mass of the enjoyment of others' wealth and pleasures, he experiences an incomparable languor within his own heart.
If the Supreme Goddess, who is the essence of the birth of the entire universe, has indeed entered within, then—alas!—may she shine forth like a full oblation.
As it is said in the *Spanda*:
"Lassitude is that which withers the body, and its course arises from ignorance;
if it is destroyed by the unfolding of that [consciousness], how could it exist without a cause?"
Thus:
"Since the emergence of another [thought] occurs for one who is intent upon a single thought, that should be known as 'unmeṣa' (the unfolding); one should perceive it by oneself."
And thus:
The auspicious ones declare that the impurity called ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is the root of the impurities of illusion (*māyīya*) and karma (*kārmika*), is indeed the *māṇava* impurity.
That very thing is the seed of the ancient tree of worldly existence; when the supreme fire of the sharpened consciousness burns it, it is consumed in an instant.
As they have said:
"They maintain that ignorance is the impurity which is the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
This very point has been stated.
p.

112) "If it [the world] is destroyed by its unfolding (unmeṣa)," and so on. It has been explained in exactly this way; otherwise, there would be the destruction of exhaustion (glāni), and this [destruction] would arise from ignorance.
"The destruction of ignorance through the manifestation of wisdom—how could these two be connected?
This would be like a king’s investigation; it is as if one were trying to extract and separate the grain from the husk of parched, flattened, and thoroughly winnowed rice.
The ruin of one's reputation through unknown misfortunes, and the failure of undertakings due to the exhaustion of one's innate strength.

Thus, the Blessed Lady, the plane of supreme speech (*parāvāgbhūmi*), contains within her womb the unfolding of the venerable goddesses Parāparā and the others, who emerge from the reality of her own sovereignty; by virtue of containing them within her, she is the unity of awakening toward the entire manifold of beings, worlds, and entities, which are fashioned without dispute through that very process of manifestation.

The primordial Great Creative Power (*mahāsṛṣṭiśakti*), whose essence is the syllable *at*, made manifest through the appearance of the Supreme Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka; her true nature is such a wondrous and real ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); she consists of the unity of infinite creation, maintenance, and withdrawal reflected in the stainless mirror of one's own Self.

It is established that the Blessed One has determined this in its entirety through the passage beginning with "Now, the first... and so forth, which describes the nature of patience (*kṣānti*). Thus it stands in that very place.

Since it is established that "everything exists," the meaning of the text is now determined: the Śiva-tattva consists of the letters from *a* to *visarga*; the five elements consist of the letters from *ka* to *ṅa*, representing earth up to ether; the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) consist of the letters from *ca* to *ña*, representing smell up to sound; and [the organs of action] consist of the letters from *ṭa* to *ṇa*, representing the feet up to speech.
The five organs of action begin with *k* and end with *ṭ*; the five instruments of cognition (the senses) beginning with the nose and ending with the ear;

the pentad known as mind, ego, intellect, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) beginning with *p* and ending with *m*; the principles denoted by the letters from *y* to *v*, beginning with air (*vāyu*) and so forth; and the principles known as passion (*rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), limited agency (*kalā*), and illusion (*māyā*).

They "maintain"—that is, they conceive of as separate entities—thus they are called *dhāraṇās*. There are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*) here due to the dual nature of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated. For indeed, all things maintain themselves within their own self, in the supreme and perfectly full state which is the nature of Light.
In the Bhairava-self,
which is the self of all— as it has been stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*.

The Self alone— whose nature is its own essence— is Śiva, whose body is consciousness that shines forth within all entities [the phrase "body of consciousness" (cidvapuḥ) meaning that all objects of knowledge have been assimilated into itself],
whose flow of will is unobstructed, and whose triad of powers of vision and action is ever-expanding.
Thus it is said; as stated in the *Spanda*:
"In that wherein all this is established.
In this way, by means of manifestation within His own self which is luminous, He sustains the existing things that are being held.
By not manifesting itself—that is, by attaining the state of being the locus of insentience (*jaḍatā*) and the sense of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*).
As it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "For those things endowed with 'this-ness' that have reached the plane of the object of knowledge (*vedya*)."
Because the essence of all phenomena is awakening, one perceives them exactly as they are.

Thus [it is said]. The Supreme Lord alone reveals [the world], and then again conceals it precisely through the sense of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*). Therefore, this state of the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva, consisting of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyāmaya*), is intimated by a single causative suffix (*ṇic*);
and therein, that which is the concealment of "this-ness" (*idantā*) by "I-ness" occurs upon the establishment of the "this-ness" that is to be concealed.

115) It is logically possible [only] when there exists this state of "thisness" (*idantā*)—consisting of forms such as the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and so forth—and not otherwise. Furthermore, this so-called "thisness," which consists of the manifestation of difference, does not exist in relation to the pure, consciousness-natured form of the Supreme Lord.

The form [of the ego] arises—thus, since that which is to be covered does not arise, by virtue of that, the state of being a cover for the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) is also untenable; consequently, the cognition of such a Lord (*īśvara*) is untenable. And if that is untenable, nothing at all would appear, due to the absence of a cause—as has been stated more than once—and yet this [world] does appear.
Although it is not distinct from its own manifestation, the world nonetheless manifests externally solely through the power of the Supreme Lord,

because no other cause is possible and because within one's own consciousness, consciousness alone manifests as being composed of everything. Thus, the world, which is one’s own essential nature, though appearing as differentiated, shines within the "I" (aham), which is of the very nature of Light.

By the phrase "in grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), this much is necessarily implied: that the Lord alone perceives various objects of knowledge as distinct from Himself through the sense of "I," and whoever that perceiver may be, he too—by virtue of being manifest—is composed of His own Self;
thus, He rests upon such powers within His own Self.
By means of those very [afflictions] such as passion (*rāga*), he would at that very moment attain the state of having the distinction between the object of cognition and the cognizer;

and since it is through passion and the like that he becomes such, it is precisely passion and the other afflictions which, being established, [bring about this state] according to the logic already stated.

Since they function as the instigating causes (*prayojaka*) with respect to the Lord who maintains [the world], they constitute the sole basis for His designation as "masculine" (*puṃstva*); thus, when a second *ṇic* affix arises— expressed by the word "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*)—
there is no loss of the connection with the meaning of the root in any case, because [the objects] continue to be maintained (*dhriyamāṇatayā*).
For it is only that which is manifesting which can be maintained; thus, the designation "manifestation" is appropriate.
As I have stated myself in the *Śivadṛṣṭyālocana*:
"Even a command would exist for one who possesses what is called 'capacity'."
Thus [it is said]. Bhartṛhari also states:
"For when there is an instigation (*praiṣa*) of one who has not yet acted, the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed after roots such as *pra-chi*;
but when the instigation is of one who has already acted, then that is the domain of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)."

Thus, in this way, by the term *dhāraṇā*, those very principles (*tattvas*) which are well-known in other scriptures under the name of "coverings" (*kañcuka*) have been described here, as it is stated in the *Śrītantrasāra*: [p. 117]

Just as they maintain the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), so too do [the powers] such as Vidyā, Māyā, and Niyati maintain states that consist of their own essence; therefore, these must be purified with effort.

Thus it is said. As for the fact that the venerable Śrī Somānanda used the word *dhāraṇā* (retention) to designate the limbs [of yoga] by resorting to an alternative interpretation [meaning by explaining them in another sense], his intention therein was to demonstrate that all other systems are merely objects of perception within the Self; for such is his style. [End of sentence fragment on style.]

Bhavāśailī maintains that "style" (*śailī*) refers to an activity preceded by a settled conclusion (*samādhāna*); others hold it to be composition (*racanā*), while still others consider it to be one's own philosophical position (*svamata*).
How can he who does not know his own positions and those of others in their entirety rescue others when he himself is sinking into the ocean of doubt?
Thus, the five principles beginning with *Śā* and ending with *Kṣā* are known as Mahāmāyā, Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti. To explain:

between the principle of Māyā above and the principle of Vidyā below, there must necessarily be another principle, wherein the Vijñānākalas reside—this is the sequence stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
The loss of freedom of consciousness and the lack of awareness within freedom—
this is the twofold atomic impurity (āṇavamala), arising from the forfeiture of one's own true nature.
Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself, due to the absence of that agency.
And these *vijñānakevalas*,
whose nature is the non-cognition of Śūnya and the other categories, are the agents known as *pralayākalas*.
This is the established position, as it has been stated:
Above Māyā and below Śuddhavidyā reside the Vijñānakevalas.

Thus it is said. For instance, in the absence of Mahāmāyā, the Pralayakevalas abide in the plane of Māyā, and the Vidyeśvaras and others abide in the plane of Vidyā. What, then, could that be which serves as the locus for the Vijñānakevalas?

Precisely for this reason, even though these have fallen from the plane of Vidyā, there arises no manifestation of distinct objects of knowledge belonging to the mass of differentiated entities consisting of duality.
When the impurity known as *māyīya* does not manifest, one is there a *vijñānakevala*, joined with only the single impurity; thus,
the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* declares that such a state is supported by the *āṇava* impurity, which consists of ignorance,
precisely because of the grace of the stage of *śuddhavidyā*.
119) They have been awakened as partakers of the state of the mantra and its lords, for it is said elsewhere: "Through awakening brought about by Ananteśa, one attains the nature of a mantra."
Thus it was said:
"There are [eight]; he awakened eight *pudgala*s who were *vijñānakevala*s," and so forth.

"Having appointed [her] to the state of the Lord of the Great Lords of Mantra," and so forth. Furthermore, in certain scriptures, that Mahāmāyā is determined to be a mere remnant of the *vidyā*-tattva by way of metaphorical designation, due to the absence of the impurity of duality (*bhedamala*); whereas in other cases, this is because of the presence of the obstruction caused by the impurity of ignorance (*ajñānamala*).

Just as in certain scriptures the principle of *rāga* (attachment) is not treated separately because it is attached to the individual soul (*pums*) as the tail of the *māyātattva*, or as in these very *Śrītrikāgamas* where *niyati* (restriction) and *kāla* (time) are not described separately; so too, in this system, the fivefold Brahman—beginning with *vidyā* and ending with *anāśritaśiva*—will be determined. And of these principles (*tattvas*)...
Vastness and the quality of expansion [arise] primarily because of having transcended duality and because of being the agent of the birth of saṃsāra;
thus are these [qualities].
The thirty-four principles (*tattvas*), existing in the form of the creative process (*prakriyā*), take the letter *a* as their primordial form.

In this regard, the following is considered: from the *śiva-tattva* at the beginning of the *a*-group, followed by the elements (*bhūtas*) and so forth, up to the *śakti-tattva* at the end—among these, which of the sequences of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), cognition (*jñapti*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and descent (*avatāra*) is this?
The sequence everywhere in the illustrious *Mālinīvijayottara*, *Siddhātantra*, *Svacchanda*, and other scriptures begins with the letter *kṣa*.

This is the sequence here: on the level of Earth (*pṛthivī*), there is the single letter *kṣa* alone, consisting of the form of a word, mantra, and phoneme; in the principles from Water (*ap*) up to the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), there are twenty-three letters beginning with *ha* and ending with *ṭa*.

There are two four-syllabled word-mantras; there are three five-syllabled [word-mantras] among those beginning with *puṃs* and ending with *māyā*, consisting of the seven letters from *gha* to *ña*. Among these, there are two word-mantras: one is five syllables and the second is two syllables. Furthermore, among *śuddhavidyā*, *īśvara*, and *sadāśiva*, there are the three letters *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*, which constitute both the word and the mantra.
Furthermore, within the Śiva-tattva, there is the single phoneme-word-mantra-tattva consisting of the three syllables and the sixteen vowels;

and because of the predominance of the nature of Śakti, it is indeed one, for Śakti cannot be distinct from the possessor of Śakti—this is the intended meaning. Then, having joined each one [of the letters] starting from the letter *kṣa* up to the thirty-four principles beginning with Earth (*kṣityādi*), as before...

Since it is appropriate for the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) during the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) that the thirty-sixth principle— which is considered all-pervasive and endowed with power— should consist of the sixteen vowels beginning from *visarga* and ending with *a*, proceeding in direct order (*ānulomyena*),
it is stated elsewhere:
Then, having established the state of being a single syllable for each principle (tattva) starting from Kṣama and so forth,
it is declared that in the supreme Śiva-principle there are sixteen syllables, beginning with the Visarga.
Thus, from [the letter] *pra* onwards up to the end of the *avarga*, the placement of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with Earth (*pārthiva*) and ending with Śiva has been described.
This is considered the first *dhārikā* (supporter), as the Great Lord stated in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"The *dhārikā*, the nourisher (*āpyāyinī*), the awakener (*boddhrī*), the purifier (*pavitrī*), and the one that provides space (*avakāśadā*)."
Thus, a single reality is held to be pervading therein;
in this way, one should contemplate each individual letter, word, and syllable separately among the phonemes.
And again, in that very same place, according to the venerable Mālinī-bhaṭṭārikā—[regarding the term *mālinī*:

as stated by the illustrious Jayadratha Rājanaka during the occasion of its commentary: "She whose *yoni* (source), characterized by the letters beginning with *ka*, is *bhinna* (divided/distinguished) by the vowels"—in that regard:

The *mālinī* mantra denotes Śakti, while the *mātṛkā* mantra denotes the Possessor of Śakti (*śaktimant*). Among these, the *mātṛkā* is well known. As for the *mālinī*, it is as follows: na, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, tha, ca, dha, ī, ṇa, u, ū, ṇa, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, i, a, va, bha, ya, ḍa, ḍha, ṭha, jha, ña, ja, ra, ṭa, pa, cha, la, ā, sa, aḥ, ha, ṣa, kṣa, ma, śa, aṃ, ta, e, ai, o, au, da, pha.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Trika-hṛdaya*:

"The *nādinī*, however, resides at the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and is designated by the syllable 'na'. It has been stated that the Blessed Lady Mālinī is indeed the primary Śākta form through the union of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the womb-syllable (*yoni*).

This name, "samastakāmadugha" (the cow of plenty that grants all desires), is significant in its meaning; it is joined with the garlands of Rudra’s powers (*rudraśaktimālā*), blossoming with fruits, possessing the bees of the resonance of the dissolution of the world's coolness, bearing both supernatural attainments (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), and endowed with the power of giving and taking—this last being due to the traditional phonetic identity between the letters *ra* and *la*. For this very reason, even a mantra whose ritual procedure has been lost becomes complete through this ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Even *sāñjana* [mantras], such as those of Garuḍa and Viṣṇu, become bestowers of liberation upon attaining the state of *nirañjana*.
This is because, through the placement of the *mātṛkā* whose source is non-different from the letter *pha* and others, they attain a stable existence within other *tattvas*.

"The nature of the elements (dhātutattva) has been indicated in sequence from the beginning to the end; there are twenty-three [elements], starting with the earth element (*pārthiva*)... and so forth, by which the application of the elements, beginning with the earth, is described. Furthermore, in that very same place, according to the three Śrīvidyās:
"That power of the Creator of the universe which is said to be inherent in Him as the triad of vidyās— that, O Goddess, becomes His will when He desires to emit the world."

Thus, by virtue of being the nature of the first surging forth, she whose essence is the desire to overflow externally and who constitutes the abode of rest for the subject is called *parā* (the Supreme); even beyond that,
there is that which is well-ascertained as "this object is thus and not otherwise."
That which makes known within this world is called the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
Thus, wherever the rays consisting of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*), which are interwoven within, converge, there the All-pervasive One alone unfolds.
That which is of such a nature is called the "Parāparā" (the Intermediate). Beyond that as well—
When, however, they bring about that very object with the thought, "May this thing become thus," it is at that very moment that action (kriyā) is said to occur in relation to that object.
Thus, that which consists of the manifold variety of various subjects, objects of knowledge, and so forth, is called the "lower" (apara).
As stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda:
"That by which this world, from Śiva down to the earth, is both sustained and perceived as being of the nature of non-conceptual pure consciousness alone."

The Supreme Lord illumines, and that is His supreme power (*parā-śakti*). That by which [He illumines] through both difference and non-difference, like a mirror and an elephant and so forth, is the supreme-non-supreme power (*parāparā-śakti*). That by which [He illumines] solely through difference, characterized by mutual distinctness, is the non-supreme power (*aparā-śakti*).
Thus ends the exposition of the threefold knowledge in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord (p.
in the Niṣkala [state], there is the single-syllable word; in the two [states of Śakti and Sadāśiva], there are the two pairs of one-syllable and three-syllable words.
Thus, according to the Parāparā-bhaṭṭārikā: "In the venerable Mālinīvijaya,
for the purification of the path regarding Māyā and in the rite of initiation in all respects,
the wise man should employ the Aparā-mantra in those ritual acts where no mantra has been specifically mentioned."
One should likewise join [the principles] from Vidyā up to Sakala; then, above Īśvara, one should join the eightfold group beginning with Niyati, which constitutes the Parāpara state.
Furthermore, the wise one should not perform any rite enjoined by the ritual rules within the six limbs above the Sakala [level], nor within the Niṣkala [level] by means of the Parā [mantra].

Thus, for those possessing extremely subtle discernment, the fundamental meaning here is indeed easily understood and need not be further determined; however, for others, even the presentation of logical arguments would be as useless as grinding what has already been ground. [The exposition of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the earthly principle and so forth, has been applied here in the sequence: *oṃkāra* as the Śiva-principle, *aghora* as the Śakti-principle, and so on. Furthermore, again—
In that very context, according to the principles of the Śrī-vidyā,
even for those [phonemes] beginning with *pha* who have attained their respective positions within the reality by means of the placement of the *mātṛkā* of the non-dual source (*abhinnayoni*),
The element of earth (pṛthivītattva) is indicated by the letters from 'ca' to 'ña' in successive order;
[these] consist of twenty-three vowels and consonants (*).

By these and other such statements, the application of the principles (*tattva-yojanā*) is established. Furthermore, according to the intention of the venerable Aparābhaṭṭārikā, two cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) are pervaded by her, with each of the two being pervaded separately.
This pervasion of Aparā has been declared in reverse order. (The summary of the meaning here is: *icchāśakti*...)
The meaning is that the triad of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is to be understood in reverse order.

By these and other such statements, the placement of the principles (*tattva*) is as follows: within the *phaṭ*-syllable are the two mundane cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*) of the earth; within the *huṃ*-syllable is the illusory egg (*māyīya*); and within the *hrīṃ*-syllable is the power-egg (*śākta*). Furthermore, in the description of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the venerable Goddess Parābhaṭṭārikā: "The triad is pervaded by the letter *sa*, and the fourth by the trident."

The supreme pervasion (*parā vyāpti*) is proclaimed by means of the emission (*visarga*) as that which transcends all. Furthermore, the intention in explaining this is as follows: when there is purification through one form, the Guru who possesses contemplative awareness (*anusandhānavān*) should effect the purification by internalizing other modalities within that very same state.
He says that even when there is an inability [to include it], there is another sequence:
"But when inclusion is impossible, the subtle is purified by the subtle;
for that, being pure, does not produce a subsequent continuity because its seed-nature has been exhausted."
Thus; and all of this is well known in the *Trikasāra*.
Thus,
the application of the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*) has been described in one way; yet, again,
according to the intention of the venerable mantras such as the *Mātṛkā-sadbhāva*, the *Ratiśekhara*, and the *Kuleśvara*, it is [described] otherwise.

Otherwise, even in the *Aparatantra* and other works, this has been described many times as being almost entirely erroneous; yet here, it appears that all of it is presented in a completely different way. Thus, a great upheaval, like a disturbance within one's own army, has arisen among those who know the scriptures—a disturbance that threatens total destruction. Nor is this merely a matter of conventional terminology, such that...
Furthermore, when described in various ways according to forms constructed under the influence of human desire, it becomes consistent in this context— for example,

Southerners designate boiled rice by the word *caura* (thief), while the Saindhavas use that same term for a robber and designate boiled rice with the word *krūra* (cruel); yet the Kashmiris use that same word for hulled barley, wheat, and rice.

For if it were merely conventional (*sāṃketika*), then because it would be unstable and non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*), the relationship between the object of purification and the purifier and so forth would be useless; thus, there would be nothing but its indefinability. Furthermore, even convention possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*) itself; for what is called "convention" is nothing other than that which is established through the will of the Supreme Lord.
For this convention is not merely fashioned by the will of the Blessed One;

rather, it results in the attainment of fruits such as pacification (*śāntika*) through the performance of rites involving nourishment (*āpyāyana*) and so forth, which are based on the names, syllables, scripts, and other elements [of the mantras]. (p. 126)
If that is so, then since all things would be accomplished by a single convention alone, what is the purpose of relying on other conventions?

Or, if one were to rely on them, there would be an infinite number [of conventions], such as those belonging to one's own school, other schools, the worldly, the assembly, the teacher, the dense [mass of tradition], and those fixed for each individual person, and so forth.

Even that [process], preceded by the establishment of conventions, must indeed be examined; yet there is no utility in such [examination], for the accomplishment of the task is achieved by this much alone—this statement, even when uttered and heard by those whose inner cavities are devoid of letters, is certainly fitting. If you argue that the unimpeded will of the Blessed One does not fall within the scope of critical inquiry, then enough!
This heavy burden should indeed be abandoned through false exertions such as memorizing, reciting, explaining, and investigating scriptures;

one should remain taking refuge in silence alone. It is the Will of the Lord that must deliver one from the flood, and it is His will alone, consisting of grace, that brings this investigation to its ultimate conclusion. Not so.
127) Indeed, by those who merely stretch out their feet while lying down comfortably, or who eat without reflecting for themselves,
[there arises] a progressively more subtle reflection produced by the supreme Lord’s grace, which is most intense with respect to their own [spiritual] requirements.

Or else, one should remain averse to the cultivation of the foundation of virtue. This must always be reflected upon: we do not abandon this much—that having ascertained it here, one should remain until we have set aside all these various objections within the supreme ground of the Supreme Goddess’s transcendental speech (*parāvāk*), which is not a reality at all.

In that [reality] whose essence is absolute sovereignty—characterized by the performance of the unsurpassably difficult—which is not tainted even by a single atom or a mere fraction of a part of dependence—it has been refuted almost entirely already; nevertheless, it is now addressed in detail: as for what was stated, "from that, the Śiva-tattva... [and so forth].

Regarding the claim that "this sequence beginning with Earth" and so forth constitutes a sequence, we say that there is no such sequence. That which is this supreme, transcendental freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord—which is without sequence, manifold, and which internalizes infinite diversity—is itself the nature of the threefold reality (*trikārtha*). For instance, this very [freedom] is the Aparā, the Parāparā, and the supreme Bhairavī (Parābhaṭṭārikā).
The supreme state of Bhairavī exists even above the principles of Sadāśiva and Anāśrita-śakti (p.
128), because even that which ends with those [principles] is made into a seat; for this sequence is intended for the purpose of reviving the divine body.
Just as elsewhere one should place a great preta, laughing and unconscious,
red in color, possessing great brilliance, and adorned with three eyes.

Namely: at the root of the foundational power (*ādhāraśaktimūla*) is the root (*mūla*), the bulb (*kanda*), and the root-essence (*āsāramūlaka*); in the *lambikrānta* is the staff (*daṇḍa*) ending with the principle of *kalā*; the knot (*granthi*) consists of *māyā*; the fourfold seat (*catuṣkikā*) is the lotus of *śuddhavidyā*, and right there is the venerable Lord Sadāśiva; he alone is the "Great Preta" (*mahāpreta*) because of his being intensely dissolved (*prakarṣeṇa līnatvāt*) and because of his preeminence through awakening.

Because of the destruction of the body consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and because it consists of the awareness of *nāda*, that [state] has arisen; having emerged through the three apertures at its crown, it reaches the triad of the Supreme (*parā*)—consisting of *śakti*, *vyāpinī*, and *samanā*—which resides within the end of *nāda*.
Above that is the pure triad of lotuses, which is the Self (*ātman*). Within this differentiated state, which consists of the entire universe...
Having visualized the deity as desired as the supported one, pervading [the seat] by way of presiding over it as its substratum, one should worship. On this point there are intermediate verses:
"This trident, with its tip reaching the *dvādaśānta*, flashes forth from its base."
Having abandoned the sequential order, one who reaches the forefront of the circle of goddesses shall attain the state of a sky-walker.
This Khecarī consists of filling the tip of the void extending from the Mūlādhāra to the end of the twelve finger-breadths;
she is so called because of her own movement and abiding, and because of her consumption of her own nectar.
Thus ends the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*). For it is said:
"The Lord, the Great Preta, laughing, insentient"—by this [verse], the seat ending with Sadāśiva, which is situated within the wing of *nāda*, is concluded in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*.
Having said, "All this is the seat," (p.
One should meditate upon the three-pronged trident of power (*śakti-śūla*) arising from its navel;

by this, the three prongs consisting of Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā are described, and even there, they are defined as being in the form of the three white lotuses of the states of Unmanā, Ūrdhva-kuṇḍalikā, and the Supreme Abode (*paramadhāma*). This is what is meant.

The *paramāsana* (the supreme seat) is so called because it is the ultimate limit (*parā-paryantatvāt*); and since the Goddesses abide above that, this very [seat] is the supreme abode of the limit of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) known as *paśyantī*,
which exists in the form of *nāda* precisely as something to be transcended, as stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*.
Now, that power of knowledge of ours which is the nature of Sadāśiva—
that is the state of Paśyantī, the supreme [state], for the virtuous grammarians.
Thus:
for the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the goddess Rudra, when directed toward the inner self (*pratyagātman*),
comes to rest only within the supreme power of knowledge of Sadāśiva, whose nature is the power of Anāśritaśiva.
Regarding the two deities Brahmā and Viṣṇu associated with the mind (*manas*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"In that state where there exists only the status of being a subject (*mātṛtāmātra*), Rudra is the presiding deity;
when the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are cited."
Thus it is said. On this point, those who desire discernment should consult the *Tantrāloka* itself.

130) In the stages of *vaikharī* and *madhyamā*, the state of the powers of Īśvara and Sadāśiva—namely, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)—belongs exclusively to the principle of Īśvara (*īśvara-tattva*).
In Sadāśiva, there is the ground of Parā-Pratiṣṭhā; this is established by scripture and reinforced by one's own self-awareness.

Above Paśyantī lies the ground of Parā, the Blessed Lady, wherein everything shines as nothing but non-dual, and where the sequence—though subtle enough to be discerned only by a refined intellect—is contemplated. For even though [this occurs] in the plane of Vidyā and the plane of Māyā, [it remains so].

Although manifestation exists there without distinction, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is otherwise. For in the stage of *vidyā* (in the Lord Īśvara), the entire collection of subjects and objects merges into the single "I" within the Self (in the Lord Sadāśiva).
Then, that which was concealed is reflected upon as "I am this. This occurs within the common conscious Self.
In the locus [of Śiva as the power of knowledge], both [the powers of action and knowledge] are reflected and appear as non-different;

this is what is called "grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya). For this very reason, in the state of Īśvara [which is the state of Śiva whose nature is knowledge], [the power] consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Just as states assume their respective conditions within the path of *māyā*— [having abandoned both the form of *śuddhavidyā* and *mahāmāyā*,
it is that very state of *Īśvara*]— it is not the case that the *aparāparā-śakti* itself becomes the *aparā* or the *parā*. This is what [is meant].

[Regarding the possibility of "otherness," he states the reason with the word *yat*: because "remoteness and proximity" (*parāparatva*) have been shown there in the principle of the Lord (*īśvara-tattva*), therefore "remoteness" (*paratva*) follows in the state of the Lord.

This was stated by the venerable feet of Utpaladeva regarding the principle of the Lord—[the phrase "stated" (*abhihitam*) should be construed as "and as having the nature of both remote and proximate"]. As it has been said:

In this state, the "inferiority" (aparatva) of entities arises from their appearing as non-self, while their "superiority" (paratā) arises from being veiled by the I-consciousness (ahantā); thus, that indeed is the intermediate state (parāpara-daśā).
Thus: "Supremacy" (*paratva*) is fullness, independence from anything else, and the sense of "I"; "inferiority" (*aparatva*) is incompleteness, dependence on another, and the sense of "this.
In the same way, it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the cognitions of 'I' and 'this' is real."
When light rests solely within itself, not directed toward anything else,

that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) characterized by resting in the luminosity of one's own self is called "I" (*so'ham*). However, that which is directed toward another is "this" (*idam*), and even that ultimately rests in a state that is not directed toward another, consisting merely in its own self-luminosity.

In that regard, in the first reflective awareness (vimarśa) there is the Śiva-principle; in the second, the state of the Vidyeśvaras; but in the middle form, the reflective awareness in which "I" and "this" are held as equal, like the pans of a balance scale, belongs to Sadāśivanātha and the venerable Lord Īśvara.
As for the distinction between these two cognitions—"I" and "this"—it is caused by the [respective] clarity or lack of clarity of the aspect of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva).

The state of having separate substrates for those two—namely, the "I" as the subject (*grāhaka*) and the "this" as the object (*grāhya*) within the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*)—is set aside; instead, their unification, which takes the form of a relationship within a single substrate, is *satī* (the Real), pure *vidyā*. This is entirely distinct from impure *vidyā*, which resides in the illusory subject. In that regard, when [there is the realization] of this "I":

That which is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) causes this "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) to manifest therein; because that [this-portion] is not yet clearly defined, it is the state of Sadāśiva. However, when the substratum has become clearly defined as "this," and one pours the reflective awareness of the "I-portion" (*ahamaṃśa-vimarśa*) into it—whether as "I am this" or "this is I"—that is the state of Īśvara; such is the distinction. That...
One should not think that what has been shown is inconsistent with the scriptures—
in the case of the Mantramaheśvaras and others, [within Śuddhavidyā and Mahāmāyā].

The great master Utpaladeva states the nature of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) as follows: "Mantra... [The form of mantra, though its ultimate reality is pure consciousness (*bodha*), is distinct from that whose ultimate reality is other than pure consciousness; it is "I," whereas this [object] is "this" again.
The word "again" indicates that this aspect of "this" is indeed different from the "I" situated above, because of which it is called *mahāmāyā* (the Great Illusion).]

"Regarding what was stated by others—that there is only the cognition of difference—it is because consciousness (*saṃvit*) lacks awakening that, even though the nature of the *vijñānākalas* consists solely in the supreme reality of pure awareness, their consciousness does not perceive 'I am not this,' but rather perceives only 'I' (*aham*);
for the *pralayakevalins*, it is 'this is I' (*idamaham*) that remains unawakened. [In this context—"here"—it refers to the *pralayākala*.]

In the state of *māyā*—that is, in all [lower levels]—although there exists within the manifestation of that non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) a corresponding reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which constitutes the very life-force [of consciousness], nevertheless, for one who engages in linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding that form...

Even for a subsequent reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—whether its existence has been obtained through grace from that [consciousness] or is non-different from it—the linguistic usage consisting of conceptualization (*vikalpātman*) occurs precisely as a form of reflective awareness characterized by duality:

"this is the body and so forth," "I am he who is the knower," "this is the jar and so forth," and "this is that which is the object of knowledge. This is so even though such a state [of non-duality] exists therein.

Since no other cause is perceived, even when a cause is postulated, it ultimately results in nothing more than an inseparable manifestation of that very same cognition; thus, such is the capacity of that very self which consists of non-conceptual awareness, and it is precisely through the possession of such capacity that it possesses the nature of infinite variety.

In this state of being, sovereignty becomes an imperishable perfection; for sovereignty is inseparable from it, since such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is possible even when there is an excess of manifestation within the self of the *vairkha* (the waking state), or within the object of knowledge (*vedya*) consisting of *māyā*, or within the abode of the *madhyamā* (the intermediate state). But here, in supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), it is exactly as it is in its manifestation.

Even the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*)—by means of that [awareness]—all entities appear as being entirely non-different, like water in water or flame in flame; they do not appear even in the manner of a reflection. It is only for the sake of instruction that even this [reflective awareness] is described as the Supreme Goddess.

To that extent, it becomes conceived as having a lower level of existence. And thus, the nature of Bhairava, which consists of light, is self-established, beginningless, primary, existing everywhere both at the beginning and at the end; what else could there be in that regard?
Let it be said: that which, consisting of the expansion of the nature of reality, manifests itself as self-luminous through its very identity with the Self,

and likewise reflects upon itself— even while not being devoid of such wonder— is that very reflection within the manifestation that directly perceives the future infinite millions, billions, and trillions of creations and dissolutions belonging to Māyā.

It would indeed become exactly of such a nature, and it would remain so, provided that in the process of creation one were to reflect upon the initial or intermediate state through its manifestation; for otherwise,
the suspicion and possibility of the latter deviating from the former would not be dispelled.
How could that which is incomplete— being severed from the mass of other entities that have not yet been manifested as non-different,

and which has not yet discharged the stain of sketching out the divisions beginning with Paśyantī and ending with the rest, all of which reside within the great abode of supreme Bhairava— be considered complete?

By virtue of not nourishing such an object, that form which has become the mere name of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) might be some kind of form; yet, in the absence of such an ascent into the stream (dhārārohaṇa), this [form] is nothing at all.
It would be proper to say: "May it shine forth expanding; may it expand so that incompleteness does not approach it;

may the mass of objective existence not remain established; may the discourse of non-duality not be fragmented; may the state of being the refuge of Bhairava not cease to exist; may it not bear the stain of duality; and may its supremacy be maintained by name alone"—this is precisely what is intended.

If it occurs and converges such that the manifestation falls [upon the object] at the very beginning and at the very end, then even through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it would fix its footing right there; for that is indeed the final portion. Thus, while bearing its own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*) for that duration, it necessarily incorporates within itself its own infinite internal portions—its prior, priorer, and so forth—which are inseparable from that very nature of its own self.
Even that preceding part, while manifesting and being reflected upon, is indeed complete; for,
through its identity with the essence of the reflection of the perfect manifestation that follows it— which occurs in the sequence of the posterior part—
it does not abandon its own perfection as that subsequent form.

The manifestation and reflective awareness of the internal aspects of one's own preceding and even more preceding parts— which are forcibly drawn forth by the necessity inherent in its own nature— is likewise undivided; thus, those manifestations belonging to each preceding stage remain so even when analyzed into their respective subsequent parts, whether two, three, or more.
