136) When each individual [part] becomes supreme and full, as far as it conforms to the force of the non-deviation from the essential nature of the state of Bhairava that has been attained, and thereby embraces the wonder (*camatkāra*) of its own respective preceding portion; until such time as...
That very form which is the closest abode of your own self-luminous, innate Bhairava,

or rather that body called Bhairava which is the resting place of your own will— you yourselves, intent on higher contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), become skilled in its discernment in a forest region, whether it be devoid of the contraction of limiting adjuncts such as lakes, mountains, and trees, or even possessed of them.
In this very way, the gaze that remains unbroken from afar, attaining a state of non-interruption,
may attain the status of a traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*) for entering into the awakening of Bhairava;
one should cast the gaze upon a place devoid of trees, mountains, walls, and the like.

And so forth; otherwise, if [the object] were to fall apart part by part starting from the first portion, or if it were indeed without parts, then what distinction would there be between this and other incomplete cognitions? The distinction, however, lies in its being as if produced by the wonder of infinite variety held within, compared to other incomplete cognitions.
"Of one who possesses the experience of the desired fullness"—let those who have received the supreme teaching understand this for themselves;
for when the lotus-heart of the bound soul has blossomed by the rays of the descent of the Supreme Lord's power (p.

Not even by our hundreds of words, nor even by needles of extremely sharp meaning, can a breach or an expansion be effected; for in this very way, the gaze falls fully upon the jar, and therein, indeed, non-conceptual consciousness (*avikalpa-saṃvit*) descends instantaneously only at the final stage. From there, however, the conceptual cognitions gradually emerge.

They enter further and further inward from the region near the periphery; what need is there for anything else? Thus, here too, it is established that the Śiva-principle is eternally free of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), yet the source of conceptual construction, possessing the essence of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), beginningless, and the primordial ground of all—there is no disagreement on this point. However, it becomes fully manifest in such a manner only if...

Indeed, the consciousness of the earth rests only upon the earth, which is the final of all [elements]; for if that consciousness were to exert itself in manifesting and reflecting upon its own essential nature, it would manifest the earth as its object through non-differentiation,
and its true reality is this very nature.

[It is] that which consists of the state of the limited sovereignty of consciousness as manifested by the power of duality— which appears as a single essence preceded by that non-duality fashioned by the full expansion of its own freedom; and which is of the nature of the non-distinction between the cycle of the grasper and the grasped of Māyā,

consisting of the primary matter (*pradhāna*), its transformations, the intellect (*dhī*), the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra*)— which is itself a transformation of that [intellect]— and the causal roots based thereon.

The earth exists by subsisting as the substratum for the group of elements beginning with space and ending with water, which are extended from the category of the individual soul (nirmātra); for as long as it persists through mere projection, it remains truly existent in its own essential nature.

To the extent that the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) must project [their causes] because they possess fivefold qualities, to that same extent, while being projected, they do not lack the continuity of the nature of their intended material cause; rather, they are connected to their own prior roots, which are linked to a succession of other original foundational roots previously projected for the sake of establishing their own specific forms.

It might be argued that while it is logical for the existence of the effect [to arise] from instrumental causes and the like, these might somehow fail to follow through; however, this point—which would undermine the present context—has already been thoroughly extracted by us elsewhere in a treatise dedicated to explaining those matters, and thus it is not elaborated upon here. Therefore, first of all, there is earth, and from that, water.

And having internalized the wonder of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through its light, one must indeed fulfill [the process] as possessing the existence of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of such a reality of the earth; that is to say, in the end, that very Blessed Lady of Full Consciousness is indeed Śiva himself—by this very means.

According to the method of the logic of instruction (*upadeśayuktinaya*), O Brahmin, it has been established in the scriptures that even a mere portion possesses every form, and that within each single principle (*tattva*) there exists the nature of consisting of all thirty-six principles. And thus, the teaching of the venerable *Spandaśāstra* remains pervading all objects at all times, as if out of a desire to be seen.
Then, what is the use of much speaking? One will understand for oneself.
Thus, this should be made to penetrate the heart; that very point is indicated here by the final quarter-verse. What more need be said?

That which does not exist without another is, for its part, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that other—just as *śiṃśapā*-ness is the essential nature of a tree. (In this context, *śiṃśapā*-ness never occurs elsewhere than in a tree; wherever there is *śiṃśapā*-ness, there...)

In this context, "tree-ness" refers to *śiṃśapā*-ness; this is its essential nature (*svarūpa*), because *śiṃśapā*-ness cannot exist without a tree. [Objection: But how can one thing be the essential nature of another? This would contradict the principle of natural necessity (*niyati*). To this, he says:

Regarding the statement that "the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśa-svātantrya*) is not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*)," it is as follows: here, it is not the case that wherever there is "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*), there must be "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātva*), because that [treeness] is absent in trees such as the *vānīra*.
Thus, treeness is not the essential nature of śiṃśapā-ness. [This occurs] when the unfolding of necessity (*niyati-vijṛmbhā*) is concealed by the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, whatever does not exist as long as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) does not exist,
necessarily exists without that [nature], just as the exclusion of "śiṃśapā-ness" does not exist without "tree-ness," and yet [qualities such as] earth and so forth do not [exist without it].

The successive higher principles do not exist without their respective preceding elements, such as water and so forth; for their very natures are such that earth cannot exist without water, since solidity is observed precisely through its support (*dhṛti*). In this sequence, how could the gross elements exist without the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), and those [subtle elements] likewise not exist without the expansion of the senses, nor the senses without that kind of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*)?

And all these [entities], beginning with this [universe], do not exist without being rooted in a subtle form that is undivided and inherent; even the *mūlaprakṛti* (root-nature) is an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) only in relation to an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), because it necessarily participates in the differentiation of those objects of enjoyment. Consequently, it is contracted, and by virtue of that contraction, the net of bonds (*pāśajāla*)—consisting of time, portions (*kalā*), and so forth, which are superimposed upon its own self—is essentially of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidātmaka*).

Otherwise, how could there be contraction for consciousness which is of an undivided nature? And how could there be the sovereignty that is the cause of contraction—synonymous with *māyā*—without [this sovereignty]?
Furthermore, regarding contraction, [consciousness] depends upon the intensity of that contraction, whose essence is the state of being contracted.
Apart from the forms of the slightly contracted, the fully contracted, the slightly expanded, and the fully expanded [states] belonging to You,
all this that manifests would not exist at all; rather, it is entirely Bhairava, whose essence is independent and perfect manifestation.
"Without anything at all, there is none"—thus this sequence of reality is established by one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). Regarding the *Śruti* as well, the meaning is this:
one should consider that "the earth also has the nature of water. Why? To this it says: "without solidity. The intention is this:
if the earth did not have the nature of water, it would lose its very stability; for solidity indeed...
Hardness is merely produced by water; it is simply their mutual cohesion. Even if one were to argue, "Where could the earth exist without being of the nature of water?
Let the former earth also be within the water," what harm would such an assertion do?
On the contrary, it would serve only to nourish the supreme consciousness whose essence is the venerable Lord Bhairava, who is the self of all things in their complete perfection.

And all this—beginning with the Supreme Goddess (Parā) and the venerable Goddess (Aparā-bhaṭṭārikā), and so forth—is according to the distinctions of the principles (tattva) that arise from the convention of existence (sattā-samaya) in Paśyantī and the other levels of speech, ranging from slightly clear to more clearly manifest. For it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "Indeed, differentiation is unmanifest in 'I-ness' (ahantā), whereas differentiation of the principles is more clearly manifest in 'this-ness' (idantā)."

In this state, the "inferiority" (aparatva) of entities arises from their appearing as non-self, while their "superiority" (paratā) arises from being veiled by the I-consciousness (ahantā); thus, that indeed is the intermediate state (parāpara-daśā).
Thus, the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā), who is Great, shines there with a body suited to that very splendor (*tejas*).
For in that state, wealth would never be found in the hand of one who is destitute, even if it were to come into being in the future. Indeed! [p. 142]

How could the distinction between the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), and so forth, be subsumed within the supreme state? For when differentiation arises, then the designations such as Paśyantī and the rest occur; but when there is no arising [of differentiation], how can those designations apply to that state?
To this he says: "Even though it is yet to be," and so on. "First" means even in the absence of its future existence. [The object, although it is] last...

In the first manifestation, there would indeed appear only that which has the nature of being clearly manifest as the essence of its unity and differentiation; thus, [the state of] "future-ness" exists. For instance, if such things as "Kalkī will arise, he will slay those devoted to unrighteousness," and so forth, had not been manifested, how could they have been recorded in the Purāṇas? In some creation, Kalkī likewise came into being.
If it is argued that [the light] is afflicted, is that very same [light] this [afflicted state], or is it something else? If it is something else, then it is unmanifest;

[if you say "it is something else," the intention is that you have arrived at our own position by your own words]. If it is that very same [light], how can there be a difference in time? If it is not delimited by time, how [can there be a difference]? If it is argued that this is because of its nature as consciousness (*cittva*) and its being the form of the universe (*viśvarūpatva*), then, in that case, regarding what is not delimited by time:

In the Supreme Lord, who is the very nature of consciousness, eternally inseparable from the power of the universe; whose singular form is non-dual, manifesting through the contraction and expansion brought about by His own sovereignty as the processes of withdrawal and emanation; and who is Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka, never departing from the tips of our tongues and the depths of our hearts.
(143) Since even this very proposition of ours, "everything exists," is being put forward, why is it not accepted with some modesty, or rather,
why is it not determined and examined by yourselves with an even more open throat? Therefore...
This Śiva-principle, which is without beginning or end, manifesting by itself, and whose essence is the sovereignty consisting solely of absolute independence characterized by fullness,
encompasses within itself the entire collection of principles whose ultimate reality is the Self alone, because they are perpetually arisen within supreme consciousness.

Because it is non-contradictory to all things and because it bestows grace upon everything, as long as the form of Bhairava remains seated— transcending all divisions of time and incapable of being designated by terms for specific states— it exists in the form of the Great Emanation (*mahāsṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which is appropriate to this scripture, and not through the sequence of limited emanations (*mitasṛṣṭi*) and so on; this is established in the context of the *saṃpuṭa* yoga.

The tradition of our teachers is this: because every single principle (*tattva*) and the entire multitude of principles are encapsulated by pure supreme existence (*śuddha-parasattā*), it will be stated that "starting from the stage of Paśyantī, there is the manifestation of parts and sub-parts consisting of the threading together of divisions. [The word *iti* is used here in the sense of a reason. From that point onward indeed—
The relationship between the object of purification and the purifier (śodhya-śodhakabhāva)—
as stated [in the verse]—
is a systematic arrangement that cannot be denied. Thus it has been said:

O lady of excellent vows, all that which begins with the earthly element and extends up to Sadāśiva—know that to be of the nature of Prakṛti, joined with birth and destruction; for this is the sequence of ascent by way of the relationship between the object to be purified and the purifier. Thus it is said: "beginning with the earthly and ending with Sadāśiva."

Perceiving this and so forth, the power of the self (*svātma-śakti*)— which is the true nature of the venerable goddess Parāparā and is like a mirror— is that wherein the very form of the venerable goddess Parā shines forth like a reflection. And indeed, even in the case of the venerable goddess Parā, there certainly exists the conceptualization of a reflection according to the principle of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*).

Since even that must be explained by means of the very expression "reflection," one might ask: is this mode of expression restricted solely to the *parāparā* [level]? To this he says: "And that which...

For there, the intention is that the form (*rūpa*) in both the original image (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*) is one and the same. The form, whose ultimate reality is always oneness in both the original image and the reflection, is like the mere act of perceiving a face; it is not said to be "reflected" in that sense.

As it has been stated by this same author elsewhere: "For this is the definition of a reflection—that which is incapable of appearing as distinct and appears only through being mixed with another; that is a reflection. However, because its true nature consists solely of that [original object], it appears there in a different way—such as the reversal of front and back, left and right—just like the form of a face.
(145) "This very one, this very one, this very one"— the meaning is that the supreme reality (*paratattva*) resides within the power that is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara-śakti*).
[It possesses] a resemblance to the form of the other without abandoning its own essential nature.
They say that it has the nature of a reflection, like [the image] in a sword-blade or the surface of a mirror.
Thus,
because it is impossible for another to be mixed with it, its differentiation cannot be manifested;
they call this a "reflection," just as a face [is seen] in a mirror.
Thus, elsewhere the true nature of the reflection is explained; here, the principle that "it has neither location nor form," and so forth, should be understood.
That which is said to be reflected possesses qualities identical to its source and is not of a different genus. And thus, within the stainless mirror of Parāparā, whose true nature is Paśyantī—
That very [reality], filled with the totality of the principles (tattva) beginning with earth and so forth, according to the aforementioned sequence,

[in which the thirty-sixfold nature resides within each single element through the differentiation of cause and effect, in due order]; it is realized precisely by embracing such an internal, innate, unartificial, ultimate, and non-perishing reflective awareness.

Even the present body of the venerable Parābhaṭṭārikā, while casting its reflection, reflects upon that which is to be contemplated as being of one form with it— earth, water, and so forth— precisely through the non-alteration of the primary awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is incapable of tolerating any change in its own nature; thus, by way of threading together the various manifestations of difference, it [reflects] within its own kind.
And as long as it reflects within the Vimalā [kalā], so long does the inversion of the principles (tattvas), beginning with Earth,
arise [this should be construed as "of its own essential nature"]; that which is the principle of Power (śaktitattva) in supreme consciousness is precisely that.

Within the supreme and non-supreme self, that which is the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) is the power-principle (*śaktitattva*); thus, beginning from the letter *kṣa*, there is the abiding of the principles starting with earth. But as for the venerable Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka, he says: "Now, just as the pervasion of the two principles by the letter *kṣa* and so forth is established by logic according to the different tantras, so too is it pervaded within the *a*-group. To this, he replies:

"O Blessed One," and so forth. He is eternally full and infinitely autonomous; he is never subject to reversal at any time. [The reason for this is: "because there is no existence apart from the nature of consciousness," and so on—this has been stated many times.
When the Supreme Self is reflected upon, the categories (*tattva*) are nothing other than the single essence of that reflection (*parāmarśa*); and that reflection begins with the letter *ka*.

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consists of the vowels from *kṣa* to *a*. In that state, there is indeed non-duality; however, in the "supreme-and-inferior" (*parāparā*) level, there is a nature consisting of both difference and non-difference according to the principle of reflection.

And that [reality], composed of supreme-and-inferior awareness (*parāparāmarśamayī*), has as its body the series of phonemes from *ka* to *kṣa*, and as long as it maintains the reflections of the principles (*tattva*) residing up to the Supreme Goddess (*Parābhaṭṭārikā*) situated above itself, for so long [does it persist].

Within those very [levels], from the non-artificial (amāyīya) realization of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—beginning with the *śrauta* and ending with *kṣānti*—the principles (*tattvas*) are established through the inversion of the upper and lower, by virtue of the majesty of the nature of the upper as the original image (*bimba*) and the lower as the reflected image (*pratibimba*).

This is the intended meaning: therefore, there is nothing contradictory in [the statement] that the earth is the letter *kṣa* and so forth, with respect to the forms to be purified (*śodhya-rūpa*), because even there the state of transcendence (*paradaśā*) does not depart. It is precisely this continuum of letters beginning with *ka*; and therein, due to the predominance of its own aspect (*svāṃśodreka*), the manifestation of the *madhyamā* stage situated within its own aspect, and the inclination toward the form of *vaikharī* abiding in its own nature.

"Because of inclination" means because of being attached. The state of consisting of phonemes, mantras, and words is the function of the portion to be purified—let this incidental matter rest; it has been determined by me alone in the commentaries (*pañcikā*) on the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures.
Although it was stated that, according to the venerable *Mālinī-bhaṭṭārikā*, the established position is one way and otherwise in other cases, even that has now been determined.

May those belonging to the Supreme Lord, whose knots of ignorance have been shattered by the instruction on the Threefold [Kula], reflect upon this as it is being examined: having transcended the ultimate limit of Paśyantī—

which consists of the power of Anāśrita and is that very Paśyantī who is the nature of the power of Anāśrita, the state at the commencement of all entities— they [abide] in the supreme consciousness of the Supreme Lord.
Your honors ought not to forget what was stated regarding the "three deities"; and thus, within the supreme consciousness...

In the state of the Middle Way (*madhyamāpade*), which is the locus of the unfolding of the Supreme-Non-Supreme Goddess (*parāparābhaṭṭārikā*), stability is contemplated. First, the Middle Way, situated in its own domain—the sovereign state (*aiśvara-pada*) consisting of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)—is of the nature of a cognition that conceals the clearly manifest object of knowledge. Therein, the signifier (*vācaka*) is superimposed upon the signified (*vācya*), and within that signifier as well, the signified is superimposed.

If, in every instance of the denoted, the denoter—which is itself the universal self—is also the universal self, then superimposition (*adhyāsa*) can proceed through this mutual concealment and blending; it cannot be otherwise. For even a deficiency of merely three or four finger-breadths would not allow one cloth to cover another. And as for its being the universal self:

Due to the mutual intermingling of their essential natures, there may be the denotative function (*vācakatva*) of the vowels in the form of seeds (*bīja*), and the denoted function (*vācyatva*) of the consonants in the form of matrices (*yoni*). This is because they sequentially consist of Śiva and Śakti;
herein, the seed is designated as Śiva and the matrix as Śakti.
Thus:
"Likewise, due to the division consisting of seed (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*), there are two kinds;
the vowels are considered the seed, and those beginning with *ka* are remembered as the womb."
Thus, according to the determination of the venerable *Pūrvaśāstra*, Śiva alone—without relinquishing his state as the subject (*pramātṛ*)—is the signifier (*vācaka*);
and Śakti alone, who penetrates the objective aspect (*prameyāṃśa*), is the signified (*vācyā*). For even in the case of difference, [Śiva] is the signifier.
It manifests as nothing other than the undivided nature of the subject, which consists of both the object to be conveyed and the conveyor;

this very state of solidification (śyānata), whose essence is Śiva and whose form is the seed-syllables of the vowels, constitutes the womb-nature of the consonants of Śakti, because the womb proceeds from the seed itself—this we shall determine immediately hereafter. Therefore:

If there were a state of mutual intermingling between the seed-syllable (bīja), whose nature is the vowels, and the womb (yoni), then, alas, the production of all fruits would occur without effort; thus, liberation and worldly enjoyment would both be drawn forth and ripened simultaneously. Since the phoneme of the seed-syllable is likewise [independent] within its own self, and the phoneme of the womb is likewise so, what could distinguish one from the other? This being stated, let it not disturb us who are devoted to the One.
Therefore, we shall utter that speech which consists of consciousness and contains within it infinite variety; as it has been said:
"There is no cognition in the world that does not follow upon words;
all knowledge is perceived as if permeated by speech."
Likewise,
if the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
manifestation would not be manifest, for it is that [speech] which performs reflective awareness.

Thus, even within the sphere of illusory worldly transaction (*māyīya-vyavahāra*), that which effects reflective awareness consists solely of the nature of a single unifying awareness (*ekaparāmarśa-svabhāva*), characterized by the clarity of conventional, sequential phonemes and words. (p. 150)

Speech is of the nature of light, and this has been established by others through great effort; here, however, it is accomplished without effort for those who possess the excellence of the continuous stream of instruction. Therefore, we have not exerted ourselves here merely to display the sanctity of our bodies resulting from visiting the houses of grammatical teachers—a result which is otherwise in vain.

In this very way, the resolution of objections regarding distinctions such as sequence and non-sequence, or priority and posteriority, is already established for the *navātmapiṇḍa* and other *mālāmantras*. Thus, it is the Blessed Lady Mālinī herself who is the mantra of Power (*śakti*), namely *hrīṃ na pha hrīṃ*; whereas *hrīṃ a kṣa hrīṃ* is the designator of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*). *Na* [is not].
To Him who, through the penetration of the Father, fills the entirety of creation;
Thus it is said in the *Durūpagarbha*:
"The letters *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* are the crest-lock (*śikhā*); then the garland of the head (*śiromālā*) and the head (*mastaka*).
The eyes are *ī* (above) and *ī* (below); the nose is *e*; and the two ears are the mudrās *ṇu* and *ṇū*."
The *ba* and *ka*-series [consonants] are located in the mouth, teeth, and tongue, as well as in speech;
*va*, *bha*, and *ya* are in the throat and the right shoulder and so forth; and *ḍa* and *ḍha* are in the two arms.
Ṭha is in the two hands; jha and ña are the fingers; jra and ṭa are the trident and skull-bowl;
pa is the heart; cha and la are the breasts; the letter ma, joined with the visarga, is the life-force (jīva) and the milk.
The letter *ta* followed by *pa* is said to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*); *ṣa* and *kṣa* reside in the belly and the navel.
*Ma*, *śa*, and *ta* are located in the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs; likewise, [the letter *ya*] is in the knees.
The letters *e* and *i* are the two shanks, and the letters *da* and *pha* are the feet that follow them.
Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Above the two ears are the two *ṇa*s, the ear-lobes, and their entry; therein are *u* and *ū*.
151) This is the true nature of the power that is the primary, ultimate, and middle locus; for this very reason, it has been stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
For the successful attainment of desired fruits by those who follow the Mantras and Tantras,
one should deposit the *mālinī* [mantra] of distinct origin for the sake of the body of Śakti.
Thus, it has been determined elsewhere as well that [this] is always of a different origin;

it does not reside in the individual soul (*puṃs*), nor in the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), nor in the power (*śakti*). As for the clear immersion (*samāveśa*) which occurs when the unfolding of the dissolution of the body takes place through the power:
This world, which unfolds while covered by the sense of "I," is joined with the notion of "this-ness."
This manifest and unmanifest sign is the potency of mantra, both supreme and non-supreme;
it emerges from the union of the individual soul (nara) and power (śakti), yet remains distinct from the form of Śiva.
As it is said elsewhere:
"A mantra applied to the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva) becomes inert; when applied to the supreme principle (paratattva), it is fruitless;
but when applied to the Power (śakti), it bestows the fruits of all actions."
Thus it is said. Herein is the distinction:
elsewhere, the birth of accomplishments (*siddhi*) arises from the manifest (*vyakta*); from both the manifest and the unmanifest (*avyakta*), there is the twofold liberation (*vimokṣa*).
From the unmanifest comes the primordial power (*bala*) of the Supreme; however, this discussion does not apply to the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
Thus one should install the mantra:
"Because of their insentience and lack of activity, they do not bestow enjoyment or liberation."

Thus, this being the case, because everything has everything as its essence (*sarvasarvātmakatvāt*), those very sounds—*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *tha*, *ca*, *dha*, *ī*, *ṇa*, *u*, *ū*, *ba*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*—which have been mentioned here in sequence with respect to the limited consciousness (*apara-saṃvit*) of this world...

The auditory organ (*śrotra*) consists of the nature of sound (*nāda*), which is of the form of the womb (*yoni*). Because it brings about the nourishment of the immortal (*amṛta*) within the Self alone, it is said to be "of the nature of the immortal.
As it is stated elsewhere: "Having fallen upon the ground that nourishes the fourfold seed, and having attained fullness, it suddenly [arises]."
Having attained the state of being composed of the essence of the flavor whose nature is grasping, and having become a specific odor in the form of the earth,

it resorts to the status of the instrument of touch right there; and this much is the power-based (śākta) and sexual (yauna) abode, which, presided over by the seed-syllable of Īśāna, is reflected within the instrumental power that is the self of speech, and from that as well—

By means of the unfolding of the power of action (*karaṇa-śakti*), which exists as the seed for ascending to higher supports, [the subject] rests upon the vegetable source in the form of the intellect (*buddhi*). Then, having entered the sources of earth, water, and fire through the form of the *paśyantī* level,
it extends into those very seeds within the hand— which is of the nature of grasping— in the form of the *cākṣuṣī* earth, sharing its commonality with that.

Having abided in the organ of smell, which is the instrument of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and the final of all instruments, and having ascended by means of the seed-syllable of Īśāna, one takes hold of the power of hearing; through the conjunction with the upward-pointing seed-syllable of Unmeṣa, that which resides in the womb of the organ of bliss becomes composed of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Śuddhavidyā.
The Śiva-tattva, which is infinite power and undivided because it pervades the beginning, middle, and end of all things, is what is described here (p.
153) in the Mālinī [vijayottara], following this supreme consciousness and following the existence that consists of Paśyantī, respectively.

Vāyu and Māyā are *pa* and *gha*; Sādākhya is *na*, *bha*, *la*, *ca*, and *ṅa*; Īśvara is *ī*. Śuddhavidyā, consisting of Śakti, is *icchā* alone; Anuttara is the independent state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*). *A* is called Śiva; *māyā* is *bha*; Śuddhavidyā is *rāga*; *sparśa* and *ya* are *kāla*; *pāyu* and *ahaṃkṛt* are *ḍa*; *niyati* is *ḍha*; and *hasta* and *manas* are the letter *ḍha*.

The faculty of bliss and intellect are *ṭha*; the male principle (*pumāṃs*) and the form of intellect (*dhīrūpa*) are *ña*; egoity (*ahaṃkṛta*) and the form of necessity (*niyatirūpa*) are *ra*; the mind (*manaḥ*), the foot-faculty, and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) are *ṭa*; the ear, the mind, and the hand are *pa*; the skin, taste, time (*kāla*), and *dha* are *la*; the tongue, the power of bliss belonging to Śiva (*ānandaśakti śaivī*), and *ā* are [the next]; the nose, the fire of knowledge (*vidyātejas*), and *sa* are [the final].

The power of speech-emission is *aḥ*; the hands are *īśa* and water is *ha*. The anus is *māyā* and air is *ṣa*; the organ of bliss is *sādākhya* and earth is *kṣa*. The feet are *pumān* and sound is *sa*; sound is *kalā* and ether is *śa*. Touch is the *baindhavī* power and *śava*; form is *aṃ*; the nose and skin are *ta*; taste is *śiva-śakti* and *sāttvī*.
The syllable *ga* is smell (*gandha*),
*ai* is ether (*nabhas*), likewise *o* is air and fire (*vāyutejasī*), *na* is the eyes, *au* is taste (*rasa*), *ā* is water (*āpaḥ*), and *da* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛt*) and the anus (*pāyu*).
And here, on this very earth, the aforementioned "entrance into the body" occurs; in this way, the state of being the self of all things (sarvasarvātmakatva) is fully established.

For it is the Supreme Goddess herself who, according to the stated method, while casting her own reflection into Paśyantī, at that very same moment [at the very time of casting the reflection into Paśyantī].
Established in identity with her own self within the central abode (*madhyamadhāman*), she assumes various origins;

due to the infinity of the manifold variety arising from the mutual intermingling of the seeds of those respective origins, she possesses innumerable modes through the distinctions of various *kula*-persons and so forth, partaking of an incalculable diversity, just as it has been described regarding Mālinī.
One should worship the goddess Mālinī, whose form is surrounded by infinite bodies of the Kula and by the Kula-śaktis themselves.
And by this very sequence, the yogi intent on practice becomes a possessor of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) within the external worlds, the *tattvas*, and the bodily wheels (*cakras*).

In whichever body or vital breath [it occurs], just as certain medicinal herbs, having arisen, perform only a specific effect, so too [is it with these mantras]. To this, he says "just as" and so forth. Just as certain medicinal herbs, having arisen, perform only a specific effect, so too [is it with these mantras].

Even if a certain accomplishment (*siddhi*) were to be bestowed by the arising of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or by the application of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth— since even here one does not transcend the operation of necessity (*niyati*)— for indeed, according to each respective scripture, preceded by the arrangement of phonemes in various ways, there is a predominance of this or that venerable phoneme (*varṇabhaṭṭāraka*) corresponding to its own specific knowledge.
The *prastāra* has been described as a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) formed by a fixed sequence resulting from the precedence of their respective letters;

and from that very [prastāra], the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) has been described. Now, in order to demonstrate that very *mātṛkā*—which, when augmented by the bestowal of such potency, brings about the manifestation of the mantra—it is said: "Just as..."
In the Śrīnityātantras,

because of the predominance of the seed-syllable of delusion (*mohana-bīja*) consisting of the letter *e*, and because of the predominance of the entry into the nature of the supreme *nāda* (the cause),
[the reading "cause, supreme *nāda*, and self" (*hetuparanādātma*) is also accepted by the wise with reference to the ultimate meaning, and not otherwise].

Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the introductory context": here, the arrangement follows precisely the sequence from the venerable *Śrīmantra* ending with the letter *pha*, as it arises in conformity with that;
this very [sequence] pertains to the *kula*-men and the *kula*-powers (*kula-śakti*).

The intention is regarding their arrangement, and the fruit is not merely the concealment of the phonemes, mantras, and so forth; likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīvājasaneyatantra* after arranging the phonemes appropriately:
"This divine wheel of the Mātṛkās is the abode of Viṣṇu’s station."
When correctly understood from the mouth of the Guru, it cuts the bonds of the bound soul.
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Śrītrikahṛdaya* as well:
"Of the wheels, tridents, lotuses, and so forth; of living beings, rivers, and men; of weapons and of the Śaktis; and of whatever else there may be."
That which is the abiding of the phonemes is their potency residing in the mantra;
by that being protected, they are protected, while the remaining phonemes are merely themselves.

Thus it is said: for instance, even when there is a change in a single syllable or mora of mantras, those very same [identical] mantras undergo transformation according to the divisions of Āṇava, Śākta, Śāmbhava, and so forth in the scriptures—just as, for example, the seed-syllable *māyā*, the *praṇava*, and all the seed-syllables of immortality (*amṛtabīja*) appear differently in Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Vāma, and other scriptures. The first [syllables] are for others, and the subsequent ones are for those following; likewise, they are like the back.
Furthermore, the rule for the Mātṛkā is considered to be as it was before, even for the preceding ones.
In accordance with this very principle, according to the nature of their different origins.
This supreme goddess Uttaramālinī is beyond the countless [deities] such as the Śāktas.
Thus, among the abodes situated above and below, which are numbered according to their divisions:
one is the Bindu; furthermore, among the others, that which was previously mentioned moves to the end.
Having placed that number which is on one's own back in one place, one should cast it;
from this, the sequence [is determined] by other desired numbers that have been touched, and again [the process is repeated].
As it has been stated regarding the procedure for perceiving the infinite [reality] of the Kula-śaktis:

by this very procedure, those practitioners of the yoga of the Kula-puruṣas and Śaktis who have become devoid of [external] offices, [attain] fully, as soon as the world— beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass— has arisen, that which was previously described.
Three and a half crores of mantras, enjoined by Śiva,
having bestowed grace upon the multitude of individual souls, have gone to the state free from affliction.

Thus, in this way, the Blessed Lady Parābhaṭṭārikā, who possesses various divisions of words, is—in her primary mode of being—the very form of the Blessed Mālinī; she is infinite, and although her own nature manifests a universal form (vaiśvarūpya) as demonstrated by enumeration, she remains so.
And there too, in the same way, because of the predominance of the three aspects within one's own self as the universal self, it should be understood that [the self] consists of phonemes, words,

and mantras by virtue of being the instrument of purification; for the fetters (pāśas), which manifest from the aspect of Paśyantī, are subtle indeed and are what must be purified, since they constitute "fettering" only while remaining internally latent.

In the expansion of Śakti, which consists of ever-arising manifestations, at the stage of Madhyamā, there is indeed the act of purification, just as the coarse external impurity is removed once the subtle internal impurities have dissolved. However, the stage of Vaikharī is contemplated as being contained within the consciousness of Parā-Bhaṭṭārikā;
for it is not that Vaikharī is impossible therein. To illustrate this, consider a child...

Although their places and organs of articulation (*sthāna-karaṇa*) become clearly manifest after two or three years, nevertheless, it remains established that for these [sounds], their production increases more and more in intensity day by day, month by month, or even daily; this being so, if [the calculation] were based on the *madhyamā* scale:

Otherwise, there would be no manifestation of the subtle portions of the phonemes— which are the undivided [elements] of the places of articulation (*sthāna*) and the organs of production (*karaṇa*) that will become manifest through the expansion of such *vaikharī* speech— for a child born on that very day, one born a month ago, or even one born a year ago, until they have attained linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*).
If it is argued that there must be a distinction—that it is precisely the middle [speech] which is distinguished by its linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*)—then let this first be examined:

one acquires linguistic proficiency while merely hearing those sounds and seeing their objects; moreover, one would reflect upon the phonemes (*varṇa*) while they are being heard, and these are indeed heard as consisting of *vaikharī* speech, and in them, that [middle speech] is manifest in form.

Therefore, like one born blind, the *vaikharī*—composed of the internal, the intermediate (*madhyamā*), and the [external] places of articulation (*sthāna*) and organs of speech (*karaṇa*)—indeed exists even in a mute person;
and the Blessed One has likewise declared that consciousness possesses this all-encompassing nature.
Thus, the very state of *vaikharī*, having attained its expansion within the substratum of *madhyamā*, [manifests] in its own portion.

When the unfolding of the relationship between the manifest signified and the signifier occurs within the self through the manifestation of mutual diversity, as long as one remains having internalized the entire web of objective reality (*tattvajāla*), so long does the state of the Goddess exist in the form of the purifier: as the *Aparā-bhaṭṭārikā* during the unfolding of the *madhyamā* level within that [state], as the *Parāparā* during the unfolding of the *paśyantī*, and as the Supreme Goddess (*bhagavatī devī*) in her essential nature.

The Purifier, who is indeed the Self of all and whose form is pervasive, abides in these three states alone; and it has been stated that extension likewise occurs in this very manner—this is purification (p.

However, agency belongs only to the Lord (Bhagavān), who, though his autonomy has assumed limitation, ultimately rests within the majesty of Śakti; whereas the state of being an object of purification belongs to that which consists solely of limitation— the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) who is inseparable from Lord Bhairava, whose singular nature transcends the thirty-seven [tattvas].

The meaning intended here is this: "The loss of freedom for consciousness, and the lack of consciousness even within freedom. [This refers to] the state of Paśyantī, which is the nature of the power of the bound soul (paśuśakti) manifested by the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) of Sadāśiva—whose essence is the agitation of deities who are equal or superior—and which consists of the first manifestation of duality.
This impurity consists of two kinds of atoms, because it causes the loss of one's own true nature.

Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of experience is that which is called *māyā*, bestowing birth and enjoyment; while the *kārma* [bond] resides in the agent's lack of awakening. All three of these exist solely through the power of *māyā*.

Thus, it has been stated that while this collection of bonds (*pāśasamūha*) is gross, the web of bonds exists even above in a subtle form; this was indicated by the first aphorism. This is the determination regarding the web of bonds of the individual self (*narātman*). As it was said by the venerable Śrī Somānanda in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
May Śiva, who has entered our very form, perform the warding off of obstacles by means of his own self through the supreme power; salutations to that pervasive Self!
Thus, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* (p. 161), it is indicated that within the entire complex of ritual actions (*sarvakriyākalāpa*), there is this very nature;
and therein also, there is the progressive dissolution even of the objects of purification and the purifiers.
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.

Thus it is said. Therefore, this entire stream is such that even the purifier and the act of purification are themselves merely the object to be purified—this has been stated in the venerable *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra*: "There is a single excellence in all three, and their simultaneous existence indeed occurs;
for while speaking of one thing, one conceptualizes another, and while conversing about one thing, one perceives another without conceptualization; but here, however, [all] is perfectly complete."
At that time, the Blessed One is indeed Bhairava— through the cultivation of the instructions of the oral tradition of experience beginning with these words—
the meaning of this, which consists of one's own consciousness, cannot be denied; therefore, it is not simultaneous, but rather,
due to its extreme subtlety, it is unperceivable, and thus there is the conceit of simultaneity, like the piercing of a hundred petals of a *śirīṣa* flower.

If this is asked, what indeed is this expression "simultaneously" (yugapat), meaning "at the same time"? If it is argued that [time exists], then within the inward-turned self of consciousness, according to the aforementioned method, what is time?

For that [consciousness] has as its very life-force the manifestation and its absence consisting of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which takes the form of the object of knowledge; thus, even though [time] is situated in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of knowledge, [it does not apply here].

If it is argued that "he [the knower] would leap into knowledge"—then what distinction is stated by way of "knowledge" regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), whether it be within its own self consisting of light or otherwise? There is a collapse into mutual dependence; for even such [arguments as] "because of intrinsic difference" (*svato bhedāt*) and so forth [are undermined].
Everything being spoken would result in nothing but the face of knowledge (*jñānamukha*); and thus, that same fault [would apply]:

even when "many" is said to mean a differentiation of hundreds of flowers and shoots, because of the connection with parts ending in atoms (*paramāṇu*), it would follow everywhere that there is no action (*karma*) due to its subtle nature, nor would there be any synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*).

It would coexist with the absence of knowledge—given that there is a distinction between the subsequent synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and memory, and that the latter depends upon experience, [memory] would be absent due to the absence of experience. I have examined this at length in my *Padārthapraveśanirṇaya-ṭīkā*; so what is the use of this web of futile talk here?
Thus,
even the goddess Parāparā, who exists as a purifier of the lower [levels] while residing within the Blessed One, is present there where the goddesses Aghorā and the others abide—
through the union with whom the practitioners (sādhakas) and Vijñānākalas become Aghora and the rest, appearing in the form of Mantramaheśvaras and so forth.
By the grace of the powers beginning with Brāhmī,
the individual practitioners (sādhaka-aṇavaḥ), such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, [attain their status]; for the Supreme Lord is indeed the venerable Bhairava.

What else can it be but that [the Lord], whose body is completely filled and overflowing with the entire mass of powers, creates the [energies] beginning with Brāhmī through His own sovereignty by the deployment of His innate power? Thus, since even the purifier is subject to purification, there is another excellence; and according to this principle, because the triad of the object to be purified, the means of purification, and the purifier exists everywhere, the *trika* (triad) is inalienable.
As I have stated myself in the *Stotra*:

"And there is no infinite regress in this way, because all of this consists solely of the supreme consciousness of the Blessed One. Thus it should be understood; even purification, or ultimately even the purifier, [is so] when the aspect of duality surges forth.

Because it consists of bonds, that which is to be purified is in fact the purifier; in the ultimate sense, the fire— which is non-different from the consciousness of Bhairava, capable of burning away all impurities— is indeed the state of fullness when it enters into everything,
as he will state later.

(164) Thus, "he who knows this in its true essence," and so forth; for that [reality] consists of the nature of all deities, such as the supreme, the intermediate, and the lower, because they are essentially one with supreme consciousness.

Based on such statements as, "The eight Yoginīs of great power are born from the limbs of the higher and the lower," even the infinite range of signifiers and signifieds belonging to worldly sciences and other systems is included. Thus, this relationship between the purifier and the purified exists precisely by encompassing an infinity of conventions—past, present, and yet to come. It is not [otherwise].
Thus it is established that there is no infinite regress, no over-extension, no over-pervasion, and no lack of ultimate reality for that which is conventionally designated.

This being so, let us return to the subject at hand: the connection is that the vowels beginning with *a* themselves, through their association with time, are those which are proclaimed as the Moon and the Sun within that;
by the word "that" (*tat*), the previously mentioned *akula* consisting of Bhairava is referred to.

By that, the Akula itself is grasped as containing within it all mental constructs (*kalanā*). Herein lies the power of Kula; for it is said: "That which abides here as the singular form of pure consciousness—that indeed is the state of the Fourth (*turyatā*).
And just as in the statement "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," the state of the Vijñānākala is indeed the state of the Fourth, if that were the case there.
The meaning is that if power were not of the nature of *kalā*, then what distinction would there be between the fourth state (*turya*) and that which transcends it? Likewise, in the *Spandaśāstra*:
"Then, in that great void, where the moon and sun have dissolved..."
Like one in the state of deep sleep, the deluded one becomes awakened and unenveloped.
Thus, by means of that power residing within the womb [of consciousness], the supreme light contains power within itself; such is the intended meaning.
For the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) consists essentially in the act of ideation (*kalanā*), for without it, even the unmanifest (*akula*) would not exist.

That which is called "beyond the fourth" (*turyātīta*) is nothing at all, because it is entered into the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptapada*), and because its continuity with the fourth state is likewise identical.
Furthermore, the reflective power (*vimarśaśakti*) is the supreme Goddess Parā. As it was said by Rājanaka Maṅgala in his *Stuti*:
O Three-eyed One, you alone are seen as the Lord, the Light, capable of governing or knowing the three worlds;
yet the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), by manifesting identity even within difference, thereby proclaims the defect of duality.
Thus, the state of the venerable Lord Bhairava— which consists of unsurpassed sovereignty—
abides as fullness, as emaciation, as both, and as neither;
for it exists by having drawn all things within its own self, and because there is nothing external to its own nature that could constitute a burden.

Since no being whatsoever exists [independently], emaciation and fullness are established as distinct; and because there is emaciation, it possesses both natures and is devoid of both. In that regard, although...

In this regard, there is no blemish whatsoever concerning the emergence of succession or simultaneity; for the emergence of succession and simultaneity is dependent upon creation and so forth, and the meaning is that creation and so forth are nothing but the non-reflection of one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*). "To such an extent" means having a measure such as fullness, thinness, and so on. And this very thing constitutes its sovereignty (*svātantrya*):
The reason why there is "this-ness" (*aitadātmyam*) even amidst the appearance of distinctions such as creation and so forth is that [Brahman] is "perfectly full" (*paripūrṇa*);

the sense is that even distinction is non-different from the Light. According to the method of the aforementioned teaching, this much of the supreme consciousness of the Goddess Parā is a single mass consisting solely of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of its own essential nature, which comprises the infinite future dissolutions and emergences.
Thus, this Lord Bhairava is independent, perfect, and all-pervasive;
there is nothing that He would not manifest within the stainless mirror of His own Self.

According to this principle, within the very nature of the Self—which cannot tolerate either succession or simultaneity—[one should not think: "If there is succession, there is a fragmentation of sovereignty; how then could there not be simultaneity? For simultaneity exists precisely through its dependence on succession; thus, there is no fault. As long as there is the manifestation of succession and non-succession, so long does this [Self] conform to that [manifestation].

The sequence must be examined; as for the non-sequence—[if the sequence is to be examined, then the non-sequence must likewise be examined, which is why it says "non-sequence" and so forth]. However, since that [non-sequence] exists only within consciousness preceded by that [sequence], it is stated [in response to the question "How then are sequence and non-sequence [distinguished]? regarding the utterance of "non-sequence"]—"In the case of the demonstration," and so on. Let it be so.

167) Since it is in every respect characterized by succession, this entire reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which consists of the form of speech (*vāgrūpa*), is indeed sequential;
however, that which consists of internal consciousness (*antaḥsaṃvit*) is non-sequential. Thus, this [consciousness] is always of such a nature, and in this very way, it is manifold.
The Supreme Goddess Parābhaṭṭārikā is the Sovereign Power; therefore, according to that sequence, there is the designation "at" and so forth.

Thus, the power of freedom consisting of Will within the self of the Supreme Lord—whose expansion of objective phenomena has not yet unfolded, and whose essence is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the nature of internal, dense consciousness—is called "a. And that state, by its very condition, is called Will.
Being designated as such, and because there is no excess of what is desired, it consists precisely of the reflective awareness of supreme existence; as it is said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"The manifestation of the Heart, being 'existent' (*san*), becomes the agent of the act of becoming."
That very [state] is the reflective awareness of action (*kriyāvimarśa*).

Thus: although this Supreme Lord, who is constantly aware of His own nature, may follow after the powers of *kula* even while contemplating a form consisting of the state of the power of *akula*, nevertheless, by virtue of His awareness of *kula*, there must indeed be a distinction for Him— this is the existence of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the possessor of power, Bhairava.

168) "Just such" means that very state consisting of mutual orientation, whose nature is vibration (*spanda*), which is the surging forth of one's own self; this is the meaning.
However, when, through the blossoming of the fragrance arising from the attributes of consciousness (*ciddharma*), [it occurs]...
Possessing manifold arrangements for the initiation of the creation of various effects.

The first *tuṭi* of will (*icchā*) is indeed the state of the mind being oriented toward [the object]. Thus, consisting of vibration (*spanda*), it takes the form of mere external orientation; it may consist of the mere will that has not yet delineated the object to be created, or, through the delineation of each respective object to be governed, it assumes the nature of effort characterized by agitation.
There is a twofold division regarding her state as one who partakes in sovereignty through the form of fire (*vahnīrūpatā*). As it has been stated concerning the Intermediate Power (*madhyā*):

she is either merely of the nature of will (*icchāmātra*), being distant from that which is to be created, or else, having attained the state of exertion (*prayatna*), she is near. In that regard, this [power] possesses the nature of Īśāna. Furthermore, the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*), as it flows forth, has issued out as *ā*.

*Paripūrṇecchā* is *i*. It is *icchā* itself, which, through its sovereignty consisting of the power of future cognition (*bhāvijñānaśakti*), desires to grasp [objects] and is thus the nature of *īśana*; it is *ī*. But when the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*) unfolds, it consists of the unfolding of all objects of desire; it is *u*. Even while unfolding, it [unfolds] those things yet to unfold as well, through forms that are exclusively the unfolding of the nature of the entire internal vital breath (*prāṇa*).
By means of the multitudes of objects appearing as portions of difference that are largely indistinct and situated within the range of the internal organ—
thereby diminishing the supreme consciousness through the power of contraction— the Supreme Deity, whose form is the insatiable longing of the bodiless one (Anaṅga), [manifests].
(169) *Ū* is the upward-facing power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which has borne the entire multitude of phenomena and is clearly manifest and expansive. Thus,
these two powers of Bhairava, the Supreme Lord— the first being "full" (*pūrṇā*) because its nature consists in the complete fulfillment of His own essence.

And because she is non-different from the power of Cāndramasī, she exists together with Umā; thus, the creative impulse (*kalanā*) called Will (*icchā*), which consists of the state of resting in one's own bliss and whose form is Soma, is designated as the "Great Emanation" (*mahāsṛṣṭi*), as will be stated there:
"I sacrifice the emanation" (28). The second [power], however, is intensified by the entry into the pouring out of the mass of existents that constitute her own nature.

By that very emission, she becomes emaciated; her activity consists in the manifestation and expansion of the circle of states (*bhāva-maṇḍala*). She is of the nature of the Sun, her own essential form, the *Kula*-consciousness whose essence is the desire to withdraw [the universe], the power of Great Withdrawal (*mahā-saṃhāra-śakti*) known as Knowledge (*jñāna*).
And even there, by virtue of reflecting upon her previously expanded form, she [manifests] within herself in due order.

Having perceived one's own nature as consciousness (*svasaṃvidātmaka*) through the state of the pair consisting of the forms of the Moon and the Sun, as well as the form called "existence" (*bhāva*), there is no contradiction even regarding the processes of emanation and withdrawal which consist of the Moon and the Sun; nor is there an infinite regress here,
even with respect to knowledge and will.

It must be stated that even for those two— expansion (*prasara*) and non-expansion (*aprasara*)— there would follow the undesirable consequence of having to postulate further internal expansions and non-expansions of will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth.
Abandon, for now, this wandering in the delusions of external objects; enter rather the subtle path of reflective inquiry.

For as soon as cognition arises even with respect to a jar or the like, knowledge manifests itself as inherently luminous, variegated by the portions of the object of knowledge—the jar and so forth—and this occurs even in that case.

Even the first subtle manifestation of a jar or other object, which is variegated by that [state of non-existence], is perceptible; for the emergence of a single entity is preceded by the manifestation of its absence from some other source. Thus, the sovereignty of consciousness itself—consisting of the desire for an entity to arise—is the power of lordship (*īśana*), which is obtained through the means of knowledge that is self-awareness (*svasaṃvit-pramāṇa*); it takes the form of the accumulation of those entities.

The plenitude of consciousness, which is the fullness of the reality of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-sattā*), is itself the object of awareness; thus, being a mass of bliss within one's own self, one becomes likewise autonomous. Therefore, even bliss is not to be denied.
And the Lord Bhairava—the Absolute (*anuttara*) whose essence is the supreme wonder beyond all designation, possessing power—is present everywhere as the agent.
Even there, it indeed shines forth in the unfolding of the will for supreme bliss; however, it does not [shine] in the self-reflection of those who are unblinking (the senses).

For those who, by investigating the dissolution of these [objects], rest upon the plane of knowledge, those very powers of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*) of the Blessed Ladies descend as non-different from their own consciousness itself— because they are undivided due to their fullness,
and because any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) acts as a divider, since that [adjunct] exists merely as something cognized through the body. For this very reason:
In the *Śrītantrasāra*, the reality of the shadow of one's own head is described as follows:

"Just as when one attempts to step over the shadow of one's own head with one's feet, the head cannot exist at the location of the feet; so too is this *baindavī* kalā. [The meaning is: the shadow of one's own head...]

Just as one who is ascending higher and higher cannot tolerate stepping upon his own feet, so too this power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) cannot tolerate dependence on an object of knowledge (jñeya) and the like, because it itself ascends higher and higher. For one who thinks that the nature of the power of knowledge is dependent on an object of knowledge and so forth— here [we reply] that this is not so, because of its self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva).
"How can such a mockery exist?"—this is indeed a great delusion on the part of those devoid of self-experience, even when it is not the proper occasion.
As it has been said:
"The power of delusion is so great that it cannot indeed be discerned."

Thus, the meaning is as follows: for those of coarse vision, the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is evident when there is the existence of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and so forth; however, even in the absence of objects of knowledge and the like, for those of subtle vision, the manifestation of the powers of knowledge and the rest certainly exists by virtue of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatvena*).
Thus, in this manner, the group of six has proceeded up to the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). Now, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), as it unfolds, is investigated:
[it consists of] will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) alone.

Action (*kriyā*) is essentially characterized by an intense effort toward the assumption of a nature consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages, which is filled with the wonder of the manifold intermingling of mutual essential natures. For action indeed consists of parts that are sequential in time. And as it was said by Bhartṛhari:
"Whether already accomplished or not yet accomplished, that which is designated as being in the process of accomplishment (*sādhyatvena*)..."
Because it possesses a sequential form based on its substrates, it is designated as "action."
Thus: "In the same way,
a collection of parts that arise in succession,
whose distinctions are mentally constructed by means of subordinate factors, is designated as 'action' (kriyā)."
And in this regard, the state of being prior and posterior occurs precisely through mutual intermingling. In that process,
whatever undergoes an intermingling mixed with another due to its connection with something else,
it becomes so by way of first entering into a nature that is predominantly void and devoid of reflective awareness.
Just as a frog or similar creature does not leave behind its body among floating objects, so too the nature consisting of unsurpassed bliss does not depart from there,
because it is of an indefinable form within all cognitions. And thus,
O small-minded one, this supreme Brahman is for you necessarily but a mere fragment of bliss.
Thus [it is said]. Likewise,
when the question is asked, "O Lord, how is supreme knowledge [attained]?"
"The supreme light contains power within its womb by virtue of the power residing within it"—this was the answer given. Furthermore, in the Gītā:
"Since I am beyond the perishable and superior even to the imperishable..."
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Thus, it culminates in being the substratum of all—
because its nature is that of a final wall, but rather because it is capable of sustaining succession; [this sequence] ending with sovereignty, will, and impetus resides within itself.

And because she is capable of expanding into the state of unsurpassed bliss (*anuttarānanda*), she, while immersing her own void-natured body, first enters a radiant form consisting of light, as in *ṛ-ṝ*. For how could the following of *i-ī* and the following of the audible *repha* in that radiant form be denied? As it has been said:
The Blessed One Puṣpadanta says:
"Or it is established because of the commonality of the name.
Indeed, in the motionless form of the void—[he clarifies this very point through the vision of the yogi, beginning with the words "In the void," etc.]—it is so.

In the desire to enter [the state of Śiva], there is already the ascent of the ladder of the perception of radiant form; then, through the entry into that immovable form, upon following the phoneme *la*—which consists of the stability of the true nature of the earthly form—the phonemes *ḷ* and *ḹ* arise.
And thus, at the ultimate limit, there is the very nature of Lordship (*īśana-rūpatā*) itself, by transcending the essential nature of all existing things.
Having flown for a longer duration, it attains a motionless and empty state; thus it "attains the state of having flown" (*plutatvam eti*).
This is because, according to the rule that there are no long vowels for the phoneme *ḷ*, whereas for the vowels beginning with *a*, there are indeed long forms.

The state of being longer (*dīrghataratā*) is its protractedness (*plutatva*), and that, according to the previous principle—meaning according to the principle beginning with "Bliss is the form of Brahman"—is nothing other than length itself; let this suffice for now. This tetrad, because it enters into the nature of emptiness, is said to be of a neuter form like a burnt seed, yet not in every respect.

Because they lack the nature of being seeds (*bīja*), they transcend both Śiva and Śakti, who consist of the seed and the womb (*yoni*). For if these did not possess the state of being seeds, then some third category would have to be designated for them. Since "being a seed" consists in both "being agitated" (*kṣubhyati*) and "causing agitation" (*kṣobhayati*), agitation certainly exists among these [powers] as well; however, because there is no causing of agitation, they are in every respect devoid of the state of being seeds.

This is the meaning. Since nothing else exists, and because it is not mentioned in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures—[as to how its absence occurs there, he says "pūrvādi" (beginning with the East)]—and since in worldly pleasures and the like, such a state of rest is itself the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), that very thing is called the "fourfold seed-syllable of nectar. Thus, will (*icchā*) and power (*īśana*) reside within the body of bliss.

And having entered into the unsurpassed supreme abode—which existed from the beginning and does not deviate from its own nature—one enters [the vowels] *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth, but not in reverse order; as it has been stated, when there is an entry such as *avarṇa* into *ivarṇa* becoming *e*, this constitutes entry into the state of the unsurpassed (*anuttarapada*).

There may indeed be a distinction: for while there is clarity in entering the state of bliss (*ānanda*), there is subtlety in the union with the unsurpassed abode (*anuttara-dhāman*). With reference to that, the Lord, the sovereign of the serpents, instructed the Chāndogas, the followers of Sātyamugri and Rāṇāyaṇīya.
"Half is the letter *e* and half is the letter *o*," so it is recited.

Even in the world, in common vernaculars and local dialects, the extensive employment of these sounds is quite evident; and even in the Pārameśvara [scriptural] traditions, when they are applied to the limbs (*aṅga*) and faces (*vaktra*) and so forth, the shortness of the letters *e* and *o* is observed in comparison to the letters *ai* and *au*.
It should be understood in this very way: this letter *e* exists as a seed-syllable (*bīja*) precisely with the intention of the letters *a* and *o*, namely as *e* and *o*;

this too is thus variegated (*śavalībhūta*), the very body of consciousness (*saṃvidvapuḥ*). And in the same manner, that very form remains as *a*, *ā*, *e*, and *ai*. Likewise, it should be stated regarding the unfolding (*unmeṣa*): *a*, *ā*, *u*, *ū* as *o*; *ā*, *o* as *au*. Only the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

Although its expansion may involve an immersion into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nevertheless, emptiness consists precisely in the entry into both forms—desire and mastery. As for desire and mastery, they consist in the transformation of one's own [nature].

"There is not"— by this very principle of what has been stated, such is the state. Thus, when desire and knowledge have attained fullness by entering into the nature of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara), one subsequently abandons the existence of the vibration of such limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and, ascending to the reality of non-dual existence, realizes the true essence of the Puruṣa-tattva, which consists of consciousness.

Thus, when the body remains as nothing more than the formless *bindu* and has dissolved into the unsurpassed state (*anuttarapada*), it is designated as "Amiti. For it is within the vowel *au* alone that the vibration of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) reaches its completion; since the powers of will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are included right here, its nature as a trident (*triśūla*) is described in the *Ṣaḍardhaśāstra*.

In such enumerations as these, the term *bindu* [is used]. Herein is the meaning: "That which is mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*) while the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*) remain is spoken of as *bindu* in the scripture; this is considered the *Śivabindu*."
According to this principle, when the universe— which, though not distinct from His own nature— emanates for the sake of attaining oneness within itself,

then that state characterized by the predominance of the form of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*) and defined as the immersion into fullness is called the *Śāmbhava* reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, when everything remains as nothing but pure consciousness (*vedanāmātra*), even though there is no distinction [in that state] from pure consciousness alone...

When the Supreme Lord emits the universe so that it may return into his own self, and emits it from his own self by means of its creation—first as the predominance of the nature of the possessor of power (śaktimat), but now... [p. 177] ...he emits it.
Because the emission of Śakti is predominant, when the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) has reached its full intensity up to the vowel *au* (ending in *aḥ*),

there remains this triad known as the powers of will, knowledge, and action, which is inherent within the essential nature of the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*), the venerable Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka.
It has been stated by the Supreme One that this [teaching] reveals the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, as soon as the universe is born from the will-power (icchā-śakti),
we declare that the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is the cause of its manifestation.
The power of action is the cause for the manifestation of external forms;
indeed, that which possesses the distinctions of beginning, middle, and end is nothing other than the single sovereignty [of consciousness].
Therefore, no separate name for these is ever found;
rather, for the sake of clear understanding, [the terms] such as *ullilasiṣā* and so forth are used right from the root text.

These consist of the initial, middle, and final stages of the vibration (*parispanda*) of the powers whose nature is knowledge and action: namely, *ullilasiṣā* (the desire to emerge), *ullasattā* (the state of emerging), and so on.
Their nature is one of radiant manifestation,
clearly characterized for yogins who have ascended to those respective stages as grasped through most subtle contemplation—
[contemplation being samādhi]— in the Śrī Svacchanda and other procedural scriptures.

These have been described as having the nature of "awakened" (*prabuddha*), "expansion" (*prasaraṇa*), and "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*), and so forth— [where "awakened" refers to will (*icchā*), "expansion" to knowledge (*jñāna*),
and "obscuration" to action (*kriyā*)]. For this very reason, it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Śivadṛṣṭiśāstra*, on page 178:
O You whose form consists of a nature filled with the weight of supreme and most intense bliss,
in whom the triad of powers is dissolved through the realization of the Supreme Self!
And so forth;
its power also has attained the state of universal form, like a lump of clay becoming a jar.
Having thus determined up to this point that there is indeed only one single reality (tattva) and no existence beyond enumeration,
that which is the very reality of Śiva (śivatattva) alone [remains].
It has been determined that the state of Bhairava is attained through the abundance of the wonder of the power of the expansion and vibration of infinite and manifold sovereignty.
In this regard, this very sequence mentioned here is also found in the first chapter of the *Saṃpradāya*:
"As long as that state of transmigratory existence—which consists of the delusion of the non-recognition of identity with Śiva—does not manifest," even then...

To that extent, the nature of Śiva as described indeed exists; and likewise, at that time, even the pentad of powers, though of a single form, exists by virtue of its effects with respect to empirical usage. For instance, in the state that is both supreme and non-supreme (parāparāvasthā), that very light which consists of the innate reflective awareness "I am" is of the nature of bliss (ānanda) because it is independent of anything else.

He remains as one whose consciousness is blissful; thus it is said that [the state] is "the delight of consciousness. Experience and manifestation occur only within the fullness of pure consciousness-bliss, and not in the external world; for this very reason, he is one whose dissolution occurs in that very [consciousness]. By this, "blissful consciousness" has been described.
However, will, knowledge, and action become manifest in dependence upon distinct objects and so forth; yet, in the supreme state (parāvasthā), they do not.

"I am full"—thus it shines forth; because it is of the nature of light, that very [light] is knowledge (*jñāna*). Because it is of the nature of intense activity (*saṃrambha*), that very [light] is action (*kriyā*).

Since its own nature is accepted as such, will (*icchā*) also exists therein; thus he says, "its will is to that extent. And this much is its essential nature and its action—this is how it should be construed. Even in the absence of distinct objects and so forth, [it remains].

Because the intensities of the manifestations of resolve, cognition, and action always remain unwavering due to their being composed of light, it has been stated that they possess the very fitness for the functional operations of will and so forth; this is called "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*) because, by virtue of its extreme subtlety, no differentiation is imagined within it due to the non-differentiation from that which is to be attained and so on. For this very reason, there is an equilibrium of powers (*śaktisāmarasya*), since its essence consists in the manifestation of pure, full consciousness alone.
And it has been stated that the highest state is the delight of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpāhlāda*).

Thus, the meaning is as follows: the manifestation of the object and subject—consisting of the jar and Devadatta, which are differentiated by the variety of the non-recognition of their non-difference from consciousness—is *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form); and this is an action (*kriyā*) whose constituent parts are arranged in a temporal sequence of before and after.
Dissolution into that consists in the experience of the mere delight of consciousness;
for His will is as great as that, His knowledge is as great as that, and His action is indeed as great as that.
It exists through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the three extremely subtle powers;
it is the supreme reality, always undivided, and characterized by the bliss of the nature of consciousness.
Thus: even at the time of perceiving a jar or other objects, one knows "I know the jar" as long as there is such a cognition;
yet, in this very act of knowing—[the word "atraiva" refers to the action]—there is no impairment of the experience for one who is free from desire.

Due to the absence of such orientation (*aunmukhya*), there is no cessation of that [object] without bliss (*nirvṛti*)—[for "orientation" refers to the prior stage of desire; and "without," because the determinations of objects are grounded in consciousness]. One does not engage with what is hateful at all, nor can one know it without consciousness (*citi*).
Thus: "In that way, whatever one desires to know or to do, action proceeds from that desire. (p. 180)
For she who existed in the past, her eastern and western portions must be conceived.
The attainment of the manifestation of that action is its unfolding; and regarding this unfolding,
for the sake of clarification through an illustration,
Śiva’s orientation has been established in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, as follows:
By casting one's gaze upon the initial movement of water that is flowing yet free of waves, its tendency toward becoming excessively wavy is indeed perceived.
As the hand moves toward the state of a fist, its initial trembling is observed;
this is the delight of consciousness established in itself regarding the act of creation.
The expansion of that conviction is what they call its orientation;
some great masters maintain that it is simply a slight swelling [of consciousness].
His will has become an effect through which he becomes possessed of will;
that gross expansion of his orientation is established as will.

Thus: "In some respects, Śiva partakes of grossness," and so forth. This has been made heart-felt through its logical consistency, as it constitutes the very life-force of the essence of all the Āgamas.
