This very one—[as it is said, "This very one," meaning he who, joined with the emission of power (*śakti-visarga*), emanates the universe]. As it has been stated:
That supreme Kaulikī power, which is said to be the desire for emission within this [consciousness],
certainly attains the nature of emission (visarga) through the force of agitation (kṣobha).
Thus,
the sixteenth digit (kalā), whose form is that of nectar,
has spread forth by means of the movement of the Bindu, which is the essential nature of both the transcendent (parā) and the immanent (apara).
She is the illumination of all things, yet she is devoid of emission (visarga). She is indeed Śaktikuṇḍalikā and likewise Prāṇakuṇḍalikā;
at the limit of emission, however, she is called Parā Kuṇḍalinī.

Thus, the Supreme Lord emits the universe, which consists of everything from the earth up to the power of Śakti, and takes the form of the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*; such is the extent of the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*).

It is sung of as the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) in the Person (*puruṣa*); they call that the sixteenth digit the "immortal" (*amṛtā*), because it causes the nourishment of even those sixteen digits, and because, being eternally risen, it does not set.

Thus, this is neither the Sāṃkhya view nor the Vedāntic view, but rather the Śaiva view alone: "The state of emission (*vaisargikī sthitiḥ*) is the natural condition of the Self casting itself into itself within itself. And it is precisely the power of emission (*visargaśakti*), belonging to the Supreme Lord, which is the seed of the ground of supreme bliss—as it has been said:
In the Siddhayogīśvarīmata,

Kuṇḍalinī is here the seed-syllable, consisting of consciousness and being the vital breath; from her arises the triad known as the Fixed (dhruva), Will (icchā), and Expansion (unmeṣa), and from that, in turn, the phonemes.
Thus, in this way, the form of the letter *a* and so forth,
by attaining density (*ghanatā*), assumes the nature of the *yoni* (womb/source), yet without falling away from its own essential nature; it remains precisely within its own essential nature.
The state of emission (*visargapada*) is said to transition into the form of the womb (*yonirūpa*), as it has been stated:
"O Great Goddess, that place where this emission attains rest is called the mouth of the Guru; it is also called the wheel of power (*śakticakra*)."
And so forth; the *ka*-group is the density (*ghanatā*) of the letter *a* itself, because it is produced in the throat. As it has been said:
"The places of articulation for the phonemes are eight: the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate."

Thus: for example, *a*, *kuh*, and *visarga* are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*). *I*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* are palatals (*tālavya*). *Ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are retroflexes (*mūrdhanya*). *Ḷ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* are dentals (*dantya*). *U*, *pu*, and the *upadhmānīya* are labials (*oṣṭhya*). *Ñ*, *ma*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ṅa* are nasals (*nāsikya*). *E* and *ai* are gutturo-palatals (*kaṇṭhatālavya*). *O* and *au* are gutturo-labials (*kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*). The *jihvāmūlīya* is [produced] at the root of the tongue. The *anusvāra*...

Regarding the term *nāsikya*: the palatal class (*cavarga*) corresponds to the vowel *i* because it is produced in the palate; the labial class (*pavarga*) corresponds to the vowel *u* because it is produced at the lips;

the retroflex class (*ṭavarga*) corresponds to the vowel *ṛ* because it is produced at the roof of the mouth (*mūrdhan*); the dental class (*tavarga*) corresponds to the vowel *ḷ* because it is produced at the teeth.

The letters *ya* and *śa* belong to the end of the palatal class; *ra* and *ṣa* belong to the retroflex class; *la* and *sa* belong to the dental class; and the letter *va* belongs to both the dental and labial classes.
p.
183) Solidity belongs to non-awareness (*abodha*), even though it is formless. As for its lack of awareness, it was stated [earlier] that this is due to the absence of sovereignty;
therein lies the Great Illusion (*māyoparimahāmāyā*), and in that state resides the *vijñānakevalins*. And by definition, they are "pure consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Just as in the *Pratyabhijñā*, a form that consists solely of consciousness but is devoid of autonomy [is described]:
"Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those for whom there is no supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the loss of their agency."

Thus, even for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that very nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) arises through the sequence of the sixfold group of powers (*śakti-ṣaṭka*) according to the method already described.
Therefore, the five [elements], when multiplied by six, become thirty; together with the six [powers], they become thirty-six.

In this way, the seed of Śiva itself, through its sovereignty (*svātantrya*), exists in some embodied form as the nature of Śakti, like a flower, by virtue of its state of solidification (*ghanībhūtatā*).

That very thing is designated as the *yoni* (womb); for, according to the previously stated method, it consists of the three corners of the grasped (*grāhya*), the grasping (*grahaṇa*), and the grasper (*grāhaka*). In reality, it becomes the locus of procreation (*prasūtipada*) precisely through its union with the seed (*bīja*), because it possesses the nature of a flower at that very moment—whereas at other times, it exists only by way of potentiality during the manifestation of this world.
The designation "thus" (tathā) refers to its being a womb (*yoni*). Thus, that very flower, by virtue of its triangular form, is the nature of the womb;
it is the manifestation of the creation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, appearing as the clearly differentiated objects of perception and so forth.

The venerable Bhairavī Bhaṭṭārikā, the Supreme Goddess, whose three corners consist of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* channels, as well as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the variegated (*śavala*), is the Mudrā;

she is designated as the "Womb" (*yoni*) because she is the substratum for that form of the womb. And so, in the *Śrīkubjikāmata*, in the investigation of the *Khaṇḍacakra*, this very point has been taught with primary emphasis.

"Māyoparimā and Mahāmāyā, whose form is the bliss of the triangle," and so forth; for this very reason, it is taught in the *Śrītrikatantrasāra* that the union of Śiva and Śakti— which is the singular, dense state of the seed and the flower of such a nature— is to be worshipped by oneself, through one's own self alone.
Through the union of Śiva and Śakti,
one whose nature consists of the compassion of Śiva and Śakti should worship the supreme triad of the union of Śiva and Śakti.

Thus, although this condensation (*ghanībhāva*) becomes manifest in the form of *vaikharī*, it nevertheless resides primarily within the body of *parāvāk*, which is the self of all things. In that regard, the distinction is that even the places of articulation (*sthāna*), the organs (*karaṇa*), such as the throat and lips, are themselves the self of all things. For indeed, it is clearly stated: "Even while internally conversing, one may see [the phonemes]."

This is indeed the experience [for the meaning is that there is no impossibility in what is desired]. Furthermore, the difference [between phonemes] is caused solely by their positions and so forth, because phonemes have the breath as their single substrate; what need is there for much [explanation], since even a child being taught perceives it within?

In such a manner—that is, by way of the nature of discursive verbalization—he reflects upon the multitude of entities through error; "error" (viparyaya) here refers to false cognition, which is the apprehension of contradictory and manifold aspects within a single substratum, while "doubt" (saṃśaya) is the same.
Or else, he reflects even through doubt, perceiving at least a partial determination; and that [reflection] is produced solely by the verbalization of speech.

For this very reason, there is also the application of closure (*saṃvāra*), opening (*vivāra*), slight breath (*alpapāṇa*), great breath (*mahāpāṇa*), aspiration (*āśvāsa*), and emission (*anupradāna*). That very vital air (*prāṇa*), rising upward and struck back at the head,
when it returns and strikes the internal cavity (*koṣṭha*), and because the opening of the throat is slightly constricted while being struck in that cavity, there is closure (*saṃvāra*).

The quality of the phoneme (*varṇadharma*) arises [therein]. Because it is open (*vivṛta*), there is openness (*vivāra*); because the resonance (*nāda*) is closed within the cavity of the throat, it is unmanifest (*avyakta*). These two—openness and resonance—are called the "accessory emissions" (*anupradāna*) in the case of breath and resonance. They are termed "accessory emissions" (*anupradāna*) because they are provided (*pradīyate*) subsequently (*anu*), after the production of the phoneme. Others, however, say that the accessory emission is the nasal resonance (*anusvāna*).

Like the resonance of a bell: just as the resonance of a bell follows after its own reverberation (*anusvāna*), so too, in that sound produced by the impact upon the vocal places (*sthāna*), the primary tone (*nāda*) is added; then, from the conjunction of the tone and the sound, a voiced sound (*ghoṣa*) arises.
When breath (*śvāsa*) is added, then from the conjunction of the breath and the sound, an unvoiced sound (*aghoṣa*) arises. This occurs when the air is great.

*Mahāprāṇa* (great breath). When the air is slight, it is *svalpaprāṇa* (very little breath). In the *Siddhāntakaumudī*, the externality (*bāhyatva*) of the articulatory efforts is established; as stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "The external efforts are eight," namely: opening (*vivāra*), closing (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), *alpaprāṇa* (aspirated), and *mahāprāṇa* (un-aspirated). In that regard:

The classification is as follows: *kha, pha, cha, ṭha, tha, ca, ṭa, ta, ka, pa, śa, ṣa, sa* are open (*vivāra*), accompanied by breath (*śvāsa*), and unvoiced (*aghoṣa*). *Ha, ya, va, ra, la, ña, ma, ṅa, ṇa, na, jha, bha, gha, dha, ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da* are closed (*saṃvāra*), accompanied by resonance (*nāda*), and voiced (*ghoṣa*). Among the classes (*varga*), the first, third, and fifth letters, as well as *ya, ra, la, va*, are of weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*).
The meaning is that the second and fourth letters of each *varga*, as well as *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, are "great breaths" (*mahāprāṇa*).

Furthermore, the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) must likewise possess their appropriate nature; otherwise, there would be no possibility of distinction among those [consonants] belonging to the same place of articulation (*sasthāna*).

The powers of making things disappear must certainly exist as well; for otherwise, the variety of mental constructs such as "I hear," "I heard," "I see," "I saw," "I will," and "I willed" would be impossible. Therefore, by this reasoning—wherein *yukti* (reasoning) is defined as an inference that follows from direct experience—one should investigate by penetrating further and further into the internal [reality].
For those who cultivate consciousness in that locus where the throat, lips, and other organs are a single mass of awareness whose nature is everything-in-everything,

there occurs the installation of the Lord of Phonemes (varṇa-bhaṭṭāraka), which consists of the great mantra whose essence is sovereignty and whose nature is the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of such a single mass of awareness.
As it is said in the *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
This consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness, is the supreme Speech (parāvāk) flowing by its own inherent force;
it is the true I-consciousness in which the entire multitude of phonemes has been withdrawn from beginning to end.
Thus, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it is said: "That reflective awareness of 'I', which, though its essence is light, has speech as its body—
that is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," [referring to] the state of being indistinguishable from the singular density of pure consciousness.
If it is asked, "How is there a distinction such that 'this is the locus,' 'this is the instrument,' and 'this is the phoneme'?"—
it is because of this very sovereignty [of consciousness] regarding its own nature in such a manner: "This is a jar," "This is pleasure," "This is knowledge."
"It manifests as 'I am the knower'. (In this regard, this point is to be discerned by subtle intelligence. There, the question and answer proceed as follows:
"But surely, the Absolute (anuttara) and Bliss (ānanda) are, by their very nature, devoid of differentiation.")
How is it that this entire manifold variety rests within one's own self?
Listen, first of all: this Lord of Consciousness is of immeasurable nature;
He is the Master of the creative power that brings about the emergence and dissolution of the manifold variety of infinite energies.
If Maheśvara were to abide with a body of a single, unchanging form,
he would have forfeited his status as Maheśvara and his nature as pure consciousness, just like a jar or other such objects.
It is indeed said that the defining characteristic of the insentient is its limited luminosity;
for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not so delimited.
Thus:

"The state of consciousness as the Knower— 'I am the Knower'— is established through the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures as independent of the collection of means such as the object of knowledge and so forth."
Thus, what effort or of what magnitude could there be for the manifestation of such diverse forms? For this very reason, all [beings... p. 188.
The stone, trees, animals, humans, gods, Rudras, Kevalins, Mantras, their Lords (Maheśvaras), and the Great Lords (Maheśas) and so forth—
all exist as the single ground of the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) alone, in the form of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) who is the self of all.

Thus, the body of sound consists of forms that are distinct or undistinct, manifest or unmanifest, and so on, which are not differentiated from the universal nature of those various locations and states.

It is proclaimed as "the potency of mantra" (*mantravīrya*). For instance, in the case of the *vīṇā*, *vipañcī*, *kacchapikā*, *muraja*, and other instruments, that very same sound, even when arising from various different locations, is said to be in a single place.
The same applies to high, middle, and low pitches, as it is stated in the *Varṇaśikṣā*: [text follows].
That vital breath, having risen from the navel and being sustained by the chest, throat, and head,
attains the state of resonance and sound through soft, medium, and intense efforts, beginning with the low (*mandra*) pitch.

For in the scriptures, it is taught that the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters are to be recited in the three daily libations (*savanas*) by means of low (*mandra*), middle (*madhyama*), and high (*tāra*) tones, respectively.

Thus, even though there is identity with the stable tone (*sthāyisvara*) residing therein—just as the single tone, whose nature is the locus (*sthāyin*), remains one despite the distinctions of high, middle, and low pitch—it must be stated that for this very reason it is that same phoneme (*varṇa*), because everything has everything as its essence.

In some living beings, even when sounds arise from different locations within the body, they occur as follows: for instance, in crows (*dhvāṅkṣa*), when the letters *ka*, *kaṭa*, and *ra* are uttered, they are all perceived as being produced by the stomach, anus, throat, and palate, despite their indistinctness. [Now, one might object: "But surely those letters, such as *ka* and the rest, because of their indistinctness, are not equal to the *ka* and other sounds produced from the throat and other locations. To this, [the author replies:]...

[Regarding the phrase "even though they are unmanifest"]: It is also incorrect to say that those very [sounds] are limited to that extent because of their being "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), and because there is no sound beyond the *mātṛkā*, and thus even an unmanifest sound beyond the *mātṛkā* is not included due to its lack of utility. Furthermore, if utility were present, everything would be well-established; and by stating that the *mātṛkā* is useful in every respect, [it is implied that] in the case of crows and so forth— [The text continues: ...for [in such cases], the *mātṛkā* is indeed useful. Therefore, since the *mātṛkā* is useful in all respects, it is established that it is the cause of all sounds. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all sounds is refuted. Consequently, the statement that "the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all sounds" is untenable. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all sounds. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all sounds, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all words (*śabda*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no word other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all words, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all words. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all words is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all words. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all words, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all letters (*varṇa*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no letter other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all letters, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all letters. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all letters is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all letters. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all letters, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all speech (*vāk*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no speech other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all speech, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all speech. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all speech is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all speech. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all speech, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all objects (*artha*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no object other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all objects, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all objects. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all objects is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all objects. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all objects, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all things (*vastu*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no thing other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all things, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all things. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all things is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all things. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all things, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all cognitions (*buddhi*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no cognition other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all cognitions, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all cognitions. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all cognitions is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all cognitions. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all cognitions, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all mental modifications (*vikalpa*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no mental modification other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all mental modifications, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all mental modifications. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all mental modifications is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all mental modifications. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all mental modifications, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no latent impression other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all latent impressions, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all latent impressions. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all latent impressions is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all latent impressions. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all latent impressions, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all seeds (*bīja*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no seed other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all seeds, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all seeds. Thus, the claim that the *mātṛkā* is not the cause of all seeds is refuted. Therefore, the *mātṛkā* is indeed the cause of all seeds. This is the meaning. [The commentary concludes: Thus, having stated the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all seeds, he now states the proof for the *mātṛkā* being the cause of all effects (*kārya*). "And because of the non-existence of anything other than the *mātṛkā*" means: since there is no effect other than the *mātṛkā*, and since the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all effects, it is established that the *mātṛkā* is the cause of all

[The objection: "Even though the letters beginning with *ka* are of a different class (*vijātīya*), they were not mentioned because they are useless; therefore, one must necessarily admit a word that transcends the *mātṛkā*. How then can you say 'they alone'? To this, he says: "This too is incorrect.
[The principle of the "stick and the apūpa" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*) should be understood here regarding even that which has the form of unmanifest phonemes.]
Even for sounds such as those of a peacock, the ocean, or the like, the capacity to produce both pleasure and pain certainly exists; what other intended utility could there be?

Furthermore, even in the *Pārameśvara*, the nature of mantra is primarily established for unmanifest sound (*avyaktadhvani*), since it is taught that the essence of the pervasion of mantra (*mantravyāpti*) consists precisely of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the other phonemes. And in that regard:
p.
190) "The sound that has reached cessation vibrates as *śu-ma-śu-ma*," and so forth—
this was stated regarding the instruction on *nāda* (resonance) concerning the sounds of bells, bronze, and the like, as well as the striking of the ear and so on.
Upon being examined,
the horse neighs as it were, and the tamed elephant seems to bolt;
the lion roars as it were, and the camel hisses as it were.
Having uttered it thus, those possessed of superior power forcibly draw out the life-breaths of the victim;
this is the application of the great mantra for the rite of summoning that which is otherwise impossible to achieve.

Thus it is stated in the *Guhyayoginītantra*; however, that is merely a provisional means (*upāya*). In reality, this mantra, whose essence is sound (*nāda*), is purely internal. This point being stated, it cannot be denied by either you or us that it applies even to mantras consisting of manifest letter-sequences (*varṇamālā*) and the like. Therefore, sound, though unmanifest, is indeed composed of letters, just as [a sound] remains [audible] even when it has traveled to a great distance.

It is established that "a jar is indeed a jar"; and it is likewise established that even as sound—consisting of phonemes—proceeds to other locations through distinctions such as breath-force (*prāṇabala*) and so forth, it remains that very same [sound]. For this very reason, the knowledge of the cries of all beings, which was taught by the Blessed One, the Sage Śeṣa, has now become deeply felt in my heart; otherwise, it would not have been so.
The mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition (p. 191),

and that which is achieved through the restraint (*saṃyama*) consisting of meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*)— this is "restraint upon that" in a single object.

[The definition of restraint: That [knowledge], which culminates in the ultimate attainment of the differentiation of those [sounds], how could it result in the knowledge of the warbling of birds and the like—which exceeds the nature of indistinct phonemes—when, in reality, those very phonemes possess denotative power characterized by identity with the object? This being so, it is logical [to conclude that the phonemes themselves are the denoters].

These very sounds, such as the cries of birds and even words like "fear" (*bhī*), are indeed meaningful, because they are taught as indicators of victory or defeat, just like the cries of birds; it is with this intention that the author of the *Śikṣāsūtra* composed his aphorisms: "The *ha*-visarga-spirants are produced from the chest, according to some. [As it has been said:]
One should know that the letter *ha* when joined with the fifth [consonants] and the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) is guttural (*urasya*); they say it is guttular (*kaṇṭhya*) when unjoined.
And so forth. Likewise, for those *ha*-vowels explicitly mentioned by name, their place of articulation is held to be their respective [consonantal] portions;
for the *ha*-vowels and the *visarga* are considered to reside in the chest, being produced from the lower part of the throat.
Thus, [the rules] beginning with "for some, the root of the teeth" (*radanamūlam ekeṣām*) function as expressive [grammatical markers], but not otherwise in any way whatsoever.
For this very reason, those who, resorting to some degree of variety, suspect that there is either difference or non-difference [between phonemes], [state]:
"from the *visarjanīya*, the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya* [arise]."
(From p.

192) From the nasals [namely, those of the form *ṅuṃ*, *ñuṃ*, *ṇuṃ*, *nuṃ*, and *muṃ*], and from the letters *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *kṣa*, [one should pronounce] those very same [nasals] with even lighter articulation (*laghuprayatnatara*). [Regarding that which is pronounced...]
"Laxity arises in the tip, the front, the middle, and the root of the tongue; that [articulation] is characterized by less effort.
Having thus conceived of them as distinct, sixty-four phonemes have been described. As for their difference, it is stated in the *Sāmbapañcāśikā*:
That [Speech] which, rising from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, manifests here sixty-three phonemes produced through the conjunction with the vital breath by means of articulatory efforts—
that Paśyantī, first arisen, I worship as the Madhyamā established in the intellect.
I take refuge in Vaikharī speech, which is articulated through the mouth with the clarity of the vocal organs.
Thus, as with the vowels and consonants, it is stated here even in the *Śrītrikaraṇakula* regarding the phonemes *ṛ* and *ra*:
"The Mātṛkā, which is described through the division of eight times eight, is that very Wheel of Kula; by it this entire world is pervaded."
Thus, this has been described in detail within the *Mātṛkā-jñāna-bheda*. As it is said:
"Will is desire, poison is knowledge, and the Goddess is action;
the immersion into these three is called Śiva-Bhairava."
The reality of desire is its fulfillment, which is explained in the *Saṃghaṭa*;
and the reality of poison is nectar when the mutual union of the atoms occurs during the state of concealment.

Thus, "immortal" (amṛta) means consisting of the state of expansion. Here, however, there is no insistence on that specific methodology, because its sole essence is fullness; such is this [reality] everywhere.

The category of the "process of penetration into consciousness" (*saṃvid-anupraveśa-krama*)—whether being conceptualized or directly realized—is established within the great splendor of the supreme mantra, which consists of the pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is the non-conventional, innate nature of Māyā;
therein all disputants proclaim the state of non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*). And from that:
In the supreme mantra, the great earth, and so forth, [the reality] consists precisely of the phonemes *ka* and the rest,

which are the nature of ultimate seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*), whether pure, mixed, or otherwise; otherwise, there would be the [absurdities of] Mount Meru being like a jujube fruit, water being fire, existence being non-existence, and a jar being pleasure, as well as non-conceptual knowledge— thus, everything would be one and the same.
Even if a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from that negligence, it should follow that very path rather than, on the contrary, fracture its essential nature.

Thus, those who perceive that very non-conventional mantra-body as having mutually diverse forms, by the omniscient ones, have resorted to the means of convention (*saṃketa*) as an object of worship. [As it is said: "The Lord said:"
O lady of excellent limbs, I shall tell you that which is always recited by me:
the Mātṛkā, whose form consists of the letters, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
Endowed with the fourteen vowels and adorned with the three *bindus*,
O Maheśvarī, you abide in the form of Śakti within the mandala of the *kalās*.
The letters from *ka* to *kṣa* are indeed of the nature of Śakti.
Because it is a consonant (vyañjana), it always endures the utterance of bliss (ānanda).
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, there is no doubt that from this [emanation] arise sounds intermingled with vowels;
by means of the fifty-fold division of phonemes, the reality known as "sound" (śabda) is produced.
O Goddess, the letter 'A' is the first, and the letter 'Kṣa' follows as the last;
she who consists of the letters of the Mātṛkā is renowned as the "Akṣamālā" (the Garland of Syllables).
This [reality] has the nature of the Śabdabrahman, yet that which transcends sound is what is recited;
that which transcends sound is the supreme abode, eternally beyond all calculation.
"Know the nature of the self; the Lord is indeed the Supreme Lord. [p.

And it is indicated that within that very non-conventional splendor of speech (*vāṅmahas*), the conventional signs of the illusory realm fall in such a way that they attain identity with the non-illusory, non-conventional mantra; for their state of being denotators consists precisely in the realization of their own true nature (*svarūpa*), and nothing else. Otherwise, [they would remain distinct] from the things to be denoted (*vācya*).

The intended meaning is: what is the distinction of the denoter? In this context, through the power of practice, there occurs a clear recognition—a recollection of the word "cow" that occurred long ago and which has attained a non-conventional status—and likewise, at the time of the convention, the recollection of the cow also falls solely within the domain of that non-delusive, non-conventional recollection.
p.

195) Even for an infant, when following after previous births, this non-conventional existence of the nature of consciousness remains established from the very beginning; otherwise, there would be no stability. It is precisely in this way that the apprehension of linguistic conventions becomes possible, and not otherwise.
Thus it has been determined by the venerable Utpaladeva in his *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-ṭīkā*: "In this regard, the method of entry is as follows:
one sees one thing, hears another, does another, and speaks yet another."
If she thinks of another while eating, that is the conventional state [of being unfaithful].
Thus the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Śrī Śrīkaṇṭha-pāda has also stated:
"The mind is cast elsewhere, the eye is directed elsewhere," and so forth; that too is the body of non-conventional mantras. For even that which is conventional is [the basis] of convention.
In an ultimate sense, the place of origin is indeed non-conventional;

thus, following its own seed, it culminates in the unsurpassed state (*anuttarapada*). That unsurpassed state, moreover, is essentially the impetus for the manifold variety of such infinite aggregates, expanding forth through the vision of emission (*visarga*).

Because the emission itself extends as far as the *hakalā*, there is also that Śakti Kuṇḍalinī known as the letter *ha*; as it is said in the first hymn of the *Śrīpañcastavī* in the *Devīstuti*: p. 196) [The passage continues: "O Goddess, you who are the supreme power of the letter *ha*... and so forth.
We meditate upon that Māyā of yours, which resides eternally in your first seed-syllable (vāgbīja), which rivals the rising of the delicate fibers of the trapusī creeper,
and which, as the power known as Kuṇḍalinī, is ever intent on the activity of generating the universe.
Knowing this, men do not again experience childhood within a mother's womb.

Thus [it is said]. The underlying meaning here is as follows: the Kuṇḍalinī, which is of the nature of the anusvāra (m) and called "Mātrā," should also be meditated upon as having the appearance of a lotus fiber; likewise, when there is a lack of focused attention, she is the "giver of the universe" (viśvajananī). However, when her true nature is known through that which is permeated by the descent of power (śaktipāta), she is the "giver of liberation. Thus he says, "having known thus," and likewise, Mātrā is of the most subtle, unsurpassed (anuttara) form.

Flowing forth through union with the *kaulikī* power, she is known as the letter *Ha*; or rather, presiding over that [power], we contemplate the *kuṇḍalinī* energy as being intent upon the activity of generating the universe.

Through the maintenance of the nature of the *bindu*, which consists in non-difference from one's own essential nature, there is a transition into the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*) itself; thus, it resides within one's own essential nature.
The consciousness of the single syllable (*ekākṣarasaṃvit*)—[that is, that which is both "one" (*ekā*) and "imperishable" (*akṣarā*), and is "consciousness" (*saṃvit*];

thus, by the rule of the *karmadhāraya* compound, there is the substitution of the masculine form; and by the maxim "in the absence of disagreement regarding the universal, when there is a prohibition of the individual instance, the universal follows"—even the calculation of space and time is of the same nature as that [consciousness]. Thus, the meaning is that it is "one," meaning all-pervasive. Indeed, this is so by its very nature.

By means of the previously mentioned principle of the "full reality" (*pūrṇatattva*), which is entirely independent of considerations such as space, time, and material cause—[as it was said that] "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*) is precisely this: the state of being conjoined with space, time, and so forth.
As it has been stated:
The nature of that [reality] is not known by those wise ones who think thus:
"The supreme state is devoid of limitations such as space and time.
And so it was said by Hari:
Salutation to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and which is known solely through direct experience.
Thus: "In the ground of emission" means in the Śāmbhava emission. (p. 197) One rushes instantaneously to the ground of emission;
this very union with the ground of emission consists of those [powers] made of bliss, will, knowledge, action, expansion, its outward flow, and its manifold creative activity.
The persistence of the vowels and so forth is that very emission (*visarga*). This emission,
by virtue of being inseparable from its own existence, flows forth with such extreme fullness of being that it immediately becomes composed of the letter *ha* (as it is said):
Thus, the emission (visarga), when drawn upward and having reached a state of solidification,
is designated as the *haṃsa*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the consonant, and the point of articulation (*sparśa*).

Thus, the actual attainment of the state consisting of *ha* and *la* is, in reality, the abiding of the entire web of principles (*tattva*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *na*; and these very *ha* and *la*, entering once again into the *bindu*, culminate in the supreme state (*anuttara-pada*).
Therefore, this supreme Goddess, the venerable Mistress of Consciousness, is one alone, whose form is non-dual and perfectly full.

O Supreme Goddess, there is no application of succession or the like here. As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "Action such as cooking is appropriate to succession because it is delimited by time; even if it is bound to its final moment, it does not attain the state of being 'cooked' [until that point]."

Thus it is said: "In the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, the sequential nature of worldly action is established through the power of time; however, this does not apply to the eternal action of the Lord, which belongs to the Sovereign (Prabhu) himself."
Thus it is said: (p.
198) "In the inversion [of the ego], when [the parts] are withdrawn, there is 'ah' and 'am'; though this duality exists, in reality this is one single consciousness alone. In this way, this...
Even when there is the manifestation of objects such as jars or pleasure, that sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*), which consists essentially in resting within one's own self, is present everywhere;
as it has been said:
"The resting of light within itself is indeed proclaimed to be the 'I-sense'."

Thus, he is in reality the self of all— according to the principle just established— as permeated by the Supreme Goddess (Parābhaṭṭārikā) and consisting of Bhairava himself, as I have stated in my own hymn in the chapter on "The Nature of All Things" (*Viśvabhāvapaṭala*): "That which is the wonder of the supreme reality, devoid of interruption, expanding everywhere..."
I naturally bow down to that Goddess, the abiding state of my own Self, whose nature is the manifestation of "I" as a full and complete activity.
Thus, this very method of instruction is to be understood in the *Advayasampattivārtika* composed by the venerable Vāmana.
By this, it is established that the letter *A* alone is the most wealthy (all-encompassing), even in cases such as the formation of joy (*harṣa*), a jar (*ghaṭa*), blue (*nīla*), and so forth.
Even the phonemes beginning with *ha* involve therein the same projection of their own infinite preceding and succeeding phonemes;

otherwise, that very collection of *ha* and the rest would be impossible. Since they are projected at the end [of the sequence], they remain latent within and do not fall within the range of conceptual thought. For this very reason, in every cognition, all deities are present simultaneously.

Maintaining a manifold aggregate, they bring about the functioning of variegated cognitive states; with this very intention, from the section on Time onwards, [the process begins] within a single breath, or even within a sixteenth part of a breath,
preceded by the emergence of sixty, twice that, and so forth, years.

The diverse arisings and dissolutions of the Mothers, Rudras, World-Protectors, Planets, Nagas, and so forth have been described; yet, precisely at the time of those diverse and infinite arisings and dissolutions, the reality—the ultimate truth—is in fact nothing other than being measured by the time of the Sun, which is the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra). At most, this much is merely that which cannot be determined by the conceptual determinations (adhyavasāya) of the realm of Māyā.

However, while one may harbor the conceit of non-existence regarding the consciousness of another, at that very moment [that consciousness] indeed shines forth. For this very reason, within a single cognitive process (*jñānakalanā*), it is said— through such instructions as "one perceives one thing and conceptualizes another"—
that the presiding of the triad of deities is present everywhere and is never absent.

Furthermore, all cognitions are in reality ultimately "I" (aham), consisting essentially of reflective awareness (vimarśa). Thus, it is established that this entire universe— residing within [the Self], filled with the power of bliss, and both emitting and devouring— is nothing other than emission (visarga).

The Supreme Lord, having become condensed and assumed the nature of the letter *ha*, attains the state of the syllable *kṣa* through the manifold variety of infinite combinations [the state of *kṣa* meaning the nature of the letters *ka*, *sa*, *a*, and the visarga]. He alone is this state of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*), which consists of the agitation (*kṣobha*) of the phonemes appropriate for the union with the womb of power (*śāktayoni*) that takes the form of the messenger (*dūtī*).
It is said that for men who are fearful by nature, success here is achieved through a messenger (*dūtī*) over the course of a year;
however, for women who have abandoned their essential nature, that same success is attained in twelve days.
Therefore, having taken a woman who is similar in form, auspicious, beautiful, and of purified intent, one should perform sacrifice, worship, and oblation.
One should first cause [the substance] to be taken from the mouth of a woman and then deposit it back into the mouth of a woman.

This is the *kulaprakriyā*. It has been stated previously as well: "The emission (*visarga*), whose nature consists of the ever-emerging multitude of infinite phenomena from the central plane of Suṣumṇā, dissolving away, enters into the abode of the eternal, which is the very state of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*). These...

The vowels beginning with *a* are established within the vital breath (*prāṇa*) according to the duration of sixteen *tuṭis*; having joined them into a single *tuṭi*, they exist by means of half-and-half divisions.

They manifest the nature of time consisting of fifteen days even outside of [the cycles of] dissolution and emergence; thus the lunar days (*tithi*) and digits (*kalā*) are spoken of. Furthermore, the sixteenth digit alone is the essence of emission (*visarga*), while the seventeenth digit, which is separating, is described in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures.
"But that seventeenth goddess has the form of half of half of the letter *ha*.

Since the visarga is half of the letter *ha*, and since even that [visarga] is half of its own [phonetic] separation, one might ask: "How can this conceptualization apply to a single phoneme (*varṇa*) that is partless? To this we reply: in our view, everything is indeed without parts.
Furthermore, since there is no excess over the manifestation as pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), even when parts manifest through its very sovereignty (*svātantrya*), partlessness remains inseparable;
let it be so here as well—what contradiction is there? In this very way, the validity of phonemes (*varṇa*) is established;
otherwise, how could the wind, spreading sequentially, be the perceiver in phonemes such as those produced by the teeth-lips, the throat, or the palate?
"Having struck the throat, one strikes the palate"—thus, even though there is simultaneous filling [of the vocal tract], there would be a sense of simultaneity;

for in every case, the form arising from the striking of the throat is produced by the striking of the palate. Furthermore, because the breath and the resonance (*nāda*) are perceived subsequently, they are called *anupradāna* (secondary contributions).

202) And in the case of two-mora and three-mora [syllables], the combination of two [moras] and so forth is implicitly contained; likewise, even in a single mora, the combination of half-moras and so forth is to be understood, as stated by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa:
"Salutation to the Aṇu, which is greater even than the half-measure above the Praṇava.

Here, however, the fifty phonemes—or even the entire universe—is considered as a single, undivided entity in some cases; yet in certain scriptures, such as the Mata, there is the acceptance that the eighteenth digit (*kalā*) consists precisely of the separation of the *visarga*, by taking recourse in the existence of the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*).

Thus, these *kalās* themselves, which cause the experience of mental fluctuations consisting solely of delight, are called "vowels" (*svaras*). They are so named because they "cause to sound" (*svarayanti*)—from the root *svṛ*, meaning "to sound" or "to afflict"—they "articulate" (*śabdayanti*) and "indicate" the mind; and by the word *sva* (meaning "self" or "one's own"), they "give" (*rānti*) their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) in this way, transmitting it into the supreme subject.

They give (*dadati*) their own, which is the form of the source beginning with *ka* (the letter *ka*), and they bestow (*rānti*—this is a form of the root *rā* meaning "to give") by manifesting externally; thus they are called vowels (*svarāḥ*). For these very sounds, consisting of resonance (*nāda*), indicate mental states (*cittavṛtti*) such as compassion, the erotic, and tranquility, in [expressions such as] lamentation, endearment, and praise.
Whether they are solitary or situated within the womb according to their respective species, they descend for the very first time even among animals, newborns on that very day, and so forth,
solely due to their proximity to consciousness, without dependence on conventions, obstacles, or the like.

Attaining the form of vocal intonation (*kāku*) and so forth, they manifest— thus, *udātta* and the others are properties of the meaning (*artha-dharma*). In that regard, when the effort (*prayatna*) follows throughout all the limbs and becomes intense,
there occurs a constriction of the body, a narrowing of the glottis (*kaṇṭhavivara*), and a harshness of the voice due to the rapid movement of the breath.

When [the effort] is intense, they call that *udātta* (high-pitched); but when the effort is weak, there occurs a relaxation of the body parts, a widening of the throat cavity, and a smoothness of the tone due to the slow movement of the breath—they call that *anudātta* (low-pitched). A *svara* (circumflex) is characterized by the proximity of these *udātta* and *anudātta* tones.

The external efforts [are as follows]: "Relaxation" (sraṃsana) means looseness, lubricity, and softness. Precisely because the aperture of the throat is large, the air exiting quickly does not dry up the water-elements; therefore, the tone becomes lubricated. Precisely because the aperture of the throat is narrow, the air exiting slowly [does not dry up] the water-elements.

It causes drying, thus it is *rūkṣatā*—it is a lack of oiliness (*asnigdhatā*). In the *Mahābhāṣya*, [the qualities] "exertion" (*āyāsa*), "harshness" (*dāruṇya*), and "minuteness" (*aṇutā*) are stated to be the means of producing sound for itself; "exertion" refers to the body, "harshness" to the roughness of the voice, and "rūkṣatā" to its own throat-cavity.
Restraint; furthermore,
the qualities of low-pitched sound are release,
softness, and largeness— release being the relaxation of the limbs, softness being the quality of the voice, and largeness being the width of the throat-cavity.
And this particular tone is to be acquired through practice, like the *pahlā* and so forth; thus says Śrī Kayyaṭa. Pāṇini, however, states:

"The high [pitch] is the udātta, the low is the anudātta, and their combination is the svarita. These [tones] have been taught because they consist of the nature of the ṣaḍja and other notes which manifest the mental fluctuations of those very [sages].
Thus, in every act of perception, all these powers— from *a* to *kṣa*, which are skillful in their various modes of activity and conduct—
descend with a competitive eagerness, each vying for precedence (*ahamahamikayā*). As it has been said:
But *ahamahamikā* is that mutual sense of "I" which arises between one another.

Thus, in the *Kośa*: "Appearing only as non-sequential, it is precisely through its nature of being constituted by mental construction (*kalana*) that it brings forth space, which is indicated solely by the transition of the sequence of cognitions; otherwise, according to the maxim that 'there would be no distinction between Mount Meru and a single atom,' the sequential form—which consists of the variety of action and the variety of spatiality contained within it—[is established]. As they say:"

Time is the delimitation of entities by means of succession or non-succession. Nor should it be thought that because entities appear only as adhering to consciousness, how could there be a connection with time for the multitude of entities associated with that [consciousness]? For even succession and non-succession are included within the Supreme Lord himself. [Objection: But if this is so, then would there not be a connection with time in the Supreme Lord?
We do not think so; why? Because that manifestation belongs to the Lord, whose power is named Kālī. As it has been said:
"Consciousness itself assumes a form differentiated from the objects of knowledge; through connection with limitation, it attains the state of being an object (*vedyatā*).

Then, by its own sovereignty, falling upon the object with an eagerness to appropriate it, it becomes the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Within that, in its primordial aspect, lies the path of time (*kālādhvan*)."
"But regarding the subsequent [distinctions], namely space and time": as it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"By means of the manifestation of a variety of forms, this Lord manifests spatial succession;
and by means of the manifestation of a variety of actions, He manifests temporal succession as well."

Thus: manifesting time externally through conjunction, and swallowing it by means of its union within one's own self, even at the moment of its full manifestation—[the phrase "at the moment of manifestation" refers to the beginning; for... p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p. 205) ...p.

In the supreme emission (visarga), which resembles a waveless ocean, which is the unsurpassed Self, and which is a single mass of light—therein first flashes forth the "I-reflection" (ahaṃ-parāmarśa), which is intent on the reflection of its own self alone; because there is an absence of anything else to be reflected upon, it is devoted solely to the consciousness-reflection (cid-vimarśa). That itself is the moment of supreme effulgence.
It is said thus so that his sovereignty may arise everywhere. This is the meaning:

by the very majesty of His own sovereignty, the Supreme Lord—whose essence is the unsurpassed Light—conceals His own nature and, abiding in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, manifests the multitude of separate objects. For example, He...
In this way, the Supreme Light, preceded by the manifestation of the stage of the contracted subject, brings forth the fourfold group of powers beginning with *udyoga* (exertion),
as follows: *udyoga* is the desire to manifest objects, [a state] in which one is always attached and turned outward.

Excluding the twelve neuter vowels, the *kalās*— beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the visarga— possess their own nature; by means of the Sun, which is the self of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) having attained its full form through that nature,
it should illuminate each individual object in the form of slightly contracted blue, pleasure, and so forth, and thus emit and fill [them] externally.
The meaning is that one should maintain [the object] for some time in its very suchness (*tathātva*), contemplate it, and then withdraw it by assimilating it into one's own self.

For any cognizer who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) must first perceive the multitude of objects as they have ascended into the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); subsequently, one should conceptualize them as "this is thus"; and thereafter, [one thinks], "this object has been known by me."

This point is witnessed by direct experience: through the pride of contentment, by dissolving external forms, one should find rest within one's own self. Thus, after the ascent of the multitude of objects—which have attained the state of manifestation and so forth—into the level of the subject (*pramātṛ*), they shine forth in their own true nature.

For one who has attained their own full nature through the sixteen digits (kalā) beginning with the intellect and the sense organs, there occurs a swallowing of emission (visarga-grāsa) characterized by the obscuration of that [innate] nature due to the onset of an inflated state. Within the limited subject, the moon of the object of knowledge— consisting of the body and so forth— is [swallowed] by the gross "life-sustaining nectar-digit" (saṃjīviny-amṛta-kalā), which exists in the form of various subjects and objects through the process of emitting [them].

This is what is meant by "the manifestation through form": whatever collection of entities there may be, each of them, preceded by the attainment of slightness, reaches the state of being an object of knowledge by ascending through the doors of the senses;
then, by performing its respective causal function and generating a repose within its own self alone, [it serves] consciousness.
"It brings about fullness. As it was said by the venerable master Utpaladeva:

"Who else is equal to me, who offers as an oblation the mandala of all states of being upon the sacrificial grass of the power consisting of universal power, performing the sacrifice that consists of the sacrifice of the universe?"
Thus, by way of their empty nature— consisting of emergence, manifestation, transition,
and dissolution— they assume a twelvefold attenuated form.

Furthermore, by means of the perfection of the four arts— beginning with effort— which reside in the women embraced therein, these [energies], having sprouted and entered with a languid grace in their full and complete form consisting of sixteen aspects, both internally and externally,
emit the fourfold art that is the essence of the reality of wonder, which consists in resting in the bliss of that nectar.

Thus experiencing this very play of the swing consisting of fullness and emaciation, they are adept at swallowing and vomiting the multitude of digits of the moon and the sun—as it is said in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"Seventeen [digits] are in the eye of the forehead; twelve and sixteen are in the other two eyes."

Thus it is said. In this context, the eye on the forehead is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), the right eye is the power of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-śakti*), and the left eye is the power of the object of knowledge (*prameya-śakti*). Furthermore, the meaning here is as follows: the solar sequence of light-spheres (*dhāma-krama*) has the twelve rays as its domain;
the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa-krama*) consists of the twelve vowels excluding the neuter ones; and these very rays are present here.
The sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) falls upon the twelve paths of emptiness, which are the first-mentioned abodes free from obscuration;
this is the pervasion of the Wheel of Light (*prakāśacakra*). In the Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*), there is the sequence of abodes (*dhāmakrama*) through the flow of the nectar of the *bindu*;

the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) occurs through the pervasion of the sixteen vowels together with the neuter vowels (*ṣaṇṭhasvara*); [and the sequence of subjects] resides in the intellect, the organs of action, the senses, and the mind.

In the sixteen [spokes], there is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*), which is the pervasion of the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*). In the wheel of forms (*mūrticakra*), within the seventeen abodes that are the unobscured domains of the wealth of sovereignty, there is likewise the sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*).
The sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) extends in seventeen ways, from the primordial phoneme up to the final letter beginning with 'A', presided over by the initial phoneme.

The stages (*bhūmikā*) belonging to the lunar [series] are seventeenfold, consisting of the sequence of consciousnesses experienced together with *amā* (the new moon), which, though turned away from the external and desiring internal reflection, remain within it. [In this series], the letter *a* alone is at the beginning, while the group born from the womb of *ka* and the other consonants is in the middle and at the end.
And bestowing the *bindu*, she is this very Blessed Lady, who is emanation itself.
As it was said by the venerable Somānandapāda in his own commentary: "Aṃ and aḥ—this very Mātṛkā is both modified and unmodified," and so forth. They, however...

This [syllable] "a" is the unsurpassed; the lunar days (tithis) begin with the letter "a. Alternatively, they explain that the dot (bindu) is the syllable "aṃ," and the lunar days begin with the letter "a," ending with the visarga. They teach that this very essence of consciousness is *spanda* (vibration). And what is this vibration? It is a slight movement from one's own nature toward another object.

That very movement is not something [apart from itself], and if it were not movement, it would be nothing at all; therefore, within its own essential nature, free from succession and the like, it is the state of surging forth whose essence is wonder— a vibration (*spanda*) indicated in the scriptures by such terms as "the wave" (*ūrmi*), "the belly of the fish" (*matsyodarī*), and so forth.
Thus it is said:
because its nature consists of slight movement, it is of the form of Śiva and Śakti, comprising both the universal and the particular.
This has been explained: the initial lunar days (*tithis*) ending with the *bindu* are, through their connection with time, the Moon and the Sun of that very [principle].

Within the family (*kula*), from the earth and the other elements up to the pentad of Brahmā, how is there the end of those vowels in due order? Moreover, the "eating" (*adana*) of that sequence is its consumption, which is the devouring by Time (*kālagrāsa*); having done so—this being an adverbial modifier—in the auspicious vow (*suvrate*), whether in enjoyment (*bhoga*) or in emptiness (*riktatva*), that is, in the cessation of enjoyment or in fullness (*pūrṇatva*).

This address should also be explained in this way: it is "rootless" (amūlā), meaning its root is the letter *a* and its root is non-existence (*avidyamāna*), because it is beginningless; it is that whose sequence, through phonetic contraction (*praśleṣa*), is of a different form or otherwise than [the original];
nevertheless, it is rootless; and its sequence is that which is the expansion (*ātana*) of what is rootless, and that very [expansion] is its sequence—this is how it should be understood.
And this very [consciousness] is the knower and the object of knowledge, because there is no other; it is the patient endurance (*kṣānta*) that is non-existent [as a separate entity],

the silent abiding (*tūṣṇīmāsana*) which, through its nature as emanation and so forth, is uninterrupted, and which— being at the end, that is, in the proximity, of the senses (*akṣāṇām*)— has no prior termination.

(209) By way of metaphorical designation, it is said that "it may come to be. In this [emanation], there is an emanation extending up to the Akṣānti level, an unprecedented bringing forth, and a nature consisting of entry into one's own self, which is of the form of withdrawal (saṃhāra). And this very [emanation] is...

Of all mantras—which are of the nature of the expansion of seeds whose essence is Śiva; which possess the qualities of *manana* (contemplation) and *trāṇa* (protection); which consist of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in the form of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), etc.; which are the very self of the Lord of Phonemes (*varṇabhaṭṭāraka*); which are the vibrations of the *yoni* whose essence is power (*śakti*); and which are of the nature of cognition produced from those seeds—[of all these...]

This [knowledge] is equal among all sciences, neither deficient nor excessive in any of the tantras, in all ritual systems, and at all times; it bestows the entire collection of accomplishments (siddhis).
It is proclaimed as having the nature of manifest manifestation, directed toward the illusory (māyīya) state. Thus, the differentiation of the phonemes is as follows: they are indeed...

The letters, which are the forms of pure mantra, first attain the state of the creation of existence (*bhāva-sṛṣṭi*), consisting of conditions such as the fivefold power of error; for creation is twofold— namely, the creation of existence and the creation of elements— and therein, the creation of existence consists of conditions, while that consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) is the creation of elements.
The creation of the elements. In this regard, the following is the state of affairs:
this creation of cognitive determinations (pratyayasarga) is known as error (viparyaya), incapacity (aśakti), contentment (tuṣṭi), and attainment (siddhi).
Due to the mutual suppression of the imbalance of the guṇas, its subdivisions are fifty.

Thus ends the creation of the mental states (bhāva-sṛṣṭi). As for the creation of the elements (bhūta-sṛṣṭi): the divine creation is of eight kinds, the animal creation is fivefold, and the human creation is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation (bhautika-sarga).
In that regard, the division of the qualities is as follows:
the creation at the top is predominantly *sattva*, and that at the root is predominantly *tamas*;
in the middle, it is predominantly *rajas*, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Thus, the divine creation (daivasarga) is eightfold: Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Aindra, Pitrya, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca.
The animal womb (tiryagyoni) is fivefold: beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary beings. This [classification] applies to the four states of existence as well.

Because there is no distinction, it is simply "humanity. (p. 210) The five—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and clinging to life (*abhiniveśa*)—which consist of darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and blind gloom (*andhatāmisra*), conceal one's true nature.

There are five known as the "miseries" (*miśra*), making eleven obstructions to the faculties (*indriyavadha*); seventeen are obstructions to the intellect (*buddhivadha*), thus totaling twenty-eight. There are nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*): four internal and five external;

and eight accomplishments (*siddhi*): reasoning (*ūha*), oral instruction (*śabda*), study (*adhyayana*), the removal of the three kinds of suffering (*trividhaduḥkhavighāta*), acquisition of a friend (*suhṛtprāpti*), and charity (*dāna*).
In that regard, the incapacities are deafness, leprosy, blindness, numbness, loss of smell, as well as muteness,
lameness, paralysis, impotence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and intoxication.

Thus, these eleven constitute the incapacity of the intellect (*buddhi*) caused by such factors. It has been stated that the incapacity of the intellect in its own nature results in the reversals of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and accomplishment (*siddhi*). Regarding contentment, there are five internal types—namely, those arising from *prakṛti*, *upādāna*, *kāla*, *bhāgya*, and the five [objects] beginning with sound—and there are likewise five types of cessation (*uparama*), for cessation consists of [the renunciation of] service and so forth.
Considering that the means of acquiring wealth cause suffering to servants and others, one should desist from such actions that bring about misery.
The varieties of error arise, as does incapacity due to the impairment of the instruments.
Contentment has twenty-eight varieties, while attainment is ninefold and eightfold.
For indeed, these very cognitions (*pratyaya*), which constitute the nature of the emission of bound souls (*pāśava-sṛṣṭi*), are primarily the fetters (*pāśa*); as it has been said:

"And his powers, ever-arisen, exist for the purpose of veiling his true nature (*svarūpāvaraṇa*), because the emergence of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of sound (*śabda-anuvedha*)."
Thus: "In that way,
the loss of the essence of the supreme nectar for him is that which arises from [ordinary] cognition."

Thus, by means of internalizing the creation of the *pratyaya* (the mental state), the creation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) belonging to *māyā*— which appear as a sequence consisting of clearly audible sounds— is described as being embraced by the primordial, ultimate, pure form, thereby bestowing the production of their respective effects and fruits.
In the Śrīpūrvaśāstra,
[it is taught] by means of such [a teaching] which contains within it the meaning of all scriptures.
Having awakened by this [Veda], the Lord, having agitated the womb according to his power,
created the castes whose learning was equal to his own, in numbers corresponding to that.
Thus embraced by various [beings] such as these, they bestow the fruits of all desires;
in this manner, though always unmanifest to those blinded by *māyā*, they are proclaimed to be ever manifest.

"O you whose nature consists of pure sensation (*śuddhavedanā*), in whom there is an unimpeded expansion everywhere manifesting the power of your own intrinsic nature"—this is the address: "O you of auspicious vows" (*śobhanavrate*). This, then, is the summary of the meaning here (p.
The supreme Goddess Bhairavī herself shines eternally, characterized solely by the wonder of immersion in the singular essence of absolute freedom.
That which is the union with its own nature is unceasing and eternally arisen,
[manifesting] through Sadāśiva, the earth, animals, blue, yellow, pleasure, and so forth.
Through its own manifesting natures, which possess self-luminosity,
consciousness— whose essence is self-awareness— manifests in the form of those very appearances.

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—meaning the manifestation of manifestation, which is the existence of such a manifestation within itself by itself—is described as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The sense is that there is no requirement for any other means of valid cognition here;
for there is no need for a means of valid cognition regarding an object that is protected by self-awareness.
That which shines forth through the very equality of the ignorant, the animals, and the omniscient—[the "ignorant" being one who knows only a little; the "animal" being the deluded].
The sense-faculties, the three-fold mark, the sequence of another's words,
similarity, the impossibility otherwise, non-arising through dependence, and restraint.
That in which everything beginning with these [senses] is perceived merely as a gateway,
and which consists of uninterrupted manifestation, is called self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Even for those animals who possess no specialized knowledge even regarding the mere names of the lunar mansions, stars, forms,
and so forth, their consciousness nevertheless shines forth equally.
Thus, speech by its very nature consists of the self-reflection of its own form;
and that which is this self-reflection of its own form is itself the body of supreme speech.
Because its nature is manifold, this [consciousness] consists of a manifold manifestation;
for in the act of manifesting, it never at any time or anywhere experiences dependence on another.

How could there be dependence on others, such as the obstruction of linguistic convention, given that it is independent? That Light is not dependent, for dependence consists in being an object of manifestation (*prakāśyatā*), and being an object of manifestation is precisely the requirement of another Light; yet no other Light exists here. Thus, Light is one and independent. Consequently, there can be no reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) therein.
It has the nature of being conceptualizable because it is not conventional;

therefore, it is devoid of convention— that is, the convention (saṃketa) consisting of the agreement (samaya) established by elders and others that "this is the denotation of this"— and it is the reflective awareness of its own essential nature.

Beyond space, time, parts, illusion, location, destruction, and action, everything is complete in itself, yet distinct from all forms. [And because of its very sovereignty, being devoid of limitation by space and time, it is pervasive, eternal, and its nature is both with and without form; thus it is stated elsewhere.]

The nature of the existent reality is characterized solely by the great consciousness of its own-being and by *saṃskāra* (as the *Bhāṣya* states: "the imposition of another quality upon an existing thing"). Its form consists of pure *vidyā* and is of a dual nature as "I" (*ahaṃ*), because the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is implied by "I-ness" (*ahantā*) itself.
That very form of the Mātṛkā is the innate body of the elements beginning with earth;
it is their ultimate form, by virtue of being the solidified state of consciousness.
It is declared to consist of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the womb-syllable (*yoni*), having the nature of Śiva and Śakti;
from the union of Śiva and Śakti, through their mutual surging forth.
The mutual union, which bestows bliss upon the world,
has as its ultimate reality a true form that encompasses everything from the internal to the limits of the universe.
That which has been determined as *vīrya* (vital energy) is the union and separation;
that is called *visarga* (emission), and it is said to be the abode of the eternal (*dhruvadhāma*). As it was stated in the *Devībhāvanā* within the *Pañcastavī* hymn:
O Bhavānī, having risen from the hollow of the root-vessel and pierced through the six lotuses like a flash of lightning,
you surely enter back into that very place in the form of the supreme nectar-water flowing from the moon of the *dhruvamaṇḍala*.
Thus [it is said].
This very method is easily accomplished for the attainment of the unsurpassed state;
it has been described from this very collection of phonemes belonging to the realm of illusion (māyā).

In the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijaya), it is taught that the imperishable emission (*sṛṣṭi*), having taken recourse to *māyā*, is indeed distinct, consisting of the generation of cognitions divided into fifty varieties. As it is said in the *Spanda*: "Just as in the case of the supreme nectar, there is a loss of its flavor when a cognition arises."
Therefore, it attains a state of non-independence, and that [consciousness] has only those [objects] as its domain.
Thus ends the evolution of the intellect (pratyayasarga).
By its very nature, it consists of bondage and has the essence of veiling one's true form.

Within this very [mass of phonemes that is free from *māyā*], those various *khecarīs* are included. Indeed, the powers such as *khecarī* are twofold; they take the forms of *khecarī*, *gocarī*, *dikcarī*, and *bhūcarī*. And their twofold nature is as follows:

For those purified by the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*), because they possess the nature of emitting the expansion of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*) and are thus untainted by time, the ultimate reality consists in the unfolding of their essential nature as non-dual, all-pervasive agency, fullness, and omnipresence;
whereas for those deluded by *māyā*, it does not bestow bliss, as they wander upon the plane of the void subject (*śūnya-pramātṛ*).

Because they consist of time, its divisions, pure discernment (*vicāra*), and *āgana* (the source of destiny), they are the binders. "Speech" (*gaur vāk*) refers to those [powers] that move within the planes of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and mind (*manas*), which are characterized by that [speech] and consist of discursive thought (*saṃjalpa*). For those who have received the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), these are the "movements" (*gocaryaḥ*) that cause the growth of pure determination, conceit, and volition; for others, however, they are the opposite. [This applies] to the directions.

They are called *dikcaryās* because they move within the ten external sense organs; for those who have been graced [by the teacher], their essence is the manifestation of non-duality, whereas for others, they fall into the perception of duality. They are called *bhūcaryās* because they move within the fivefold objects of cognition—earth, form, and so forth—and by means of the solidification of that mental engagement, they have attained identity with them; this refers to those who are awakened.

There is a twofold state: [consciousness] manifests as having the body of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), and it displays the total limitation (*nyavacchedatā*) of other things from all sides. Here, however, the state exists solely with the intention of bondage, because it is said to be "consisting of objects" (*viṣayātmikā*), in accordance with the verbal root *ṣiñ*, meaning "to bind. Thus, they consist of objects.
They weave a manifold cycle of existence, consisting of the subtle power of karma and māyā.
Its similarity to its own nature consists in this: it is a pure manifestation of the external.
The state of being a living soul and the state of liberation have already been declared as ultimately real;
and the supreme body is non-different from that [reality], even though the creation of castes appears distinct.

What has been called "vīrya" right here is that by whose protection the mantra remains secret; this very [vīrya] is the nature of the unsurpassed emission (visarga), consisting of the thought "I am this."
The wise one who, knowing the supreme nature of his own self, is liberated while living, is never again bound;
whereas those desiring supernatural powers and the like remain ensnared by the constraints fashioned by that [ignorance].
We yogins worship the space within the heart, which is like an earring at the navel;
this has indeed been briefly determined according to the tradition of the Guru’s teachings.
Relying upon this realization, let that which arises be asked of your own inner wisdom;
for by this much alone the path has not been fully weighed, though its portion has been shown.
For who could indeed delimit this Bhairavī consciousness as being "only this much"?
This very extent of the descent of power (śaktipāta) has manifested within us.
By virtue of the authority bestowed upon us, we have now revealed this [teaching] for ourselves and for our other mothers, whether today or at some other time.
Therefore, reasoning (tarka), even in its most subtle form, comes into being after not having been, and will continue to exist;
it is that which possesses rays of light illuminating all the components and methods of yoga.
That by which the one who is liberated and the one who liberates is determined in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra must be accepted and reflected upon in every way by those who desire the Supreme.
Wise men, having abandoned for a moment that envy so easily found among mortals,
should maintain that state within themselves which arises after the moment of reflection.

The fragments of clouds over the sun of consciousness are naturally pacified by their own essence. Enough with this appearance of the perception of another; let there be no further wandering about. O you who possess the splendor of the supreme realization, abandon the state of being a dependent, and indeed embrace the supreme color.
The great power of the dwelling-place, agitated by the ocean of suffering, flows forth; it is the unaccomplished ground of existence, the essence of the earth, the supreme state beyond all.
It is described as the external sphere of activity, the field of emission, free from affliction. Having seen this stainless path of entry, the sphere of activity is rendered pure;
it is the unsurpassed, the ultimate, which, having become that very reality, shines like a drop of ash.

(217) O daughter, you have been attached to him; therefore, having previously abandoned the seven impurities, you shall fearlessly laugh at the darkness. O Tamālī, having thus spoken to her son, he said: "O Aila, enjoy the earth; may you rule over the entire world, free from enemies, until the end of time. Thus he spoke, his heart overflowing with affection for his son.
O you who have departed from this pair, your beauty is now like a fading splendor; you are the object of that non-violence and supreme purity.
O deer-eyed one, alas, you are a stage for lamentations, a restless fawn with eyes full of tears, whose essence is sorrow.
You are intoxicated by the nectar of passion, yet now you are parched by the separation from your beloved; alas, you are not being drunk by him, for he is now utterly indifferent to your caresses.

Thus, regarding what was stated—that the "Unsurpassed" (anuttara) is also [derived] from the "Surpassed" (uttara)—that Śākta expansion of emanation, which consists of that [Surpassed] and is comprised by the aspect of the "Surpassed," has been determined in detail as being of the nature of Kula. Furthermore, that "Surpassed" has been described in such a way that it is itself the "Unsurpassed.
Now, however, the "Unsurpassed" itself must be examined in detail according to its own essential nature; such is the manner of injunction and restatement.
If, in the process of fulfillment, both the part being restated and the part being enjoined were to be characterized by their own essential nature—
as in the case where "the very remembrance of Śiva’s name is itself the surging forth of all happiness," and thus both parts are the objects of characterization— then [the fault would apply].
