p. 218) However, although here there is no other entity whatsoever called "the unsurpassed" (anuttara)— since if it were something else, it would necessarily follow that it too is "surpassed" (uttara)— nevertheless, this [designation] is used with the intention of establishing the relationship between the teacher and the taught through the construction of autonomy (svātantrya).

The systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) was mentioned previously; therefore, for the purpose of defining the nature of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) in detail, there is the introduction of another text. It defines that [nature] as follows:
"O Blessed One, [it consists of] fourteen joined with the end of the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśa*). (9)
O lady of beautiful hips, this third Brahman is the heart of the Bhairava-Self;
it is clearly not obtained by one who is not born of a Yoginī, nor by one who is not Rudra.
This heart-mantra of the God of gods bestows yoga and liberation instantly;
when it is properly uttered, the great multitude of mantras and mudrās is fully realized.

(219) He who is sealed by the Kisser (Cumbaka) remembers for a moment that he attains the state of having that [deity’s] very face, which is characterized by the entry of his own body [into the deity]. 12.
Then that person binds the entire assembly of mantras and mudrās;
when questioned, he even speaks of matters past and future.
Reciting whatever form of a deity he desires at the beginning of the watch and so forth,
he sees it directly and without doubt, drawn forth by the powers of Rudra.
By remembering [this] for merely two watches (six hours), one becomes situated in the sky;
by three [watches], all the Mothers, the powerful mistresses of yoga, [appear]. 15.
The heroes, the lords of heroes, the perfected ones, and the powerful host of Śākinīs,
having been impelled by Bhairava, arrived and offered their pledge. (16)
They bestow supreme accomplishment, or whatever fruit is desired; by means of this, accomplished practitioners have attained success, will attain it, and are attaining it. || 17 ||
Whatever is found in the Bhairava Tantra, all of that is accomplished through this;
even one who has not seen the maṇḍala attains [success] in this very way. || 18 ||

The Śākta [nature] is the essence of the universe— which, though appearing in the form of Bhairava, has been established through the reasoning and scriptures as having the nature of the Supreme Goddess (Aparābhaṭṭārikā) in her human form;
its heart, its core, is the form of Śiva, embraced by the Supreme Sovereign, the venerable Parābhaṭṭārikā.

By the word *bhairava*, [is meant] the form of power (*śakti*) which is the nature of the universal identity of all things within the universe; [this refers to] a single differentiation with respect to the Self that is conjoined with that [power]. (p. 221)

The heart of this one in human form consists of Śiva to such an extent that, through supreme non-duality, there is indeed the state of being the self of all; for without that [non-duality] and by means of it, this very duality would be impossible, as was stated previously. The address “O fair-hipped one” (suśroṇi) refers to that heart which, even within the nature of the inauspicious Māyā, is never departed from and consists of pure consciousness.
The nature of the Yoni has been described as that which is filled within by all the great lords of mantras (Maheśas) and others,

and which consists of the fullness of the self of Bhairava for us— those whose identity is the "I"— and who possess the appropriate designations such as "this" or "ours," extending to the entire network of subjects ending with the immobile world.
Brahman is the single mass of the power of bliss arising from the separation of the emission (*visarga*), which consists of the surging forth of the universal potency inherent within it;
it is vast, pervasive, and expanded—not like the vision of Brahman held by the readers of the Vedānta, which does not stand far removed from the doctrine of absolute nihilism. And this...

The third [level] is of a single form centered on Śiva in relation to humans and others; for this very reason, in these scriptures and here [in this work], that alone is taught as the primary heart (*hṛdaya*) to be worshipped. Even those whose heart—the essence consisting of the pervasion of such potency (*vīrya*)—has not yet entered [into that state], by the mere practice of external conduct to that extent...
When the bonds of the fetters of animal existence (*pāśava-niyama*) have become loosened by the power of the gradual process— becoming slack, further slackened, split, and utterly shattered—
they themselves come to rest within the pervasion of this Heart; then, that indeed is the very entry into this Heart.

"I have entered into this very heart; this Goddess is the Supreme"—these [notions] are merely constructed by verbal conceptualization. On the contrary, it has been explained at length that they do not lead to the search for the inner core of the Heart;
rather, the snares of the scriptures contract the Heart. Indeed, neither these scriptural bonds nor this worldly existence should defile one's consciousness.
That very state would be one filled with the weight of shimmering absorption (laya), its form perfected by the path of the true nature (samyaksvabhāva).
As I myself have stated in my hymn:
"Due to the intense immersion in devotion to you, this state— whose clarity has arisen within the mind— instantly and clearly comes to dwell within the heart."

Thus, for this very reason, the three [goddesses] are to be worshipped in the corners, while in the center is the Goddess whose nature is the churning of Parānandabhairava; she exists through the very flow of the essence of eternal bliss (*nityānanda-rasa*), by means of the emission (*visarga*) characterized by agitation. This is the tradition of the deities regarding the *yāmalayoga*. For the heroes (*vīra*s) as well, it arises from the union with the *dūtī*s, which consists of the agitation of the sense-organ of bliss and eternal bliss.
Even in the state of being a solitary hero (ekavīratā),
by virtue of resting in the bliss of one's own essential nature (svarūpānanda), even for a man...

Because the mind is fixed upon the triangular bulbous root (*kanda*), which is the abode of the emergence of the bliss-faculties, it produces the arousal of bliss; this occurs when there is a dense friction between the base of those faculties and their extremity. Regarding this, it is said: "In the midst of fire and poison... [etc.]
Thus, the yoga of bliss itself is the worship of the heart; as it is stated in the *Trikatantrasāra*:
"The flow of bliss is worship; one should perform that within the triangle, using flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth, which bring satisfaction to one's own heart."

Thus, everything is indeed permeated by the two mudrās, because their essence consists of the powers of knowledge (jñāna) and action (kriyā). Among the deities, the knowledge-mudrā is predominant internally while the action-mudrā is predominant externally; among the heroes (vīras), it is the reverse. However, entry occurs through equality and through the reversal [of these states]. It is with this very intention that [the deity is established] in the *liṅga*, which consists of the power of knowledge.

Thus, the bestowal of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) has been explained. This [system] is joined with and integrated into the fourteen [tattvas], consisting of fifteen [units], and is endowed with the sixteenth, the emission (visarga), which is the Lord of the lunar days (tithīśa).

Alternatively, "endowed with fourteen" refers to the pair [of vowels] joined with the fourteenth; the "Lord of the fifteen lunar days" is the Visarga, and its "end" is the seventeenth, the unsurpassed Kalā (Anuttara). The Heart is conjoined with that. It has been stated that all things, such as pots, pleasure, and so forth, pervade that very essence of the seed (bījasattā) in its ultimate form.

In detail, for this very reason, that heart is thus sixteenfold. This heart, in accordance with the *Anuttara* [Tantra], is that primordial state of non-differentiation which is the union of Brahman and the identity of the object and subject (*vedya-vedaka*), the aggregate of the four states beginning with *udyoga*; endowed with that non-differentiation are these lords of the lunar days (*tithi*).
Because everything else originates from them, they end with the vowel *ū*; for it has been stated: "In this succession of phonemes, the group of six vowels alone shall be the root.
Thus, the four nectar-phonemes (*amṛtavarṇa*) are at the end of those lords of the lunar days (*tithīśa*). By means of these...

And that third [state] is correctly associated [with the fourth]: with respect to humans and others, it is the supreme form of Śiva, the knower, shining forth through four stages; while the object of knowledge itself, through those [stages], consists of the nature of nourishment and curiosity—unifying those very nectarian digits within one's own self by means of the attainment of the agitation between the known and the knower.

One should enter the unsurpassed heart of the universe, whose nature is Bhairava, by means of the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna* characterized by the realization of oneness (*aikātmya*), or through repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa*). As it has been said:

"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self. Thus, within the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), whose nature is the radiance of will (*icchā*), that which is the third form—the essence of will (*icchātman*)—arises by withdrawing [the other powers] and following after the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). This very form, at its initial stage (*prākkoṭau*), is untainted by anything yet to be willed. At its initial stage...
Since [the universe] is defiled by being subject to the *hīṣya* and other [states], how can it be Brahman? To this, the intended meaning is that in the eastern portion it is "undefiled" (*akaluṣa*).

And regarding Brahman, there are forty-four divisions in the fourth [tattva], which, with respect to the divisions of Bhairava, include the principles (*tattvas*) together with the three supreme powers of Parabhairava, as has been stated.
There are thirty-six things to be purified, and the supreme Bhairava is the purifier. As was established at the beginning regarding the Supreme Triad:
the Mother is the great new creation resting upon the stainless digit (*vimalakalā*), whose body is full; and the Father is he of beautiful, secret splendor with five faces.
May my heart, which consists of the natural outpouring of the radiance of that union of the two, and which is the family of the unsurpassed nectar, shine forth!
Thus, the *karaṇa* (instrument) is the means of purification; this initiation, however, is the ultimate *karaṇa*.

(226) Thus, that which is joined with these—the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which is indeed full and devoid of prior or posterior form—how could it be associated with the lords of the lunar days (*tithīśa*) as seeds, and with those ending in the womb-forms (*yonirūpa*) and so forth? This is an adverbial modifier; that alone is the Heart.

In this context, the form that is everywhere and simultaneously manifest, which is accessible through higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), is the primary [object]; however, for those who are fit for it—

having been purified by the descent of the supreme power (*paraśaktipāta*)— or even for those who are merely eager for the illusory displays of a magician, it should be understood as the practice of yoga.
By the intention of "desire" (icchā), the third is desire; and that [desire] is augmented by the non-differentiated, full Brahman which is the object of desire.

There are fourteen times forty [units] which possess no division. Since the word *yuta* also denotes "divided," as in the phrase "because of being established separately" (*yutasiddhatvāt*), [it is used here in the sense of non-separation], as in the definition: "The relation between two things that are not established separately is inherence" (*ayutasiddhayoḥ sambandhaḥ samavāyaḥ*).

The meaning is "of two things that are established as conjoined" (*yutasiddha*) yet not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha*). Having kept this very intention in mind, it is stated in the *Siddhāntakaumudī*:

"the root *yu* is used in the sense of mixing and non-mixing. Within the Lord of the lunar day (*tithīśvara*), who consists of the supreme *kalā* of the *Kula*, there is bliss; following that (*anu*), it is correctly attained (*samita*) as consisting of consciousness.
In relation to Īśāna, the third [form], which is of the nature of will (*icchā*), becomes vast by the force of its expansion and attains the state of Īśāna;
[this occurs] for the fourteen [worlds] and forty [kalās].

Where there is a mutual intermingling of what has been described, and where the dissolution of the Lord of the lunar day (*tithīśvara*) occurs within the *Anuttara* calculation of the *Akula*, it is conjoined with that first vibration of the power of *Kula*.
Through union with the power of knowledge whose nature is expansion (*unmeṣa*), the third is indeed Brahmā-Īśāna; when [it is] thus [of Īśāna].

He establishes the third state of Brahman with the words beginning "yadā" [when]. It is that wherein the first division of those very fourteen [principles] out of the forty-four principles is joined; likewise, it is endowed with the first vibration (*spanda*) of the Kula-śakti ending with Tithīśa, by virtue of being properly possessed of the desire to ascend. Here, the word "saṃ" [is used].
Dependent on sustenance;

through the ascent of the intense state supported by the *ūkāra-kalā* previously determined as the central limit of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*), that which is this Brahman— whatever is moving or unmoving— [is realized].

Then, with respect to the impure, the pure-impure, and the pure creation, there is a third [creation] consisting of the pure creation; for this very reason, it is endowed with the Lords of the Lunar Days (*tithīśvara*) as its heart, and with the letters from *ka* to *kṣa* at its end. Now, following the sequence of the four voids (*śūnya*), there exists therein the ten states of destruction belonging to the four elements beginning with earth.
That void, joined with that [fire], is the third Brahma, known as Will (icchā), endowed with the external radiance of the Sun, the Lord of the lunar days (tithīśvara).
According to the explained sequence, this third [deity], Brahmeśana, is also exactly like this.

The third is called Brahmecha; it is that which is joined as a support for the internal periods (*antardaśā*) of the four beginning with space (*nabhas*), and it is accompanied by the form of the fire (*tejas*) of the Lord of the Tithis (*tithīśa*) which follows after it.
The nature of space; likewise, the third Brahma, joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the lunar days (Amāvasyā),
is the nature of Bhairava through the leap into the form of the full void.
Indeed, when desire— accompanied by the power of its own inherent nature (*īśana*)— ascends toward the state of space (*vyoma*) within the realm of the knowable,

it first rests upon the ground of slight illumination and then suddenly enters the boundless, motionless plane of space, which consists primarily of wood and stone; therein, one enters the great void of dreamless sleep (*suṣupta*) where no object of knowledge remains.
It is said in response to the yogi: "Even the sound of a kettledrum or a brass gong is not conducive to emergence," and so forth.

229) Now, regarding this aforementioned variety consisting of the mutual intermingling of the forms of the powers (*śakti*), it is with reference to this that such a will arises when it is characterized by entry into the state of the Absolute (*anuttara*); at that time, [there occurs] the agitation of the power (*śaktikṣobha*).

Immediately after the discussion of the tongue and so forth, it is said therein: where there exists the fourth state, characterized by the four sounds, which consists of the general vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*) of the specific vibrations of consciousness (*cid-viśeṣa-spanda*) associated with *sattva* and the other qualities;
that is *Akula*. Being conjoined with that *Anuttara* (the Unsurpassed), the third *Brahman*, whose nature is Will (*icchātman*), is accompanied by Sovereignty (*īśana*).

Joined at the end of the vowel *ā*, the lord of the lunar days (*tithīśa*), which is of the nature of the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*), that [vowel] likewise again enters back into the supreme existence (*parāṃ sattām*). When that occurs, it becomes the self of Bhairava, complete and elongated—“for us” (*naḥ*) as before. For this very reason, this alone is the pair of seed-syllables (*bījayugma*).
Because it enters into such a variety of seeds, it is said to be capable of both concealing and bringing forth through the application of the principles of desire and speech:
"One should desire desires with desire; one should join desire to desires."
And so forth (p.
The seed-syllable situated in the letter *e* is solely for the purpose of the manifestation of speech.

Thus, by means of the fifth and sixth letters, that which was stated— namely, the third Brahman joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the lunar-day lord (tithīśa)— is precisely this very Brahman, having entered the unsurpassed state (anuttara-pada) whose essence is Bhairava; according to the aforementioned method,
it is joined with the fortieth and endowed with the end of the lunar-day lord, insofar as its nature is the realization of the essence of Bhairava.
This entire web of principles, whose essence is the *bindu*, surges forth as the nature of Bhairava;

therefore, when projected outward, it becomes the expanded Brahman consisting of emission (*visarga*). Abiding externally, it becomes one with the nature of Bhairava by means of removing the poverty of differentiation through the exclusion of dualistic distinctions.
"Augmented by the attainment of the state that is the self of all things"—thus has this state of emission (*visarga*) been determined through careful attention.

In this way, the sixteenfold pervasion of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) has been described. As for the pervasion of the womb-syllables (*yoni*), however, it has already been explained with respect to each individual letter; it shall now be further examined from the perspective of their systematic classification.
The third [aspect] is Brahman, consisting of the aggregate of the four stages— childhood, youth, old age, and the assumption of another body—
and composed of the five elements; it is joined internally with the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) characterized by entry and exit, ending with the lord of the lunar days (the *tithīśa*),
and consists of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).

And because of its vastness, that which is the void here is the Heart whose essence is Śakti; thus all these are of the nature of the body, the vital breath, the *puryaṣṭaka*, the void, and the Fourth Śakti.

The subjects—designated as the external self (*bāhyātman*), the embodied self (*ātmabhūtātman*), the subtle body (*ātivāhikātman*), the inner self (*antarātman*), and the supreme self (*paramātman*)—are those who have attained, through a gradual process, a state of being that is progressively more intense and dense than the seed of Śiva which consists of awakening (*bodha*).
The means of entry here into this Heart, which is the nature of Bhairava, is as follows: "all the planes of the subject" (*sarvāḥ pramātṛbhūmīḥ*).
As it has been said:
"Having completely exhausted all powers— such as seeing, touching, and so forth— simultaneously within their respective objects of knowledge,
You alone shine forth in the center like a crystal pillar, the support of the universe."
Thus it is said: "O Caṇḍikā, by whichever of the fourteen poisons one may travel— those residing in the external organs, the intellect, the ego, the mind, and the suṣumnā— "
O Mother, casting aside all arts, such a state as that arises there; alas, it is difficult to find in the world, even for the gods!

Thus, one should traverse the planes of the subject without limitation: the thirteen internal and external organs together with primordial nature (*prakṛti*) make fourteen; doubled, they are twenty-eight; increased by forty, they are sixty-eight; the lunar days (*tithi*) are fifteen; and the lords (*īśāḥ*) are [nine]. (p. 232)
The eleven Rudras are joined with the three Kālas; thus,

[one contemplates] the very existence of the body as consisting of the agitation (*kṣobha*) resulting from the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*) and separation (*viśleṣaṇa*) of the emission (*visarga*), which is made to vibrate by the expansion of the potency of the mantra— the nature of the gross, subtle, and supreme Śākta pulsation— residing within the one hundred and twelve vital points (*marmans*).

One should cultivate the form of Bhairava through the method of simultaneous immersion (*yugapanniveśa-saṃpradāya*). That wine, *surā*, *āsava*, or the like, which possesses the four states of sweet, astringent, bitter, and sour—[as it has been said:
"One should practice with the prohibited [substances] the goddesses residing in the intellect, the senses, and the organs"].
That which is forbidden and loathed by the world... [is not to be done].
Thus it is said:
"Even though this supreme power is eternally manifest, nevertheless,
for one devoid of external ritual practice, the state of Kaula is difficult to attain."
Thus it is said elsewhere:
"One should employ everything here, both worldly and supramundane;
but if one is trembling while [the other] is unshakable, one should forcibly diminish that trembling."
And it should not be thought that this [practice] must necessarily be performed here:
"Where is meat, and where is devotion to Śiva? Where is liquor, and where is the worship of Śiva? Indeed, Śaṅkara is very difficult to attain for those intent on worship with liquor and such."

Because of such contradictions as these, what then should be understood here? That for those whose true nature has been recognized through re-cognition, no stain of doubt should be entertained. Even one who is free from suspicion, though a knower of reality, [should act] toward the seeker of liberation regarding the method of practice.
One should not abandon the boundaries of the scriptures; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Thus, because of the clear prohibition of [worship by] gods and others, therefore, in this matter, the *Mahārthamañjarī* alone is the authority in every respect, as in the passage beginning, "according to where one's inclination lies," and so forth. That [mantra] ends with the Lord of the lunar days (tithīśa).

That third impurity (*mala*), which consists of the substance of both emissions and resides within the two organs, is denoted by the word "flower" (*kusuma*); it is the ash remaining after the burning of the fuel of the world, whose nature is Bhairava, which is the nourishing water of full form, and the heart,
which is of a dual nature consisting of the congealed essence residing within all the senses.

Therefore, these substances, as they may be obtained, are for the purpose of dissolving impurities and stains; as it has been said: "By whatever means and by whichever method, whether gradually or even simultaneously, one should exert effort so that doubt within dissolves."

Thus it is; for this very sequence is indeed observed: this very doubt, consisting of contraction, as it arises, takes root and reaches its fruition, becoming the first sprout of the seed-tree of transmigratory existence. As it was said previously in this very work:
"The wise and auspicious ones declare that the impurity called 'contraction' (*āṇavamala*), which is the root of the impurities of *māyā* and *karman*, is indeed the primary cause."
"That alone is the root of the ancient tree of existence.

Herein is the summary: as has been stated by this very [author], one should not weary one's own self here with the discrimination between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit, or between purity and impurity—[discriminations] that are devoid of the true nature of reality.
Purity and impurity are not the inherent nature of an object from the perspective of ultimate reality, because they are observed to be mutually exclusive.
That which is considered purity by the wise is regarded as impurity by others,
just as giving is prescribed [as pure] for one who is not initiated, yet is considered impure for one who has been initiated.
This is merely a mental construction; therefore, let it be accepted as such by the wise. There is no certainty that a construction is real, for it is indeed false.
Therefore, in this investigation of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), the status of being the "answer" belongs to this alone;
indeed, this is beyond doubt for both the proponent and the opponent.

Thus it is said. In this regard, the following inquiry arises: if it is argued that [the world] is not impure because of the Mīmāṃsaka statement that "the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is indeed uncontradicted," we reply that it is established by reasoning that the Śiva-injunction itself is contradicted, just as it has been stated that the knowledge of the bound (*pāśava-jñāna*) is expressed through varying degrees of contraction.
However, the cognition of the cloth, by virtue of the varying degrees of its manifestation, is a sublater [of that notion].

Thus it is said; likewise, in the Śivopaniṣad: "That purification which is prescribed by those of limited knowledge is not considered true purification in the vision of Śambhu. [The text continues: "In the vision of Śambhu, purification is [attained] through... [the rest of the verse follows].
Thus it is said: "The conviction of the bound soul— that 'I am inert, I am fettered by karma, I am impure, I am driven by others'—
is instantly transformed into the state of the Lord, whose body is the universe and whose nature is consciousness, through the attainment of a different, firm conviction."
Thus, that state exists for those who are unawakened;
it is imagined by the awakened and is likewise being imagined for the sake of the ignorant, yet it remains established for them through its very diversity.

For this very reason, because of the conceptualization of diversity, that [power] is designated by various terms such as "dharmas" and so forth; it appears in different forms in each scripture and in each region, as it has been said:
"Languor is a plunderer" (as in the *Spanda*).
Illness is a plunderer of the body, and its course arises from ignorance; if that [ignorance] is destroyed by the unfolding of [true] consciousness, how could such illness exist without a cause?
Thus [regarding the body...

Thus, when this [body] suddenly dissolves, one becomes free from the stain of the fetters of the animal state (pāśava) and enters the heart of Bhairava; therefore, one should strive by all means in this practice.
This is the intended meaning in the *Śrītilakaśāstra*. It is also stated in the *Śrībhargaśikhā*:
"One should welcome the Vīra-vow and practice it accordingly," and so forth. It is likewise stated in the *Śrīsarvācāra*.
Out of ignorance, the deluded person fears; from that [ignorance] proceed both creation and dissolution.
All mantras consist of phonemes, and all phonemes are of the nature of Śiva.
Water is known as that which is drinkable and undrinkable; the earth consists of what is edible and inedible;
and all that is beautiful and ugly is said to be fire.
Wind is remembered as the touchable and the intangible; the void is called space.
The offering and the offerer, as well as that which is received as the offering—[all these are one].
O Goddess, everything consists of the five elements; nothing anywhere is devoid of them.
Since the Self produces desire, how can doubt be entertained?

Thus it is said. This same intention is also expressed in the *Śrīvīrāvaliśāstra*, and it is stated in the *Kramastotra*: "I bow to Kālī, who draws back [into herself] the body of Yama—the restrainer of the universe and the one who withdraws all objects—while she is intent upon the playful act of the great devouring of that form."

Thus it has been explained by me at length in my commentary on the *Kramakeli* itself. For this very reason, in the Trika scriptures (*ṣaḍardhaśāstra*), this same ritual action is primarily worship because it is free from restrictive constraints; and for the sake of fulfilling that [worship] alone, when all the necessary substances are unavailable, the procedure for the *pavitraka* (the sacred thread) is prescribed to be performed four times, three times, twice, or once within the course of a year.
He who performs [the rite] four times or even once for the sake of completing the ritual action and for fulfilling the command of the sacrifice, his *pavitra* is fruitless.

Thus, the sequence of consciousness has been explained in detail. Furthermore, the Blessed One stated that there is no fixed status for castes such as the Brāhmaṇas and so forth— because they are conceptually constructed— and that [the claim] they are manifested through instruction is intended only to lead those of dull intellect, who are like beasts, astray.

This has been determined in detail in the *Mukuṭasaṃhitā*, but here it is established without effort. The qualities, beginning with Will (*icchā*), have been determined as fourteen; from among the vowels, [the seed-syllable] is that which stands between the letters *o* and *au*, ending with the Lord of the Tithis (*tithīśa*) as the *visarga*, and containing the third Brahman (*ṣa-ha*) in its midst. This is the seed-syllable of the universe in reality; for whatever exists— *Note: The specific seed-mantra (bīja) derived from the description is "oṃ" (or "oṃ" depending on the interpretation of the "third Brahman" as the letter "ṣ"), though the commentary suggests a more complex derivation involving the phonemes o, au, visarga, and ṣ-ha.*

That form, consisting of the earthly, the elemental, and the illusory, appears; although it falls within will, knowledge, or action, because it is the self of all, it is threefold in nature. It is emitted into the supreme state of Śiva, and everything is emitted from the state of Śiva—thus this very uninterrupted flow is non-conceptual, even though it is a conceptualization.

The group beginning with women and enemies is thus an object of action; for this very reason, one becomes a doer of such [actions], thinking "I was a doer of such [actions]," "I am a doer of such [actions]," and "I will be a doer of such [actions]"—thus, through the connection of the three times, emission (*visarga*) exists precisely as the ultimate reality of differentiation.
Thus, on the contrary, for those cursed by fate, the very ground of auspicious liberation has always become a vast desert forest of fear for the cycle of existence;
from the waters arises a mass of the submarine fire, dense with flickering flames, while from the moon comes [only] a store of nectar.

How wondrous is this marvel: that from the tenth lunar day, through the fullness of the moon until the end of the full moon—according to the scriptures, from which [fullness] comes the shattering by the thunderbolt—and from the path of the expansion of sovereignty arising from conceptual thought, there is the destruction of transmigratory existence! How truly marvelous!
It flows forth from the destruction of the expansion of ritual injunctions.
It is also stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

"For one who fully recognizes, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs regarding the universal self; for the inner Self is certainly not some other kind of bound soul (*paśu*)."
"Is there anyone else? No, even I am that very one who is a dense mass of light wherein the grasped and the grasper have been fully integrated;
I am that Being, and I alone, not anyone else. Therefore, even the creation of conceptual constructs is my own sovereign power (vibhava), characterized by absolute freedom.
When such a realization becomes firm, one is liberated while still living, even if conceptual thought has not yet entirely ceased. As it has been said:
Even doubt would not be suspected; this state of being free from doubt is manifest.
Thus.

Thus, just as within the very midst of forms there are forms such as the four-armed and three-eyed, or the full and the emaciated, and within the very midst of substances there are substances such as wine and spirits (p.
As if forcibly causing that very existence to rest within them, they are like written syllables;

thus, these [referring to the four-armed forms and so forth, as well as the written syllables] possess excellence. In this way, even among all phonemes (*varṇa*), this phoneme [the word "phoneme" implies: this possesses excellence] is likewise. For instance:
The letter *sa* is, first of all, the nature of the nectar of supreme bliss. As it has been said:
"The reality of the fullness of desire is explained as occurring in the union (*saṃghaṭṭa*);
the reality of the nectar of the object arises when the atom (*aṇu*) is released from its state of being concealed."
Thus, while shining forth, it seizes the entire collection of phonemes and shines as that very ultimate essence of truth, bliss, plenitude, and existence—
which is characterized by the emission of the *sītkāra* sound, trembling, and the contraction and expansion of the generative organ. For that alone is [the ultimate reality].

The non-illusory, real nature of truth and the other [categories] is as follows: for instance, those who are skilled in discerning the intentions of others' hearts can achieve their desired goal from the mere perception of the letter *ga* alone— even when that *ga* occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of an infinite series of words such as "gaganagavaya" (sky-cow) or "gava" (cow)— provided it is present within that much.
p.
240) Because of the entry into the locus of truth, in this way each individual phoneme possesses real denotative power, as it has been said:
"There is a confusion [of identity] due to the mutual superimposition of word, meaning, and cognition."

Through *saṃyama* on their differentiation, there arises knowledge of the cries of all beings. [The differentiation of those sounds, meanings, and cognitions—*saṃyama* upon that is the technical definition of *saṃyama*: "the three together in one place" is the conventional designation for *saṃyama*.]
(Yoginīhṛdayasūtra 3-17).

For this very reason, these particles (*nipāta*), case-endings (*vibhakti*), and so forth—which consist of single phonemes such as *a*, *ca*, and others—are generally [treated thus]; for instance, they are called "particles" (*nipāta*) because they "fall down" (*nipatanti*) upon meanings established by another.
Regarding the claim that [the Self] is non-substantial (*asattva*) because it lacks distinctions produced by gender, number, and case-role (*kāraka*), as stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"There is no otherness for this Self from the I-consciousness (*ahantā*) and so forth, due to the absence of differentiation in its reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
It exists solely as the object of the 'I'-reflection, like an object denoted by a verbal suffix (*tiṅvācya-karman*)."
Thus [it is said]. Here, for the sake of applying it to the subject at hand, one must conceive of a reversal between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Just as by means of the powers of particles (*nipāta*), which are non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*) and consist of the forms of suffixes (*pratyaya*), option (*vikalpa*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*), no meaning distinct from that which is negated or conjoined is denoted. Just as...

In the state of Māyā as well, an object that is not distinct from the creation is designated by terms such as "I," "Lord" (Īśvara), or "Self" (Ātman) precisely because it is perceived as "I"; yet this is not the [actual] Lord or Self. It is as if ultimately real, merged within the state of the subject, turned away from "this-ness" (idantā), and characterized by non-existence.

This very point is the view of the venerable Bhartṛhari, who said (p. 241): "Words express such meanings as the negation of what is being negated, the collection [of things] being collected, and the negation or collection of non-different forms."
"Every word is distinct, and every word is expectant [of others] due to mutual superimposition"—
thus it is said in the investigation of sentences (*vākyavicāra*). And so it is stated in the *Pārameśvara* scriptures on Vedic grammar.
In words such as *mantra* and *dīkṣā*, an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is justified due to the similarity of their constituent letters and phonemes. But [an objection may be raised]:

"If this is so, then since everything is rooted in letters and phonemes, it would follow that an etymological derivation could be applied everywhere simply through the similarity of letters and phonemes, because words and sentences are rooted in those [letters]. One who abandons the root and grasps the branches..."

For there would be a great disadvantage [if it were not so]; therefore he says "But that" (*tattu*) and so forth. He states the reason for this by asking "Why? (*kutaḥ*), saying: "By the power of necessity" (*niyativaśāt*).

For everything has been established by the Supreme Lord through the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*); thus, the meaning is that there is a restriction (*niyama*) such that, through the combination of the syllables *brahma*, the meaning of this word is exactly this. It is not conventional (*na rūḍham*)—that is, not [so] by the power of necessity.
Thus, the letter *sakāra* extends to the end of the world; the letters *au* and the *visarga* have also been explained. As it is said in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"The triad is pervaded by the letter *sa*, and the fourth by the trident (*triśūla*)."

The supreme pervasion (*parā vyāpti*) is declared to be that which transcends all by means of the emission (*visarga*). This number consists of three parts, hence it is a "triad" (*tritaya*), a sphere (*aṇḍa*) characterized by the number three; therein, the designations of the earthly (*pārthiva*), the primordial nature (*prākṛta*), and *māyā* are pervaded by the phoneme *sa*.
The meaning is that the pervasion of the letter *sa* extends up to that limit, by means of the trident (*triśūla*).

"Fourth" means the fourth Śākta-maṇḍala; and that [is performed] with the trident—the seed-syllable *au*—as before, by means of the thirty-six-fold utterance. He states that which transcends this [level] with the word "all," which is clear. The sense is that "this is the supreme initiation (*parā-dīkṣā*)."
Thus, likewise,
the disciple too should receive [the teaching] only when the guru has been satisfied.
[By means of] body, substance, consciousness, birth, karma, qualities, and so forth, [and by training in other treatises].
But when she has been pierced by that Guru with a joyful heart,
then she should be known as the bestower of accomplishment, and not otherwise, O Goddess worshipped by heroes.
Thus it is said. Elsewhere also, there is one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, as it has been stated:
"There is one seed-syllable consisting of emanation, and one mudrā, namely Khecarī."
He in whom these two arise abides in the state of supreme peace.
Thus [it is said]. * * * * * * * * (?

| Thus. For this very reason, there is a rule in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra* that it should not be written in a book: "The living principle (jīva), endowed with the left shank, has come down through the lineage of oral tradition."
Thus it is said. Here too it will be stated:
"Just as [the tree] resides within the seed of the banyan...
and so forth. This is the heart of the Bhairava-self; because of its nature as the letter *na* in relation to the *Mālinī*, yet in reality...
From the letter *a* and the Yoginī Visargaśakti (p. 243), Rudra is born; he is the manifestation of the subject who is both the obstructor and the dissolver of bonds.
Only that person—namely, a *nā* (female) or a *puruṣa* (male)—clearly attains this; neither one who is not Rudra nor one born from the womb of a non-yoginī can attain it.

Immediate yoga (*sadyoyoga*), which is identity with Bhairava, is itself liberation. As it has been said: "And what is called liberation is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature."
And the essential nature of the self is consciousness... [text missing].

Thus it is determined: he who receives that [teaching] is one of this kind and no other; and he who is of this kind is "born of a Yoginī" and is Rudra—this meaning is established by implication. He certainly attains it clearly; thus he attains the Heart itself—that which grants immediate union and liberation. This is the universal rule. The mantras are the venerable lords of the phonemes (*varṇabhaṭṭāraka*).

The *mudrās*—consisting of worldly forms such as those of Pārameśvarī and others, which derive their names from the verbal roots *manu* (to understand) and *trai* (to protect)—are composed of conceptual consciousness (*vikalpa-saṃvit*).

Being of the nature of the activity of all the instruments, such as the hands and feet, they are of the form of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). The "group" (*gaṇa*) is that which is formed by these.
Having a single form consisting of the supreme power (*paraśakti*) which is the essence of the aggregate, [he is] of his own self—
of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), the void (*śūnya*), and so forth— as described in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
And this very principle of consciousness (cittattva), consisting of agency, when intensified by *kalā*,
exists as a limited attribute of insentient entities such as the void (*śūnya*).
The primacy of agency and consciousness belongs to the conscious self (cidātman);
when knowledge arises regarding the void and other qualities [of the elements], it is characterized by absorption into that [conscious self].

The meaning here is as follows: because the aspect of consciousness is submerged by impurity (mala), the reality of the nature of consciousness—which consists of agency and is called "sovereignty" (svātantrya)—is supported by the principle called "limited agency" (kalā). Although this [agency] is suppressed by impurity, it is nevertheless uplifted when it becomes immersed in the objective portion, ranging from the body to the void (śūnya), which has attained the state of "this-ness" (idantā). Even then...

When the state of being "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is pierced—along with everything from the void (śūnya) to the body—by means of the penetration of such qualities as the sovereignty of the eternal manifestation of reality as it truly is, that is the Fourth State (turyatā). Regarding the "penetration" (āveśa) of the body: it is the instantaneous entry into the supreme nature, through which the insentience consisting of dependence is obscured.

The emergence of the subject (pramātṛ) is permeated by autonomous agency (*svatantra-kartṛtā*). Likewise, because it bestows its own nature upon the object, it is "self-giving" (*svadā*); this refers to the activity beginning with will (*icchā*) and ending with action (*kriyā*). An immersion (*āveśa*) characterized by that very [activity] is established; having thus performed it, that which arises is [the state] when this vowel *a* is in the state of being uttered (*uccāra*), that is, in its upward movement (*ūrdhvacaraṇa*). Just as this is so for this [vowel], so it is [for the others].
This has been determined many times; by the word "immediately" (sadyas), the penetration [of the Self] into that [object] is indicated.
It attains the state of being oriented toward that and the predominance of its supreme form; however, unlike bound souls (paśus), it does not manifest that form, but rather conceals it.

Therefore, for a *muhūrta*—even though it is not limited by time, it is merely an *unmeṣa* (opening) in relation to the supreme reckoning—he who remembers—that is, connects with—it, he alone binds the previously explained multitude of mantras and mudrās;
he unifies them within his own self through non-duality. How? By means of the *cumbaka* [the "kisser"], as in the rule *cuvi vaktrasaṃyoge* ("*cu* is used for the joining of mouths").

[This is] according to the sequence of the elements (*dhātu*). Having performed the sealing (*mudraṇa*) on all sides—that is, everywhere—by means of the Śākta form which touches the universe, the particle *tu* (indeed) serves for emphasis: he alone who is thus sealed by the vibration of Śakti (*śāktaspanda*), and who contemplates the nature of Śiva as consisting of such reality (*tattva*), acts in this way; but one whose nature is solely that of a limited individual (*nara*) does not.

He explains that which is past, such as stones and the like, and that which is future, as well as that which is of the nature of non-benefit because of its prior absence; he brings even the other [topics] to their ultimate conclusion through non-conceptualization.
How so? When asked, there is a desire to know in the question; "one who is asked" (pṛṣṭa) refers to one who possesses that [desire] when questioned.
Whatever one indeed intends to know, that very thing he brings forth from within.
As it has been said:

"Just as the Creator, when entreated according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the attainment of objects residing in their hearts by causing the rising of the moon and the sun while they are awake."
p.

246) and so forth. For this [consciousness] is indeed one; even in memory, imagination, and the like, it remains just as much as when present, and the past and future do not exist, as has been stated.
"Unconditioned by time and both [space and object]," and so forth.

For that which was previously existent, yet devoid of any additional form and incapable of enduring such limitations as "this now knows" or "this now acts," there is a state of being once-and-for-all manifest (*sakṛdvibhātatva*). It is for this very reason that it has been described in relation to the past and so on.

Since, in the absence of that [time], the present time is in fact never applicable, it has been stated more than once that the true nature of reality is indeed its being untouched by time; for it is that very [Reality] which manifests the variegated power of time.
Furthermore, even that which is considered a "ghatikā" (a unit of time) during waking consciousness—
In that very state, the cognizers who have entered the dream-world experience its manifold variety; they even perceive the diversity of days, watches, years, and so forth.

According to this principle, *hara* is the supreme withdrawal known as *akula*; immediately following that, with an orientation toward the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) situated in the *sadāśiva-tattva*, which is denoted by the term *preta*.

The form of the deity’s will is the fashioning of forms; it is the eating—that is, the devouring—of the form of the witness together with the senses, and it is the continuous movement [based on the roots *ad* "to eat" and *at* "to move continuously"].
Having performed this continuous movement, one sees, drawn forth by the powers whose nature is obstruction and liquefaction; having made this certain, the following is said:

That which is called "vision" (darśana) belongs to the Lord who possesses the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), having ascended to a state of being whose nature is undisturbed by the subsidence of all waves [of manifestation] due to His union with infinite majesty and sovereignty.

That very will, through the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)— which consists in the appearance of a slight, indistinct differentiation of the object to be willed that is contained within itself— attains the nature of that [power].
The external withdrawal of all the senses—which consist in the vibration of the specific power of that [supreme] knowledge—is precisely this constant movement;

and that very movement is liquefaction, which is itself consumption. These two—vomiting and consumption—belong to vision, because all manifestation is of the nature of a single expansion, and because that expansion possesses such manifold variety.
Furthermore, the state of having both as an indeterminate object of apprehension is also undoubtedly present in cases such as a post or a person; thus, [the mind] consists of evil deeds.

The Supreme Lord’s power is indeed thus; he is Bhairava, the possessor of the power of memory whose nature is both supreme and non-supreme. Thus he says, "for two watches," and so forth. By remembering in this way, one becomes the void (*vyoma*) wherein [the self] exists within the *puryaṣṭaka* and the empty state, assuming the form of that subject. When, moreover, the form called "vision" (*darśana*), characterized by a watch [of time], [is maintained] again...

Furthermore, he reflects and even remembers, as before, and sees directly and without doubt, being drawn by the powers of Rudra; such is the connection [of the words]. For it has been stated that even then, that is indeed a form of vision.
Thus, however, he is said to be "endowed with the power of conceptualization consisting of the lower [nature]" by means of this triad—when, while seeing and remembering, he stands in the void.

Furthermore, he perceives again that by means of these three observations characterized by the watch, the Mothers—who consist of the internal subject—are the powers of the Supreme Lord; and because they are subjects, they are established as such, independent of the establishment of objects for other subjects. Thus, through yoga characterized by identity with their nature, [he attains] sovereignty.

Those rays of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which have assumed a portion of autonomy and possess power (*bala*)— meaning their unimpeded expansion everywhere in relation to the functions of the great external senses— are also indeed perfected (*siddha*).
This is because they consist of an impetuous activity that is entirely independent of the constraints of the fetters of bondage (*pāśava-śāsana-yantraṇā*) throughout the universe.

The *vīras*—those known as the organs of cognition and action—are indeed perfected beings (*siddhas*); their lords, whose nature consists of the phonemes beginning with *ka*, are also perfected beings. Furthermore, that which arises from the extraction of the phonemes beginning with *ka* has the nature of the deities such as Brāhmī and the rest.

That collection of powers (*śaktisamūha*), which consists of the various mental fluctuations such as aversion and attachment, is likewise established; for this very reason, it is powerful. All these, acting together by the command of the Supreme (*parājñayā*)—the Supreme being the realization consisting of the conceptualization "I am He" (*mānamayīm asau para iti vikalpātmikām siddhim*), or rather, the desired fruit itself—bestow or grant [it], their causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) being unknown [to the limited subject].
And when the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has been known, this application of conceptualization occurs sequentially; what need is there for more?

Even those mantra-practitioners who have attained mastery over mantras belonging to other lineages—even they shall attain perfection through this Heart-mantra and become liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). The intended meaning is that without this, supreme (*pāramārthikī*) perfection does not occur.

"Whatever [is taught] beginning with 'O Bhairava,' likewise those who have attained perfection, those who are attaining it, and those who will attain it through the yoga of *aṇimā* and the other powers—they too [attain their goal] by this very yoga; for there is no entry into the Heart apart from this.

For even worldly accomplishment (*vyāvahārikī siddhi*) is [attained] from this; because whatever collection of accomplishments exists within the *Bhairava* tantra—the tantra whose self is the universe—it arises from that very source.

Thus, this Supreme Lord alone is conceived as the very essence of the Heart, possessing a unity with infinite consciousness that is constantly arising and being withdrawn, nourished by the triad of powers (*śaktitritaya*).

Thus, the "non-perception of what was not seen"—which consists of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*)—destroys the egg of the impurity of *māyā* and the essence of phenomena known as "differentiation. In this way, even this "heart-egg" (*hṛdayamaṇḍala*), which is the unseen, is the destruction or contraction of the four eggs; that which is joined with this is thus composed of both *vidyā* and *māyā*.
The Supreme Lord is indeed one, a mass of consciousness; as it has been said:
"Vision is the Supreme Goddess, recollection is the Intermediate Goddess, and conceptual thought is the Lower Goddess; the Lord consists of the power of the Triad."
Both Māyā and Vidyā belong to Him; Māyā consists of the four eggs (aṇḍas), while Vidyā is the self-awareness of His own nature, auspicious and consisting of grace.

Thus [it is said]. However, if yoga is the primary factor, then one should first perform the vows and so forth as prescribed in the *Śrīpūrva* and other scriptures; then, when this [mantra] is uttered, the rest should be clearly explained as follows (p.

In matters where the result is already perceived, the entire collection of actions is projected as being entirely dependent on necessity; for even for yogins, there is indeed a fixed rule through the application of the practice and realization of the system of channels (*nāḍīcakra*). 17.
Now, regarding this threefold subject matter, he explains the unsurpassed nature of that which was called "the triad higher than the Kula," which is the most supreme of all:
"Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala, whoever knows this in its true essence..."
He shall eternally possess accomplishment; he is a yogi and he is truly initiated.
The *maṇḍala*—the circle of deities—even though not being perceived and even though the union (*melaka*) has not been attained [the intention here is this:

each individual goddess of the channels brings about a union within her respective domain through her own natural spontaneity by means of the empowerment of the Primordial Goddess; thus, there is a union of the twelve sense-deities].

Even while directly realizing through yogic practice the mandalas—which consist of the body’s channels (*nāḍī*) and their subsidiary wheels (*cakra*)—by means of practices such as *caryā*, *niśāṭana*, and *haṭha*, one does so even without having previously seen the mandalas of the trident, lotus, and so forth.
In this case, there is no need for initiation through a mandala or other such means. Thus, one who is favored by the descent of the supreme power (para-śaktipāta) knows this;

indeed, this very knowledge is initiation—what other initiation could there be? Therefore, knowing it thus, he is initiated by the all-pervasive Lord Bhairava-bhaṭṭāraka; for this very reason, he himself [as it has been said]:
Those of small intelligence who have taken up mantras on their own suffer;
for a mantra that remains merely as written text is considered here to be devoid of power.
"By the power of convention, his greatness does not spread from a book. Likewise:
"Those who have studied the sciences from books but are devoid of initiation and the observances (*samaya*)."
Ascetics who wander here excessively under the influence of harming others and the like do not know the truth; therefore, it is clear that they are partakers of fault.

Thus: "And one who has received the mantra"—this refers to mantras other than the Heart (hṛdaya). For this [Heart] is not a mantra, because its nature is the Heart itself, and because it transcends the forms of the Mantramaheshvaras and their Maheshvaras; it is determined that this Heart is indeed not to be written in books, and that its attainment occurs in reality only through the grace of the supreme descent of power (para-śaktipāta). Likewise, "whosoever... [refers to] anyone at all.
—In this context, independence from [distinctions such as] caste, vows, and conduct is intended;
for here, realization alone is primary. That yogi is the possessor of accomplishment, because it is said: "They desire yoga to be oneness. (p. 253)
And its initiation (dīkṣā) is characterized by the bestowing of knowledge and the destruction of illusion; as it has been said: "It bestows the true essence of knowledge and destroys all impurity.
Because its nature is that of bestowing and destroying, it is indeed proclaimed as 'initiation' (dīkṣā)."

Thus [ends the citation]. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis; therefore, it should be understood as applying to everything. Thus he says: "He alone is the yogi destined for success, he alone is the initiated one, eternally. (18)
By the mere knowledge of this, he is known by all powers;

he is known by all deities and by all powers, and by all-knowing ones. Even that which is known by them is known by him merely through the knowledge of this—just as before. [This applies] to "by all powers."
The third case ending is used in the sense of the instrument.
In the same way,
one becomes a member of the common family of the Śākinīs even without yoga. (19)

By the mere knowledge of this, even without the practice of yoga— which consists of attaining identity [with the Absolute] upon the fall of the illusory body— one becomes the Lord of the Wheel of Power (Śakticakreśvara), whose nature is the universal vibration (sāmānyaspanda) and the form of Akula, belonging to the lineage of the Śākinīs, which is characterized by the specific vibration (viśeṣaspanda). || 19 ||
Moreover,
one who is ignorant of the injunctions becomes a knower of the injunctions regarding the performance of sacrifice.
The ritual procedure (*vidhi*) consists of action and knowledge; he who lacks this twofold [nature] is a bound soul (*paśu*). As it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The bound soul is eternal, indeed formless, ignorant, inactive, devoid of qualities, yet sovereign;
all-pervading, situated within the belly of Māyā, and contemplating the means for experience."

Thus, even that animal, by the mere knowledge of this, becomes one who knows the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*); he is both the agent and the knower, the instrument for the connection with the object. (p. 255)
Sacrifice is born again for him, and even what was incomplete becomes complete—because the heart consists of everything.
For instance, beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Māyā, which resides within the body of Brahmā;
and from Śiva, who begins with the universe (Viśva) and ends with Ananta, up to the Supreme, there is what is considered the triad of powers (śaktitraya). || 21 ||

From the world-realm of the *dharātattva* (earth-principle) and others belonging to Kālāgni up to the *māyātattva*, O Brahman, is the domain of the letter *sa*; from the world of Viśva within the body [of the letter *ha*] beginning with the *vidyātattva* up to Śiva in the form of the *anāśritaśakti*, is the domain of the letter *a*. Within the end of Ananta—the letter *a*—is the supreme triad of powers (*śaktitraya*) consisting of the *visarga*. And that supreme [state] has been described by Sāraṅga and others.
Whatever exists within that, established on the pure path,
the purified individual soul soon attains divine knowledge.
Whatever object is established—that is, that which has come to possess various states—is established;

[the suffix -itac is applied here according to the rule beginning with *tārakā*]. That very thing, though existing in diverse states, would be pure when situated within the seed-syllable of the heart (*hṛdayabīja*). It is precisely that.

The divine knowledge is *aṇu*: it is called *aṇu* because it breathes (*aṇiti*), it vibrates (*aṇati*), and it resounds (*nadati*) due to its limited articulation; being palatal (*mūrdhanya*) through the power of the Lord, one attains divine knowledge in no time at all—attaining it by becoming palatal in the form of resonance, but not otherwise.
Even though they consist of pure consciousness, those who do not possess supreme agency have been created by the Lord as distinct from Himself due to the absence of that agency.
According to this principle, [the self] consists precisely of pure awakening; as it is stated in the *Śrīspandasūtras*:
"Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved, the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep."
Thus, this indeed is the mutual distinction between the knowledge of Brahman and the knowledge of Śiva. To explain:
when one has transcended *māyā*, in one case there is the attainment of Brahman, while in the other there is the state of a *vijñānākala*;
having thus distinguished this subtle state of awakening, such a sequence is to be understood. Even in the case of lower-level awakening (*aparābodha*), there is no fault whatsoever. || 22 ||
p.
257) How is he the impeller of that? [The intention here is as follows: Śiva alone, the Guru, is to be known as the impeller of that sovereignty.]

Once the state of pure essential nature has been attained, although sovereignty characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) is indeed established without effort, there are nevertheless two possible courses therein: that which arises from necessity (*niyati*), as it has been said: "All those such as the Vaiṣṇavas and others are colored by the passion for limited knowledge (*vidyā-rāga*)."
There exists no higher reality than this.
Thus, for that very purpose it was said, "and that impeller," and likewise stated:
"It attains the status of mantra through the awakening fashioned by Ananteśa.
For that same reason, it is said here "that impeller"; therefore, it is not merely knowledge characterized by its own self-reflection [that constitutes the mantra].
Because it is stated that [the cause] is the "essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*), the primacy of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is taught in the Śaiva scriptures; therefore, it is said:
"Right knowledge [arises] from oneself, from the scripture, and from the teacher. Śiva is to be known as all-pervading, stainless, transparent, satisfied, self-abiding, and pure. (23)

He who is the teacher (guru) who impels one toward that [Śiva] should be known as Śiva himself; Śiva himself is that impeller. And he is to be known as "the knower" (jñātṛ), for he alone is the "abode of his own" (svāyatana)—so called because he extends (tanoti) his own "ayanas," which are states consisting of pure consciousness. All of this has indeed been determined in detail. || 23 ||
Having thus explained in detail, he concludes with the essential meaning: "He concludes"—

the five members of reasoning for the sake of another's understanding are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).
In that context, the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the probandum by way of incorporating the established meaning of the four members [of the syllogism].
By this, it establishes the proven object; thus, the meaning is that it brings the matter to its final resolution.
As it is said: "Just as the great tree exists within the banyan seed in the form of a potentiality..."
In this way, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.
Thus, for one who knows this in its true essence, initiation leading to nirvāṇa occurs without doubt, even though it is devoid of oblations of sesame and clarified butter.
In this context, "non-existent" refers to things such as the horn of a hare; as it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Thus, even by means of the horn of a hare and the like, there is a pervasive connection with the All-pervasive One.
Likewise...
If non-manifestation does not appear as something slight, then manifestation alone remains;
if manifestation appears as something slight, then because it has the nature of form, solidity alone remains.
Likewise,
what specific excellence of existence does a sky-flower possess over a [real] flower, such that the world is animated by its manifestation? And yet, manifestation is common to all things.
Thus,
whatever expansion belongs to the Lord of Teachers during the state of the unfolding of the universe,
that same [expansion] occurs during the state of the cosmic egg (kalila), even in the closing of the universe.
Thus, it should be understood that the analogy of the liquid inside a peacock's egg is clearly established here; at that time, nothing [exists]—thus it is said that the universe [is non-existent].

And because it is the soul of the universe, just as within a banyan seed the sprout, branches, leaves, and fruits exist in their appropriate forms, so too does this entire universe exist within the heart; such thorough knowledge is itself the indubitable initiation into liberation, as it has been said:
This alone is the attainment of the nectar of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva.

Thus, although other forms of initiation might also bestow worldly enjoyments, this very thorough knowledge alone is initiation in its true sense; therefore, it possesses supreme excellence here, as it surpasses even the Kula scriptures. For instance, among the marks on a scale, even though the increments of height are measured step by step, there exists an infinite difference in the resulting measurement.
p.
260) Thus, in the higher and higher levels of reality (*tattva*), the interval between the perceptions of space, time, and experience is indeed infinite;
in this very way, it increases, becoming even greater than the thirty-six [levels]. And because perception itself is initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Therefore, this has been stated: a hero or a yoginī who has entered into this consciousness, having performed initiation and so forth, is sustained by that nature of "I" which is determined as consisting of the Lord Parabhairava— the Lord of the wheel of twelve deities who are the rays of the internal and external organs of Māyā— and whose essence is the constant arising of one's own supreme existence.

Thus, the unsurpassed state has been extensively determined through both detailed and concise explanations, precisely as it occurs without abandoning its supreme form; now, however, this which must be said is being declared: first of all, in all the scriptures, those Supreme Lords abide concealed, having assumed human bodies.
Those who worship the threefold object within the heart, even if it lacks vigor, [attain their goal].
Thus, how can there be worship of this [deity]? Nevertheless, one must contemplate it here as well by means of its unsurpassed existence, precisely because of its unsurpassed nature.
Desiring to resolve the inquiry as to how that [worship] occurs, he introduces another passage:
"In the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and likewise in the body..."
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and tied the topknot consecrated twenty-seven times with mantras. || 26 ||
One should apply the binding of each of the ten directions individually,
having first performed three audible claps for the pacification of obstacles. (27)
Then, one should sprinkle with water consecrated by reciting the Śikhā-mantra the appropriate number of times all the offerings,
such as flowers and so forth, in due order, upon either the Liṅga or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower consecrated fourteen times; there the hero should worship the Emanation, and thereafter the seat once again. (29)

Having enclosed the emanation within the *saṃpuṭa* (the union of the seed-syllables), one should thereafter begin the worship [of the goddess] who is perfectly complete with all the *tattvas* and adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship the Goddess Maheśānī, consecrated with twenty-seven mantras;
thereafter, one should honor her with fragrant flowers according to one's capacity. (31)
One should worship with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well;
thus is sacrifice described, and this same procedure applies to the fire-rite as well.

The crown of the head and the other [limbs], though appearing externally as appropriate forms, are in reality nothing other than the manifestations of consciousness, will, knowledge, and action— whose essence consists of Īśāna and the others, and whose true nature extends from space to earth and is designated as the fivefold Supreme Brahman; this is known from the indicative mark of the mantra, just as it is with the mantras themselves.
1. To the head of Īśāna; 2. To the face of Tatpuruṣa; 3. To the heart of Aghora; 4. To the secret organ of Vāmadeva; 5. To the form of Sadyojāta.

Thus, in this context, that which consists of the non-division of the pentad is the form at the beginning and the conclusion; in the middle, when the state of division manifests, each one of the five possesses a fivefold nature—thus there are twenty-five.
Into this very [system] is the entry of the *mālinī* and other mantras, as well as the three goddesses.

Each of these, through association with the triad beginning with desire (icchā), attains a ninefold nature; furthermore, by virtue of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, they fall into a threefold state—thus, by means of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*) remembered as twenty-seven, there is the sovereignty consisting of the conceptualization of everything from the form-bearing [earth] up to the end. Of that [sovereignty], [this is the application] to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Bondage consists in being treated as having the forms of the intellect (*buddhi*), touch (*sparśa*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and the exit (*vahirūpa*).

This is an identity whose essence is the non-differentiation of all things. Even when [the senses] are considered individually in the head and other locations, all [faculties] such as speech and the rest are mutual qualifications; and this has indeed already been determined through the very determination that everything is the self of everything.

The directions are nothing other than the jars and so forth being pointed out; and these, in relation to one's own sleep, are exactly ten. Even there, this alone is the bondage—consisting of the direct realization of the Self—and this is accomplished by three *tālas*, where a *tāla* is the resting in *pratiṣṭhā*.
Therein, the heart begins with the letter *sa*, and that is indeed the heart itself.
p.

264) That which is accompanied by sound (*saśabda*) is the end of the middle state (*madhyamānta*), for "sound" (*śabda*) is the act of sounding, and that is indeed the middle state itself—because *vaikharī* consists of its remnants—as has been stated many times. And this [middle state] belongs to the obstacles (*vighna*s), within the undivided, non-dual Self.

In the Supreme Self, there is the pacification of the stains of the waves of differentiation—the essence of which is the contraction consisting of fragmentation—namely, identity with the ocean of the non-dual Bhairava; as the venerable Somānanda-pāda has said: "Pervaded by our own nature, [the Self] acts through its own self for the sake of its own self-restraint."
May Śiva, who is the pervasive Self, act through his supreme power of adoration.

Thus [ends the citation]. In this very manner, water consecrated twenty-seven times constitutes the rite of the *argha* vessel. Here, all water is of the nature of the fluid of the Heart (*hṛdaya*), because it is unrestricted and because it bestows non-constriction. This has been explained as the flower;
and the *liṅga*—this too has already been determined—as the substratum and the agent of the act of sitting within the reality that is the Universal Self (*viśvātman*). Regarding the seat:
The state of being conceived through autonomy by that which is conceived through autonomy (p.
265) is [indicated] by the fourteenth vowel, *au*, because it has been stated that this very [vowel] is the form of the trident (*triśūla*). This is emission (*sṛṣṭi*).

The Heart consists of the identity with everything from A to Kṣa; it is Power (śakti), the Secret, and thus Heroism (vīratva). For this very reason, the entire seat (āsana) is also located therein, because of the mutual identity between the support and that which is supported, as it has been said:
"The Self, abiding in all beings... [and so forth].

And so forth: because each letter from *a* to *kṣa* of the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) of the "enveloping" (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) shines forth and is withdrawn within the Heart-seed syllable (*hṛdayabīja*)—which is the Supreme Reality (Paratattva) itself—there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as has already been stated.

Furthermore, the "enveloping" of the emanation consists of the bliss arising from the agitation (*kṣobha*) of the union of both [polarities]; even the consumption of substances produced therefrom is performed by means of that [bliss].

In this context, regarding the mere sequence of the cognition of words, there is "fullness" (pūrṇatva) by all principles (tattvas) being perfectly non-differentiated, correctly, and irreversibly; and "filling" (bharaṇa) occurs everywhere, even in a single atom, when it is encompassed on all sides—
that is, when everything is made one's own— by all [subjects] in the forms of the jar, pleasure, animals, humans, Brahmā (Viriñci), Viṣṇu, Rudra, Mantra, Sadāśiva, and so forth.
Since my state as a composite whole consisting of parts has already been determined through the measurements of those very parts,

for this reason, meditation on specific forms, weapons, and so forth is not mentioned here; for that [meditation] is something to be constructed, and one who desires to ascend [to the higher stage], as well as one who merely desires the threefold purpose, [require only what has been stated].
If it is asked, "How can one ascend?"—to whom does this state of being a seeker belong? Let him then not ascend;

rather, let him rely solely upon the ritual procedures of the *Siddhātantra* and other such texts, which are delineated according to that very limited perspective consisting of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth.

For indeed, in the uncontracted supreme state (*anuttarapada*), this very yoga—which is ever-arisen—is not even subject to formal injunction; as has been determined regarding the incense, flowers, and so forth, the word "yathā" is used in the sense of "together with," and the instrumental case ending is likewise stated in that same context. One should worship by means of the Supreme [Energy] whose nature is the Heart. How? By devotion—that is, by means of devotion consisting of the self-surrender of one whose soul is intent on entering into identity [with Her], fashioned by oneself.

Through the distinction between the object of worship and the worshipper, it is indeed the Object of Worship itself that creates [the worshipper]; for He is the supreme ultimate reality consisting of autonomous consciousness.
By virtue of the power of unsurpassed sovereignty, He is not insentient like a jar or other such objects—this is the distinction here.
As it has been said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:

The Lord, having fashioned his own self— which is liberated through autonomy— from that non-dual nature of autonomy by means of volitions such as "I am Īśvara" and so forth, carries out worldly activity. (This has already been stated previously in the commentary on the verse "the Unsurpassed of even the Surpassed.")
Thus, by means of devotion (*bhakti*), secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and worship, the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattva*) is indicated;

for in all actions, the recognition of this very nature serves as the means (*upāya*). Just as in the mastery of the letters of the world of illusion (*māyīya-varṇa-vyutpatti*), one should offer oneself just as those [letters] enter into the potency (*vīrya*) of the phonemes, like a written syllable.
p.
267) Since there is no other offering (*nivedya*) [to be presented], one should thus cause oneself alone to be known in its entirety as the unsurpassed state—

using the optative (*liṅ*) here in the sense of possibility according to the principle of the unsurpassed existence (*anuttarasattā*), because one abides eternally in this very state of being so constituted.

Thus it has been said that, according to the practice of contemplation (*upāsā*), this applies even to ritual injunctions and the like. In this way, that which is everywhere and always manifest as the manifestation of the nature of ultimate, pure Śiva— that very manifestation is itself the sacrifice (*yajana*) to the deity of supreme Bhairava-consciousness, because of being worshipped by means of that [manifestation].

Because it effects the state of being identical with and correctly attaining [the Supreme], and because it consists of the giving— which, by everywhere withdrawing the limited sense of "mine" and "self" as one's own property, brings about the supreme ownership consisting of the form of "mine" that is the nature of Śiva’s power, which is the full mass of consciousness.

This indeed is the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*): [it is performed] within the great splendor of Supreme Bhairava, which arises incessantly from the friction-sticks (*araṇi*) of the Supreme Power— shaken by the agitation of the union with Śiva— and which blazes with a voracious appetite for devouring the fuel of all objects and the seeds of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

The intended meaning is this: because of the offering (*havana*) into the great heat of the abundant clarified butter of intense attachment (*mahāsneha*), which takes the form of all worldly clinging, and because of the internal burning (*antardāha*), this very procedure for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) extends even to the initiation (*dīkṣā*); there is no other separate ritual whatsoever.
The thorough knowledge of one's own true nature is this ultimate mantra;
it is initiation, it is yoga, and it is unsurpassed even in ritual action.

Or rather, it has already been stated [here]: "In this context, the word 'na' (not) should be applied according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold; thus, the meaning is that it brings neither a quality (*guṇa*) nor a refutation (*khaṇḍana*).

As for what was said in the *sūtra*: "The answer is also no answer," namely, that elsewhere one crosses over the knot of knowledge following the practice of mantra-worship and so forth, but it is not so here.

This very point has been established by the preceding section of the text, because the *hṛdaya* (Heart) itself consists of the nature of sacrifice (*yāga*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and ritual action (*kriyā*).

[According to the grammatical rule that "a word heard at the end of a dvandva compound is connected with each member," the term *rūpatva* (the state of being the form) is connected here with each of these. And this is because it is the Absolute (*anuttara*). As for the venerable Śrī Somānandapāda, however...
