The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth—[for indeed, the *sruk* and *sruva* are the forms of Śiva and Śakti, and they should be established in a state of mutual orientation; such is the sequence even in the external ritual]—is described by way of demonstrating all-endurance (*sarvaṃsahatva*), with the intention of establishing its indivisibility (*akhaṇḍitatva*). In this same manner, the piercing of the limbs (*aṅgabhedha*), the piercing of the heart (*hṛdbhedha*), the piercing of the dust (*dhūlibhedha*), and so forth, are also [to be understood].

[The distinction between the *cūrṇikā* and so forth consists in its nature as a deposit. That such a form is appropriate here is not the case; neither is it logically tenable, nor does it exist, nor is there any dependence upon it by virtue of being included within a lower treatise—this is essentially already determined.
"What happens when one meditates in this way?"— with this question,
the following is introduced: having properly performed the ritual of worship and correctly recollecting the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one attains accomplishment.
Thus, even amidst constant worldly activities, remembering the seed-syllable alone— and having performed the ritual of worship through that very remembrance—
he becomes fully possessed by the form of the venerable Lord Bhairava Bhaṭṭāraka, pre-eminently and beyond all other scriptures, from the Kula texts down to the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava systems.

It has been stated that the memory [of this] is as follows: "Only one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) becomes, according to the method previously described, a manifestation of the grand display of the play of objective existence created by the power of the wonder of the consciousness of self and other; this is a revolving experience itself, and nothing else whatsoever. In the scriptures of the *Śrīmata* tradition, it is said that even a practitioner whose heart has not yet entered the essence of the reality of *vīrya* (vital potency) [is like this].

By the greatness of the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*), while correctly recollecting the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one who has attained the potency of the reality-mantra (*tattvamantra*) known as the Heart (*hṛdaya*) achieves perfection preeminently— either through the very greatness of the sequential worship due to its superior gradation, or spontaneously from the lotus-face of a gracious venerable Guru.
p.

270) One attains the potency of the mantra (*mantravīrya*), which is of the nature of the Heart, and becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); this is the meaning. Here, the worship of the door-keepers, the retinue, and the Guru is a merit; having contracted and turned inward the *khaṇḍanā* (the state of fragmentation), one expands it.

Having turned outward, one rejoices and experiences an excess of bliss within one's own self; likewise, there is the great bliss (*mahānanda*) of both Bhairava and Bhairavī, which means the state of emission (*visargabhū*). For this indeed is the unique, non-common form of this supreme Light, which is its constant capacity to effect both emanation and withdrawal.

Otherwise, indeed, there would be no distinction between this [consciousness] and insentient things. Or rather, it does not flow [in that way], for which very reason it was described by the venerable Bhaṭṭa-pāda. Here, however, are the *kulaparvan*s: "A *parvan* is so called because of the fulfillment (*pūraṇa*) of the injunction; and that is sixfold: the general (*sāmānya*), the general-general (*sāmānyasāmānya*), the general-particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), the particular-general (*viśeṣasāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and the particular-particular (*viśeṣaviśeṣa*)."

This has been explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding its procedure: even one who has not seen the mandala, by worshipping on the festival days, attains within a year the fruit described for a *putraka*, even without the performance of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth; likewise, the procedure for the *pavitraka* [rite], when performed according to rule and fulfilling the command of the Supreme Lord, is as stated: "Without the *pavitraka*, everything..."
Since it would otherwise be fruitless, the specific timing for this must be sought elsewhere; its procedure is as follows:

one should prepare it starting from those fashioned with gold, pearls, and gems, down to those made of silk thread, cotton, or kuśa grass; it should have knots equal in number to the [twenty-five] principles (*tattva*). When resources permit, this *pavitraka* should be offered every month, or else every four months.

Or, if it is not performed even once, one should mutter the expiation (*prāyaścitta*); for even a wise man, even if he possesses wealth, incurs sin by its non-performance, and there is the risk of falling into the censure of wisdom. And [it is called] "purifying" because it is the perfection of the ritual of worship, wherein everything internal shines and which shines everywhere.
For that alone is the single throbbing reality; O wise ones, it is indeed the supreme heart.

Whether she be a female donkey or a mare, having simultaneously expanded and then contracted that which is her own source for the birth of the world— characterized by virility— she rejoices in her heart.
Likewise, within the *nara* [channel] at the heart of the *suṣumṇā*, which is the great bliss of both,
one should worship the throbbing heart characterized by emanation.
Whether one is meditating, recollecting, reflecting, or acting anywhere at all, that in which one finds rest and from which the heart exults—that is it. As it has been said:
"In the heart, where the great root and the piercing shaft have been unified within the state of emission..."
One finds rest in that which is beyond, through the yoga of filling all things.
Now, let it be seen that through the very full functioning of that [consciousness], which consists of the immersion into the universe, there is the state "I" in the self-resting of the Light.
In the supreme reflective awareness (anuttara-vimarśa), which is initially devoid of activity and the like,
the reflective awareness of consciousness— the supreme I-consciousness— should flash forth as it first unfolds.
Thus [it is said].
That alone is the one supreme reality wherein this knowledge is conceptualized:
the principles (tattvas), the expansion of the worlds (bhuvanābhoga), and the bound souls (paśus) beginning with Śiva.
Discovering their own respective diverse ultimate natures,
they indeed manifest in variety and proceed toward that supreme, variegated consciousness.
Even regarding the knowledge of the ten substances, the ritual actions,
and the sacred sites, his worship is perpetually manifest through a transition [of consciousness] that is entirely free from doubt.

In this Trika teaching, it is declared that perfect realization arises through worship consisting of the sequential ritual alone, together with the Kula festivals and the sacred thread ceremonies (pavitraka).
As it has been said:
"Grammar is the bodily state of sounds, as it were; Mīmāṃsā is the sentence; Logic (Tarka) is the means of valid cognition;
and [Yoga] is the seed-syllable for the creation of phonemes."
Among teachings, the Trika is the supreme scripture; among liberations, the state of Bhairavī is the ultimate.
The attainment of the state of a lay devotee, the observance of vows, and heroic conduct— likewise, within the sacred festivals, there are the family festivals in the Teaching.
The *pavitraka* is for the fulfillment of all sacrifices;
those who do not perform the *pavitraka* rite four, three, two, or even once [are deficient].

They do not know the sacred festival of the Kula, and thus their spiritual vigor does not take root. They experience only flickering flashes; they do not attain the supreme light of the Self. Know that the innate state is the worship of the Self at all times, free from doubt—this is the true path of the adepts. *Phura-i phuraṇama alaha kā-abbaha para deu sohi ausa magāha savya kāla nīsaṃkasa-ū sahajā jāṇu pūjasa pajja i i u u ha*.
Thus, the nature of the unsurpassed has been determined in detail— that state wherein there is no room for cultivation or other such means,
but only *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative realization),
culminating in the firmness of comprehension characterized by a deep-seated wonder that reaches the very heart.
Regarding this, yoga must be explained for those desiring spiritual perfection (*siddhi*), as it possesses a continuous stream of preeminent means.

For even when the perfections of manifest yoga are brought about through one's own autonomy, and even though they transcend worldly consensus and necessity, they do not overstep the necessity that consists in the established order of the Supreme Lord. As it has been said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
Nevertheless, for the sake of the work of painting, the method must be stated with care;

yet even in that regard, there is no contradiction whatsoever for one whose form is unsurpassed—because, just as in the case of one who strives for the attainment of a visible perfection, there is the resting in the fruit of its attainment, all of which consists solely of the Supreme (para). However, this is said from the perspective of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
This is said to be a weak descent of power (śaktipāta) because it is for the most part incomplete.
To define that path of yoga, the remainder of the text proceeds:
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable devoid of beginning and end, blossoming in the midst of the lunar days, situated within the heart-lotus; one should practice this constantly. (33)
p.

274) This very seed of the Heart, because it is devoid of the light of a lamp, because it is empty of coming and going, and because it is perpetually arisen, is without beginning or end; that very [seed], blossoming, has attained fullness and resides in the midst of the lunar days (tithis), because it is the Heart.

One should meditate upon that very [lotus] in its state of being metaphorically designated as a lotus through the properties of contraction and expansion—located in the bulb (kanda), the secret place, or the heart. Furthermore, regarding its meditation, he says: one should "emit" or project the portion of Soma, consisting of sixteen digits and having the form of the moon, all around—that is, from every side—by means of this digit situated in the pericarp of the heart of this full moon.

Sealed by the mudrā of the crow’s beak (*kākacañcupuṭamudrā*), characterized by the kissing [of the breath] following the upward-rising *nāda* that has brought about the touch of nectar from the place of its arising— the flowers and so forth— at one's own respective *dvādaśānta*,
and further stirred by the *nāda* flowing from the moon of the heart, which expands through the tasting of the cool essence of nectar receding from that [place].

Bhaṭṭa Dhaneśvara Śarmā maintains that one should practice until the moon is filled with the drinking of nectar, and then resting solely upon the letter *sa*— which is the rising of a digit of the sun and is without vowels— one’s body is graced by horripilation, trembling, jumping, tears, shaking, paralysis, and so forth. This consists of the letter *sa* alone, devoid of beginning and end, accompanied by the sixteen forms starting from the first lunar day (*tithi*).

One should cast [the breath] into the interior of the heart by means of the sequence of swallowing the *kalā*s, like drawing water through a tube, while it is permeated with movement, trembling, and vibration within the *mūlādhāra*, the triangle (*trikoṇa*), the auspicious bulb (*bhadra-kanda*), and the seals (*mudrā*) of the heart and face.
Simultaneously, through the power of attaining the streams of [the breath] in slow, medium, fast, and even faster-than-fast tempos, the clusters of lunar and solar digits (kalās) are dissolved;

having rendered it devoid of beginning and end— meaning, in relation to this seed-mantra (*bīja*) and the Mother-alphabet (*mātṛkā*), it is free from the vowels *au* and the consonant *sa*— it is the eternal (*dhruva*) mantra whose familiarity with potency is obtained through the technique of separation (*viśleṣaṇa*).

One should meditate upon that very nectarine portion of the moon, consisting of sixteen parts, which is the seventeenth digit (kalā) said to transcend even the sixteenth— the time of eclipse situated in the midst of the fifteen expanding lunar days (tithis), which is devoid of a lunar day (tithi)—
within the heart-lotus.

"One should practice this constantly," so say our teachers. For instance: the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka Soma exists as the friction resulting from the union (*samāpatti*) with the Blessed Lady Umā—a friction consisting of the churning of the *tattvas*. He is a portion of that whole entity, the complete "I-consciousness" (*ahamātman*).

Blue, pleasure, and so forth— thus one practices by means of the rosary of the axle and the revolving wheel of emanation and withdrawal that turns back toward one's own essential nature; that which is contemplated as the truth is itself this "ever-arisen heart-recitation" (*hṛdayajapa*), where the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
Others, however, [hold that] the movement from the heart-center to the *dvādaśānta*, which consists of thirty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),
shines forth there in the form of the sun and, having rested for only half a *tuṭi* outside, [returns].

In each successive *tuṭi*—measuring two fingers and a quarter—at the rise of the lunar digit (*somakalā*) which is the form of emission (*visarga*), indestructible and called "immortal" (*amṛta*), the moon-digit is filled; and when the fifteenth *tuṭi* is full, it becomes full within the heart-lotus. There too, the repose lasts for half a *tuṭi*. Thus, it consists of sixteen *tuṭis*.

When the movement [of the breath] consists of thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas), at that stage—one which is devoid of beginning and end because it has not set—one should practice the "swallowing of the digits" (kalāgrāsābhyāsa).

Having dissolved within the center of the heart-lotus the lunar portion (somāṃśa) in the form of the visarga, which is contained within the expanding second [digit] and so forth, one should meditate upon it as consisting of seventeen [principles] through repeated cultivation. Thus it is said.
All of this that has been taught should be understood as entirely logical. Furthermore, an infinite commentary on this [text] is appropriate because it is a *sūtra*;

for it has been said by the masters that "it is a *sūtra* because it strings together (*sūtraṇāt*) infinite meanings," and that "the *Triṃśikā* is the unsurpassed *sūtra*. This applies likewise to the preceding verses and *sūtras*. (33)
What happens when one practices in this manner? He says:
"Whatever desires one may long for, those very desires one shall swiftly attain."
From this, omniscience becomes manifest; of this there is no doubt. || 34 ||

Thus, through such practice, whatever one desires, that very thing is attained without delay; for by the repeated cultivation of the state of being firmly established in that [object], one possesses the specific power of the support of the surging flow of will—the essence of a heart composed of all things—and exerts oneself with intense energy and enthusiasm. What more need be said?

"Omniscience is the state of being identical with Supreme Bhairava by means of this very body"—having thus stated everything, the conclusion is drawn at the end: for in the withdrawal of the expansion, there is the attainment of the reality of Akula, which is the nature of repose; that is the state of Bhairava, as has been stated more than once. (34)
This is the concluding section: "In this way, the fruit of the mantra is attained; this is the Rudrayāmala.
Through the practice of this, perfection and omniscience are obtained. (35)

(278) Thus is the fruit of the mantras belonging to other scriptures and of the phonemes obtained, and not otherwise; so it is at the conclusion. If there is a *yāmala*—that is, a union—of Rudra and Rudrāṇī.

Beginning from the expansion of the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature in the form of questions and answers that are indivisible, up until the manifestation within of hundreds of external creations and dissolutions—endless and beyond counting—all this is indeed withdrawn into Akula; such is the conclusion of the enumeration. Through the practice of this, omniscience is attained.
The conclusion regarding the fruit of yoga: for this [yoga] is ever-arisen in everyone; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus, he whose bee-like feet were ever hovering over the lotus-feet of the illustrious Maheśvara— who is intent on uplifting the people who have sought refuge— composed this commentary,
which contains within it an investigation of the *Trika-rahasya*, having received his birth from Cukhalaka of Kaśmīra.
Who could forcibly weigh this [reality], saying "it is only this much," when the words of the illustrious Śambhu have transcended all limits?
Nevertheless, that which has appeared to me shines within the Self of all; therefore, the wise should not turn their backs on this.

This work of such a kind produces correct knowledge, free from wavering, for the ignorant or for one subject to doubt and error; and for one who has already attained firm conviction, it establishes a consistent grounding within the heart. (3)
With a heart ascended by a continuous stream of contemplation upon the synthesis of these meanings and aesthetic essences, one should reflect even further than this;
for even that [reflection] would not suffice as a stepping-stone for one desiring to ascend to that stainless state.
In Kaśmīra, there was a preeminent minister of King Yaśaskara named the illustrious Vallabha, a twice-born man whose form was renowned for its excellence; his own son,
Śrī Śauri, became a worthy recipient of the path of universal fame through all his virtues.
He is the sole ocean of jewels for those devoted to meditation on the feet of the one who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel.
She is the abode of virtue, the source of another’s fame, the ground for the blossoming of playfulness, and the birthplace and sustainer of compassion for the entire world;
she is the illustrious companion named Vatsalikā, whose inner disposition is overflowing with devotion in the praise of Śaṅkara.
She whose mind expands. || 6 ||

His very self was one who had realized the creation and maintenance of the world; a twice-born man named Karṇa, whose sole delight lay in the meditation upon, worship of, and contemplation of Śaṅkara, who,
having abandoned attachment to sense-objects even in childhood and youth, takes refuge in this steadfast [path].
The path of discernment which uproots the cycle of worldly existence.
My own brother, whose mind is firmly established in the teaching of Śiva, named Manorathagupta,
desires to attain the supreme state of Śiva and wishes to discern the entirety of the scriptures and tantras.
For the sake of breaking through existence. || 8 ||
He was one who took singular delight in the Śiva scriptures, was learned in grammar, logic, and epistemology,
was named Rāmadeva, and had adorned his noble birth.

May this exposition of the path, which has been composed by me with a heart deeply rooted in performing what is dear and beneficial [to others], serve for the attainment of auspiciousness for all. (10)
Having attained birth, he who was named Atrigupta in his previous life entered the glorious Kaśmīra region,
whose borders had been sanctified by countless incarnations of the Moon-crested Lord.
Born into that great lineage from Varāhagupta, he was named Cukha;
his mind was turned away from the affairs of worldly existence and was fixed solely on Śiva.
Therefore, having attained the state of being purified by the Supreme Lord from the entire collection of categories once they had been clearly distinguished,
he who is named Abhinavagupta— having obtained fearlessness— caused this hidden reality of the Trika to enter [into the world].
Salutation is better for those whose hearts are barren of solitude; yet others, though they seek solitude, have not reached its further shore—shame on those dull-witted ones!
But as for that other person who stands firm in the conviction of the path whose essence is profound investigation—even a single such individual is truly someone extraordinary.
One should make my effort bear fruit. || 14 ||
For those who bear indolence even toward discerning their own selves, a prayer directed at them will yield no fruit other than self-mortification; however,
for those of steady intellect who exert themselves for the discernment of this entire universe, this [treatise] has been composed by me as a request.
Respectful prostration with the head [is the mark of] reverence. || 15 ||

Wandering about themselves, those of dull intellect cause the inert wheel of living beings to wander; having made it their own through the power of designating the *guṇas*, they bind it firmly with bonds.
Seeing thus that these animals follow one after another for the sake of bearing a heavy burden, [one should act] for the purpose of cutting asunder their fetters.
I have fashioned this trident of knowledge.
I alone have been led astray by many who consider themselves teachers of reality,
even though the pair of syllables "tat-tvam" has never touched their tongues.
The supreme lord Śambhu, the glorious god whose heart was moved by compassion to uplift those who have sought refuge, has appointed me to this reality.

Having reflected upon the doctrine of the venerable Somānanda, which has entered as it were of its own accord into my heart— wherein the divisions of existence have been purified by that very reality— I have composed this. (19)
O Goddesses, filled with the intense bliss produced by the movement within the wheel of the heart, you whose upward-pointing shafts of knowledge are skilled in shattering the millions of our bonds—
this mind, speech, and body of mine, from which the arising of the fear of worldly existence has departed, is perfectly woven into you; therefore, depart!
It is said that he forcibly brought about immediate grace within the heart. || 20 ||

Having entered into the state of a teacher, I have been appointed by you to the sequence of duties such as exposition; therefore, O Goddesses, whose beautiful and skillful abodes are that very mandala, please forgive this restlessness of my speech and mind. (21)
This *Tattvavivaraṇa* on the *Parātriṃśikā* is completed.
This *Triṃśikā*, analyzed by one hundred and nineteen [verses],
shall shatter the knots within all the Trika scriptures.
Thus ends the venerable *Parātriṃśikā*,
along with its commentary composed thereon by the illustrious and most eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the venerable Abhinavagupta.
(283) As time passes, there occurs a decline in the assembly of texts and scholars who are the refuge of the six sciences;
[this work is undertaken] for the sake of professional activity by one endowed with the vigor of true discernment, whose sole intent is the desire to uphold those various True Dharmas. || 1 ||

Having deliberated with his chief ministers who were devoted to the Dharma, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established the primary office for the purpose of extracting the texts containing the essence of spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom. || 2 ||
May this work, refined by the livelihood of those virtuous ones who enter into it under the supervision of Mukunda Rāma,
and perfected through its completion, purification, and commentary, lead to the welfare of the good.
(Tilaka)
May there be the offering of one's own glorious self unto Śiva.
